descs.en: He made a rule: the two of them stay flat, like a line on a graph. She gave the line an end date, drew an atom for every day until it, and a week later he kissed her on the back stairs.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Dr. Miles Wei, 31, lecturer in physics, holds office hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Shen Yu Jie, final-year student and the best mind in the department, comes on Wednesdays. Every Wednesday. With problems she has already solved.

He has one rule: nothing happens while she is a student in his department. He draws it on his chalkboard as a flat line. She adds an end date. 20 June, 16:00. Then she makes a calendar, two hundred and fifty-five squares long, with a physically inaccurate atom in every one. He counts them twice. A week later, the rule doesn’t survive the back stairs.

Between them stand sticky-note physics jokes, a supervisor who smokes on a balcony nobody is allowed on, a mother who calls her daughter the Perfect Jewel in front of guests, a diplomat with a secret, a forum photograph, and a grant nobody applied for.

Proof by Induction is a bright campus romance about being taken seriously, and about a man who stopped laughing at seventeen and a woman who makes him start again.

The main story is told across four volumes. New chapters are added as they are written; the side stories at the end can be read any time. Miles first appears in Every Flower in the Shop, but this book stands on its own.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a gentle book, but it has some hard moments:

• Emotional control and coercion by a parent, including being cut off financially and made to leave home (Volume Two and Volume Three)

• Online gossip and rumours about a student’s degree (Rumours in the Department Kitchen)

• A character coming out to his family at a dinner table, and a parent walking out (The Perfect Jewel Says No)

• Illness with a high fever (Miles Gets Sick and Nobody Notices)

• A relationship between a lecturer and a student in his department, kept secret and then declared to the department (Miles Recuses Himself). He never teaches, supervises or marks her.

• Love scenes, sensual but not explicit (The Thesis Draft Covered in Red Pen, Miles Recuses Himself, and later chapters)

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Miles Wei walked into Every Flower in the Shop for one scene, dropped his clicker, asked Elowen if she was happy, and wouldn’t leave my head. This is his book.

I wanted a love story where the most romantic thing anyone does is take the other person’s mind seriously. The physics is real, kept at the level of a story: the harmonic oscillator, entropy as counting, strained graphene, and analogue black holes made in water tanks, which real laboratories build.

The jokes are, regrettably, also real. Thank you for reading.

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Wednesday — The day Yu Jie comes to office hours, which are on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
The harmonic oscillator — The problem she brings on her first Wednesday. Its lowest energy, ½ħω, is never zero: nothing is ever completely at rest.
Lecture Theatre C — Where Miles teaches second-year quantum mechanics at ten, to a hundred and forty students.
The rule — Miles’s one rule: not while she is a student in his department.
20 June, 16:00 — The end of the interval: graduation. Written in chalk in the corner of his board, and left there.

White Rabbit — The milk sweets he buys her, “on offer”. Also what she saves him as in her phone.
The Perfect Jewel — What her mother calls her in front of guests.
Shen Holdings — Her family’s company. It owns half the harbour and a forty-storey building downtown.

Bell Street — The street by the old wall, with the bakery called Ling’s.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Was Definitely Not Stuck on Quantum Mechanics
chapters.desc: Shen Yu Jie turns up on the wrong day with a problem she has already solved. Dr. Miles Wei solves it anyway, the long way, and keeps the pen she drops.
chapters.epigraph: “Next time, bring a problem you haven’t solved.”
chapters.content:
Shen Yu Jie had a perfectly reasonable explanation for why she was sitting in Dr. Miles Wei’s office on a Wednesday afternoon, when everyone in the building knew his office hours were Tuesdays and Thursdays.

She was stuck.

She was stuck on a problem she had solved three days ago and checked twice, once in pencil and once in pen, with a small cat drawn at the bottom of the page to celebrate.

None of that helped her now, because Dr. Wei was reading the page with the kind of quiet attention that made her regret every decision that had brought her up four flights of stairs.

“You’re having trouble with the harmonic oscillator?”

His voice was low and unhurried. He sounded like a man who had never once been late for anything and wouldn’t hold it against you if you were.

“Yes, Professor.”

He looked at her over the top of his glasses. They were thin and round and slightly too old-fashioned for his face, which was the face of a postgraduate who had wandered into the wrong office and decided to stay. Soft brown hair fell over his forehead in a fringe that needed cutting. He wore a black turtleneck under a dark blazer, and there was a faint stripe of chalk on the left cuff.

He looked back at the page. “Which part?”

She’d prepared for this. “The wave function.”

“Which part of the wave function?”

“The normalisation.”

There was a small pause.

“Interesting,” said Dr. Wei.

Yu Jie folded her hands on her knee and tried to look like a girl who didn’t understand integrals.

He picked up a stick of chalk and turned to the board behind his desk. It was a real chalkboard, dark green and worn grey in the middle where a thousand derivations had been rubbed out with the side of somebody’s hand. The fourth floor had been offered whiteboards two years ago. According to department legend, Dr. Wei had been the only one to say no.

“All right,” he said. “Let’s start from the beginning.”

“The beginning?”

“Unless you’d prefer the middle.”

“No. The beginning’s fine.”

He wrote the time-independent Schrödinger equation across the top of the board in handwriting so neat it was almost rude.

−(ħ²/2m) d²ψ/dx² + ½ mω²x² ψ = Eψ

“The potential goes as the square of the displacement,” he said, and drew a little parabola underneath with a ball sitting at the bottom of it. “So the further the particle moves from the centre, the harder it’s pulled back.”

Yu Jie had expected a hint. Possibly a gentle question about where she’d gone wrong. She had not expected a full lecture, delivered to an audience of one, with diagrams.

She knew all of this. She could have recited it in her sleep, and in her second year, during a fever, she more or less had. But he was explaining it so seriously, and with such care, and his sleeves had ridden up to show a pair of nice wrists, and interrupting him felt like a crime.

“Now,” he said, “we change to a dimensionless variable, and the equation becomes easier to handle. What happens at the boundaries?”

“Only the solutions that fall off fast enough can be normalised.”

The chalk stopped.

He turned his head.

“Correct.”

She smiled before she could stop herself.

He looked at her for a second longer than he needed to, and then he turned back to the board. “Then perhaps you aren’t as stuck as you think.”

Her smile wobbled.

Oh no. He knew.

No. Surely not. She looked down at her own page, as if the answer might change if she stared at it hard enough.

It didn’t. Neither did Dr. Wei. He went on to take the longest possible road through the derivation, every step of it, and worked the normalisation integral out in full while her own neat version of it sat on his desk two feet from his elbow. By the time he put the chalk down, Yu Jie had learned nothing at all about the harmonic oscillator.

She had learned that Dr. Miles Wei was hard to fool.

“Does that help?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Good. Then I assume you’ll manage the next one on your own.”

“Probably.”

His eyebrows rose a little.

“Definitely,” she said.

A faint smile pulled at one corner of his mouth. It made him look about twenty-five. “That’s reassuring.”

It was deeply unfair, she thought, that a man could look so ordinary while explaining quantum mechanics and then ruin everything by smiling.

“Anything else?” he asked.

“No, Professor. Thank you.”

She gathered her notebook, her bag and what was left of her dignity. She had her hand on the door when he spoke again.

“Miss Shen.”

She turned. He was already looking down at the page she’d left on his desk.

“Next time, bring a problem you haven’t solved.”

She went out with her face hot.

✦ ✦ ✦

The door closed.

Miles stood beside his desk and looked at it.

Then he looked down at the page she’d left behind.

The calculations were correct. They weren’t correct with a few lucky guesses or correct apart from a sign. They were clean from the first line to the last, in small upright handwriting, and at the bottom of the final page, under the answer, a round cat sat with its tail curled around its feet.

Something went out of him through his nose. It was nearly a laugh.

He put the page in a folder and the folder in his bag, and when he pushed his chair back to sit down, his shoe knocked something across the floor.

He bent and picked it up. It was a purple pen with a fat cat on the end of it, wearing a small gold crown.

He looked at the door again.

✦ ✦ ✦

“She came to your office?”

Professor Weng didn’t look up from his coffee. He had come in to borrow a book, which he did about twice a week, and stayed to sit on the edge of Miles’s spare chair and complain about the timetable, which he did every time.

“Yes,” said Miles.

“On a Wednesday.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“She had a question.”

“About what?”

“The harmonic oscillator.”

Now Professor Weng looked up. He was sixty-one, with thick grey eyebrows and a cardigan that had been with the department longer than most of the furniture.

“Shen Yu Jie? From my Quantum Two?”

“How many Shen Yu Jies do we have?”

“She scored a hundred.” Professor Weng put his cup down. “On the final. A hundred, no deductions. I remember because she was the only undergraduate in four years who got the perturbation question right, and she did it in a third of the space I gave her.”

Miles’s fingers had stopped on the keyboard.

“What did she ask you?” said Professor Weng.

“Normalisation.”

Professor Weng stared at him. “You’re joking.”

“I’m not.”

“She knows normalisation. She knows it better than half my doctoral students.”

“That would explain the solution she left behind.”

Professor Weng laughed, a short delighted bark. “She was pretending?”

“I didn’t say that.”

“You didn’t have to.” Professor Weng picked his coffee up again and looked at Miles over it for a while, and slowly the delight went out of his face. “She’s a very good student, Wei. And she’s in her final year.”

“I know.”

“Then you know the department’s policy.”

“I do.”

“Good.” He stood up and tucked the book under his arm. “Keep things professional.”

He went out. Miles sat with his hands on the keyboard and didn’t type anything.

After a while he opened his top drawer and looked at the purple cat.

“That’s the intention,” he said, to nobody, and shut the drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

His office hours were Thursday from two until four.

At a quarter past two a doctoral student came in about a paper. At twenty to three a second-year needed help with the problem sheet. At three Professor Weng returned the book and took a different one. At twenty past three Miles answered two emails, and at twenty to four he looked at the clock.

Then, before he’d decided to, he looked at the door.

Nobody came.

He looked back at his screen. Three minutes later he looked at the door again, and it was still a door.

At four he closed the laptop. There was no reason for the small, flat disappointment sitting behind his ribs. Shen Yu Jie had no obligation to come to his office hours. She wasn’t even supposed to have a problem.

He reached into the top drawer for a folder, and his fingers found the pen.

He could take it to her. She’d be in a lecture somewhere in the building. He could leave it in the undergraduate office with her name on an envelope, which was the correct thing to do and would take no time at all.

He turned it over. The cat looked back at him, smug in its crown.

Next Wednesday, perhaps.

He put it back in the drawer, under the folder, where nobody would see it, and turned off the lamp.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across campus, Yu Jie was in the library, on the third floor by the window, staring at a harmonic oscillator problem she had now solved three times.

Her phone buzzed.

Tao Tao: Did you go and see Dr. Wei?

Yu Jie looked at the message. Then at her notebook. Then into her pencil case, where her purple cat pen should have been and wasn’t, and hadn’t been since yesterday.

Yu Jie: No.

Yu Jie: I have self-respect.

Tao Tao: Then why is his office hours page open on your laptop? I can see it from here. I’m two tables behind you.

Yu Jie turned round. Tao Tao waved at her with a highlighter.

Yu Jie shut the laptop and turned back.

She did have an answer. She just wasn’t ready to say it, even to Tao Tao, who had known her since they were twelve and would only laugh.

Dr. Wei had a way of listening. He never interrupted and never pretended to understand when he didn’t. When he looked at you, you felt as though every word you said deserved his full attention, even the stupid ones, even the fake ones. It was hard not to want more of that, especially from a man who wore round glasses and spoke quietly and smiled as if he’d been caught doing something.

Yu Jie unwrapped a strawberry sweet, put it in her mouth, and opened her notebook to a clean page.

Reasons to go back to Dr. Wei’s office.

She looked at it for a while. Then she crossed it out and wrote underneath:

Reasons not to.

She managed three.

1. He knows I’m pretending.

2. He teaches in my department.

3. I graduate in June.

She bit down on the sweet and considered the list, and then she added a fourth.

4. He has my pen.

Probably. Almost certainly. It had to be somewhere in that office, under a chair or behind the radiator, and the only fair thing to do was go back and look for it.

On a Wednesday, obviously. She wouldn’t want to waste his real office hours.

Yu Jie looked at the fourth reason until she was smiling at it, and then she turned to the next problem and solved it, in pencil, and drew a small cat at the bottom.

chapters.title: Office Hours Are Tuesdays and Thursdays
chapters.desc: She keeps coming on Wednesdays. He lies about the pen, buys a second mug, and starts leaving the door open.
chapters.content:
Shen Yu Jie had a plan, and the beauty of it was how simple it was.

Find a hard problem. Pretend she couldn’t do it. Take it to Dr. Miles Wei on a Wednesday afternoon, when he had no office hours and nobody else would be there. Make him remember her.

“The flaw in your plan,” said Tao Tao, “is that you’re terrible at pretending to be stupid.”

They were in the library café, at the table under the stairs where the wifi was bad and nobody they knew ever sat. Tao Tao had an iced coffee, two textbooks and the face of a woman being made to drive the getaway car.

“I’m a wonderful actress,” said Yu Jie.

“You scored a hundred in Quantum Two.”

“That was last year.”

“That was June.”

“People change.”

“Not that fast.” Tao Tao pointed her straw at her. “And why Wednesday?”

“Because his office hours are Tuesdays and Thursdays.”

“I know how a week works.”

“Then you see the problem. On Tuesdays and Thursdays there’s a queue of second-years outside his door holding problem sheets. On Wednesdays his research group meets in the morning, and in the afternoon he sits in his office on his own.” Yu Jie scrolled down the department page and turned the laptop round so Tao Tao could see his photograph, which was terrible and made him look like a startled librarian. “It’s a perfectly academic piece of reasoning.”

“You’re going to a man with a doctorate in physics,” said Tao Tao, “whose whole job is noticing things other people miss.”

Yu Jie looked at the photograph for a while.

“That’s a very unpleasant way of putting it,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seventeen minutes past two the following Wednesday she knocked on the door of office 412.

He opened it in a black turtleneck, holding a pencil, with his glasses halfway down his nose. He looked at her over the top of them for a moment before his face caught up.

“Miss Shen.”

“Good afternoon, Professor.”

He glanced past her at the empty corridor, then back at her. “Is something wrong?”

“Academically speaking.”

“Academically speaking,” he repeated, and stepped aside.

She’d chosen the problem carefully. It came from the back of the supplementary sheet: an oscillator with an extra term that made it lopsided, and a second-order correction that took a page and a half to grind out. It was hard enough to get lost in, and not so hard that he’d think she was showing off.

He read it. Then he looked at her. “Where did you get stuck?”

She pointed at the third line. “Here.”

“Why?”

“Because...” She looked at the third line. It looked back at her, entirely correct. “Because I don’t understand where the second-order term comes from.”

“All right. Show me what you’ve done.”

That was where the plan began to fall apart, because Dr. Wei didn’t explain anything. He asked questions.

“Why this basis?”

“Because the unperturbed part is just the ordinary oscillator.”

“Good. And what does that tell you about the matrix elements?”

She told him.

“And the parity of the extra term?”

She told him that too.

“Then where exactly are you confused?”

Yu Jie opened her mouth and nothing came out of it.

He pulled the notebook closer and went down her working with the end of his pencil, a line at a time. “This is correct,” he said. “So is this. And this substitution. And the algebra.” The pencil stopped at the bottom of the page, where she’d done the whole thing a second time in blue ink to check it, and had forgotten to turn the page over.

He looked at the black version. Then at the blue one. Then at her.

“Miss Shen,” he said, “are you asking me to explain a problem you’ve solved twice?”

Her ears went hot.

“Not necessarily.”

He didn’t laugh. That was worse. He only put the pencil down gently, as though it might go off, and said, “Well. It’s good to be thorough.”

She could not tell, then or later, whether he was making fun of her.

“Since you’ve come all this way,” he said, “let’s do the second-order term properly.”

He did it properly, at length, which was cruel. At the door she turned round.

“Professor? Did I leave a pen here last week? It’s purple. It has a cat on it.”

He was already looking down at his desk. “I haven’t seen it.”

“Oh.” She waited. He kept reading. “If you find it...”

“I’ll let you know.”

When she’d gone, Miles sat still for a moment. Then he opened the top drawer an inch, looked at the cat in its crown, and shut it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next Wednesday she brought something she really couldn’t do.

It was a research problem she’d found in the back of an old graduate textbook in the library basement: an oscillator in a potential that had been bent out of shape, so that the usual approximation worked near the bottom and fell apart further out. She’d spent two evenings on it and got a contradiction in the third-order term both times.

He read it and his face changed. It wasn’t much. His eyebrows came together and he sat forward.

“Where did you find this?”

“Library.”

“It isn’t an undergraduate problem.”

“I know. That’s why I liked it.”

He looked at her for a second longer than he needed to. Then he pulled his chair in. “Tell me what you think’s going wrong.”

She told him, and he listened without interrupting, and when she’d finished he circled one of her terms. “You’ve assumed the correction stays small across the whole range.”

“So I restrict the range.”

“Then you’ve got a different problem at the edges.”

“Locally it should still hold.”

“Not with this potential.”

“Why not?”

“Because it isn’t behaving the way you want it to.”

Yu Jie looked at the circle. Then at him. Then she picked up her own pencil.

“I disagree,” she said.

There was a short silence. He didn’t seem offended. If anything he looked interested, the way a cat looks interested when something moves under a rug.

“All right,” he said, and pushed the page across to her. “Convince me.”

That was how they spent the rest of the afternoon. By half past three she had one foot tucked under her on the chair. By four he’d taken his glasses off and put them on the keyboard, and he looked younger without them and slightly lost, the way short-sighted people do, and she had to stop looking at him to think. By five they were both standing at the chalkboard and he had filled half of it with a derivation of his own, and she was jabbing her finger at his fourth line.

“That doesn’t follow.”

“It does in the limit.”

“The limit isn’t the system. You can’t use the limit to prove something about the system.”

“I’m not proving it. I’m approximating it.”

“You’re ignoring the difference because it makes your sums shorter.”

He looked at the board. He looked at her.

Then he looked down, and a sound came out of him. It was short and quiet and it surprised him as much as it surprised her. It was nearly a laugh.

“What?” she said.

“Nothing.”

“You laughed.”

“Did I?” He held out the chalk to her. “Show me your way.”

She took the chalk and wrote fast, because she’d been waiting all afternoon to do it. He stood beside her with his arms folded and asked questions, and she answered them, and he asked harder ones, and she answered those too. When she reached the last line she stopped, slightly out of breath, and stood back.

He read it from the top. He took his time.

“You’re right,” he said.

She turned. “What?”

“You’re right. It holds on the domain you’ve restricted it to. I was treating it as a global condition.” He put his glasses back on and looked at her through them. “You’re right, Miss Shen.”

Her whole face lit up. She could feel it happen and couldn’t stop it. “I knew it. I told you.”

“You did.”

“I was right and you were wrong.”

“Don’t become unbearable about it.”

“Too late.”

He was smiling, properly, and it did something to the shape of his face that she would have liked a few minutes alone with.

It was only when he turned to rub out the top of the board that she saw the back of him. He’d leaned on the chalk ledge at some point, or she’d leaned into him while she was writing and he’d moved out of the way into the board, because there were two long white stripes down the left side of his black turtleneck, and a perfect chalk handprint on his shoulder blade. The handprint was small. It was, she realised, hers.

She opened her mouth to tell him.

Then she closed it.

“It’s six,” he said, looking at the clock. “I’ve kept you.”

“You didn’t.”

“We were discussing a problem. That’s what office hours are for.”

“Even on Wednesdays?”

He looked at her. “Apparently even on Wednesdays.”

He walked her to the lift, because he was going down to the post room, and she stood behind him all the way along the corridor looking at the handprint on his back and biting the inside of her cheek. Two doctoral students passed them and stared.

“Good evening, Miss Shen,” he said when the lift came.

“Good evening, Professor.”

The doors closed on him, chalky and dignified. She leaned on the wall and laughed until she had to sit down on the stairs.

He found out at eight the next morning, when Professor Weng put his head round the door, looked at the turtleneck hanging on the back of Miles’s chair, and said, “Somebody’s had a busy Wednesday.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles had never thought of himself as sentimental. He owned five identical black turtlenecks and a shelf of conference mugs he hadn’t chosen. He liked things that worked and didn’t need looking after.

Which didn’t explain why he was standing in a department store on Friday evening in front of a shelf of mugs.

He’d come for printer paper. The mugs were next to the stationery. That was all.

He picked up a plain white one, a little wider than his own, with a good heavy handle. He turned it over. He put it in the basket. On the shelf beside it there were small tins of jasmine tea, and after a moment one of those went in the basket too.

That should have been enough. But the way to the till went past a stand of sweets, and halfway up it, in their blue-and-white paper, were White Rabbits.

He stopped.

On Wednesday a bag of them had fallen out of her handbag while she was looking for a pencil. She’d scooped it up and stuffed it back in and gone on arguing about boundary conditions with one already in her cheek. She’d smelt of it all afternoon, milk and sugar, under something like peaches.

He stood looking at the stand for longer than he could account for.

It was absurd. He was buying sweets for a student who had no business being in his office outside office hours, who was graduating in June, whom he’d been specifically told to keep at a professional distance. He knew all of that perfectly well.

He took two bags.

“Gift wrap?” said the woman at the till.

“No, thank you.”

“Are they for someone?”

He looked down at the white mug.

“They’re for the office,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the following Wednesday Yu Jie changed her blouse three times. She told herself she wasn’t excited about going to the physics department. She settled on her usual white shirt and black blazer, so it couldn’t look as though she’d tried.

She turned into the fourth-floor corridor and stopped.

The door of office 412 was open.

Somebody had wedged it open with a stack of old journals, so that a long slice of afternoon sun lay out across the corridor floor.

He was at his desk. He looked up when he heard her heels. “Miss Shen.”

“Good afternoon, Professor.”

“Come in.”

On the desk there were two mugs. One was his dark blue one with the chipped rim. The other was new and white. Beside them was a small tin of jasmine tea and a bag of White Rabbits, opened, with the sweets tipped out into a saucer.

Yu Jie looked at them. Then at him.

“Are you expecting someone?”

“No.”

“Then why are there two mugs?”

He moved a sheet of paper an inch to the left. “The other one’s new.”

“I can see that.”

“I bought it.”

“Also clear.” She looked at the saucer. “Do you like White Rabbits?”

“Not particularly.”

“Then why have you got them?”

“They were on offer.”

“Both bags?”

He didn’t answer that.

“Sit down, Miss Shen,” he said.

She sat. She was trying hard not to smile, and it wasn’t going well. He took the lid off the tin and the smell of jasmine came up into the room, and he put a spoonful in the white mug and filled it from the little kettle on the bookshelf, without any fuss at all, the way you’d make tea for someone who’d been coming for years. He set it down in front of her with the handle turned towards her right hand.

“Careful,” he said. “It’s hot.”

She wrapped both hands round it. “Is this one mine?”

“It’s a spare.”

“Of course.”

“For the office. You can use it if you want tea.”

She ducked her head over the mug. She was smiling so hard it hurt.

“Are you going to show me your problem,” he said, “or did you come to audit my shopping?”

She nearly inhaled the tea. “Professor!”

His face was perfectly calm. His eyes weren’t.

They worked until four. It was an easy problem, by her standards, and she managed to turn it into an argument anyway, about what the second-order correction actually meant, and he let her. She ate four White Rabbits in a row. He noticed.

“Are those helping?”

“They improve morale.”

“Whose?”

“Mine. Obviously.”

He shook his head and went back to the page, and the corner of his mouth didn’t go back with him.

At four she packed up. She had a lecture. He got up to take a book down from the shelf behind him and said, without looking round, “Bring the revised derivation next week.”

“Next week?”

“Yes.”

“Wednesday?”

He turned round with the book in his hand. For a moment neither of them said anything at all.

“If you have a question,” he said, “you can come during office hours.”

“Tuesdays and Thursdays.”

“Correct.”

“Not Wednesdays.”

“Correct.”

“Very strict.”

“Somebody has to be.”

She laughed, and picked up her bag, and at the door she turned round again. “Thank you for the tea. And the sweets.”

“They were on offer.”

“Of course they were,” said Yu Jie, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past five Professor Weng walked past, stopped, and came back.

“You’ve got your door open.”

“It’s warm,” said Miles, without looking up.

Professor Weng looked at the window. It was the first of October and there was a wind coming off the hill that had the leaves going sideways.

“Is it.”

“Yes.”

Professor Weng looked at the two mugs drying by the sink. At the tin of jasmine. At the saucer, which still had two White Rabbits in it, and a little heap of folded wrappers somebody had made into tiny paper cranes.

He raised his thick grey eyebrows as high as they would go and walked off down the corridor without a word, which from Professor Weng was a speech.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening Yu Jie lay on her bed with her face in the pillow and her phone on speaker. Tao Tao, her flatmate, was at the biology lab with her cell cultures until midnight.

“He bought you a mug?” said Tao Tao.

“He said it was a spare.”

“He bought you a mug and your favourite tea and your favourite sweets, and he said they were on offer?”

“Both bags.”

Tao Tao made a noise like a kettle.

“Don’t,” said Yu Jie.

“I’m being extremely reasonable. You’re the one making up quantum problems to visit a man who has now furnished his office for you.”

“He hasn’t furnished anything.”

“He bought a second mug!”

Yu Jie rolled onto her back and looked at the ceiling. She couldn’t get the smile off her face. She’d been trying since four o’clock.

“He noticed the sweets,” she said. “I dropped them once, and he noticed.”

Tao Tao was quiet for a moment. When she spoke again she’d stopped laughing.

“Yu Jie. You know what you’re doing, don’t you? You’ve got a thesis due in May, and he’s in your department.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

On the bedside table her notebook lay open at the revised derivation. In the corner of the last page there was a small purple cat, drawn in ordinary biro, because her good pen was still missing.

“I’m going back next Wednesday,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

In office 412 Miles washed the white mug and put it upside down beside his own. He put the lid back on the tea. He picked up the paper cranes, all four of them, and stood holding them in his palm.

Then he opened the top drawer and put them in beside the pen.

On his way out he looked at the stack of journals holding the door. Then he picked them up, shut the door, and put the journals on the floor just inside it, against the wall, where they’d be handy next Wednesday.

chapters.title: The Harmonic Oscillator Is Not a Metaphor
chapters.desc: In front of a hundred and forty second-years she asks if zero-point energy applies to people. He answers honestly, and the whole fourth floor knows by lunch.
chapters.content:
There were a hundred and forty second-years in Lecture Theatre C at ten on a Tuesday morning, and they made the noise a hundred and forty people make when they’ve all been told to sit down at once and none of them wants to.

Miles stood at the front with his notes in one hand and a stick of chalk in the other, and looked up at the back row.

She was there.

Shen Yu Jie had no business in a second-year lecture. She’d taken Quantum Two last year and scored a hundred, and Professor Weng still told people about it. But she was sitting in the back row on the left, in her white shirt and black blazer, with her hair over one shoulder and a notebook open on her knee, wearing the face of a girl who had come purely to revise.

He looked at her for about one second. Then he turned to the board. He’d learned over the last month that looking at Shen Yu Jie for longer than a second didn’t help anybody.

“Good morning. Last week we built the ladder operators. Today we’re going to use them to find out what the oscillator does when it’s got as little energy as it can possibly have.”

He wrote the energy levels across the board, big enough for the back row.

Eₙ = ħω (n + ½)

“So. What happens when n is zero?”

A boy in the second row put his hand up. “The energy’s still not zero.”

“Why not?”

“Uncertainty principle.”

“More precisely?”

The boy went pink. Miles waited, because there was nothing worse than a lecturer who answered his own questions.

“If it sat perfectly still at the bottom,” the boy said slowly, “we’d know the position and the momentum exactly. And we can’t.”

“Good.” Miles wrote underneath:

E₀ = ½ ħω

“The lowest state still has energy in it. We call it the zero-point energy. The system can’t be completely still. Quantum mechanics won’t allow it.”

He went through the ground-state wave function and drew the little bell curve of where the particle was likely to be, and explained it twice, the second time with his hands, because he could see a girl in the fourth row who’d stopped writing and was looking at the board the way people look at a train that’s left.

At the back, Yu Jie was paying attention. To begin with.

He’d worn a black turtleneck again, with a dark grey blazer over it, and when he turned to the board the light from the high windows caught the edge of his glasses. He hardly looked at his notes. He was good at this, she thought, unfairly good. He could explain something hard without making you feel stupid for not knowing it already, and before he answered a question he always paused for a second, as though the question deserved to be considered properly, even when it was the boy in the third row asking whether this would be on the exam.

She’d started to associate that pause with the possibility of making him smile. That was becoming a problem.

“Any questions?”

A hand went up at the back.

He knew whose it was before he looked.

“Miss Shen.”

“If the oscillator still has energy in its lowest state,” said Yu Jie, quite seriously, “does that mean the energy’s never really zero?”

“For the quantum oscillator, yes.”

She considered this. Then she asked, in the same voice, “Does that apply to people too?”

A hundred and forty heads turned round.

Miles stood with the chalk in his hand. He could have said several sensible things. That people weren’t harmonic oscillators. That analogies had limits. That if she had questions about the syllabus his door was open on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

He looked up at the back row instead, at her, and said, “It’s never zero.”

The room went quiet in a different way.

“Even when they’re resting?” said Yu Jie.

“Especially then.”

Somebody laughed, and then a lot of people did. Miles turned back to the board.

“I’d advise against using the harmonic oscillator for your love lives,” he said. “The maths gets much less reliable.”

The theatre laughed properly then. At the back, Yu Jie sat down with her face burning and bent over her notebook. She wrote three words, which weren’t physics, and drew a small heart beside them, and immediately scribbled it out so hard the paper tore.

✦ ✦ ✦

A lecture theatre with a hundred and forty people in it keeps a secret for about twelve minutes.

By a quarter to twelve it was on the student forum, under Physics Confessions, with a photograph of the board.

Lecture 7 was not about physics today. Somebody asked Dr. Wei if zero-point energy applies to people and he said, completely seriously, “It’s never zero.” Our lecturer is a lonely quantum particle. His energy is never zero but his social life is.

By lunch it had two hundred likes and the comments were worse.

cat_in_lab: lonely quantum particle 😭😭

physics_nerd_22: he isn’t romantic, he just talks like a textbook with excellent posture

xiaoyu_phys: he’s the only man alive who can make the ground state sound romantic. nobody has excited his energy state yet. applications open?

Yu Jie read the last one three times.

“You’ve got a face on,” said Tao Tao, across the canteen table.

“What face?”

“The face you had when that girl at school copied your science fair project.”

Yu Jie put her phone face down. “Somebody posted something stupid.”

“About Dr. Wei?”

Yu Jie said nothing.

“Show me,” said Tao Tao.

“No.”

Tao Tao held out her hand and waited, and Yu Jie, who had been losing to Tao Tao since they were twelve, pushed the phone across. Tao Tao read it and laughed so hard a boy at the next table moved his tray.

“’Applications open’!”

“It isn’t funny.”

“It’s extremely funny.” Tao Tao wiped her eyes. “Who’s xiaoyu?”

“Nobody.” Yu Jie took the phone back and tapped on the name, because apparently her thumb had stopped asking her permission for things. The profile was public. A second-year, with long hair and a lovely smile, who had posted a photograph of herself in the front row of Lecture Theatre C holding up her notes with a heart drawn on them, three weeks ago, captioned my favourite class.

“You’re looking at her profile,” said Tao Tao.

“I’m checking whether she actually understands quantum mechanics.”

“Of course you are.”

Yu Jie scrolled. A birthday cake. A cat. A study group. Nothing that gave her a single good reason to dislike the girl, which was annoying.

He wasn’t her boyfriend. He wasn’t even her friend, technically. He was a man in her department who bought her jasmine tea and remembered which sweets she liked and had just said it’s never zero to her in front of a hundred and forty people.

She locked the phone.

“You’re smiling,” said Tao Tao.

“I’m chewing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday afternoons Miles had real office hours, and there was a queue.

A second-year wanted to go through the problem sheet. Another wanted to know if the slides would be up before the weekend. A third had come, as far as Miles could tell, to stand in the doorway and look at him and then leave, and he had a horrible feeling she’d read the forum.

At twenty past two his phone buzzed.

Ling Hao: Have you seen the forum

Ling Hao: You’re a lonely quantum particle

Ling Hao: I’ve printed it out for the staff room

He put the phone face down.

At half past two there was a knock, and when he said “Come in,” Yu Jie came in.

On a Tuesday. In his actual office hours, like a normal student, with her notebook held in front of her in both hands.

“Good afternoon, Professor.”

“Miss Shen. You know what day it is.”

“I thought I’d try the official ones. To see what they’re like.”

“And?”

She looked round the empty office. “Quieter than I expected.”

She sat down and opened the notebook at a page about the zero-point energy, and asked him a real question, which was whether a system in its ground state was doing anything if you couldn’t see it doing it, and he spent a good twenty minutes on the difference between a particle wobbling about and a particle simply not being in one place. She listened properly. She asked two more questions, both good.

Then she said, “Did you see the forum?”

His pen stopped for half a second.

“Unfortunately.”

“You’re famous.”

“I don’t think that’s an improvement.”

“They’re calling you a lonely quantum particle.”

He took his glasses off and pinched the bridge of his nose, and she watched him do it with an attention he’d have found alarming if he’d seen it.

“You do spend a lot of time on your own in this office,” she said.

“That’s how research works.”

“And you drink tea on your own.”

“That’s how tea works.”

“Not always.”

He put his glasses back on and looked at her through them. “Did you come about quantum mechanics or about my social life?”

“Can’t it be both?”

“No.”

“That’s a shame,” said Yu Jie, and turned the page.

At half past three, while he was reading her derivation, she took a White Rabbit from the saucer on his desk, ate it, and sat folding the wrapper into smaller and smaller squares. When she’d made it as small as it would go she took the purple biro out of her pencil case, wrote something on it in tiny letters, and put it on the corner of his desk without a word.

He didn’t look at it until she’d gone.

never zero

It was a sweet wrapper. It was rubbish. He held it for a while and then opened his wallet and slid it in behind his staff card, where nobody would ever see it, and closed the wallet and went back to marking problem sheets, and marked the next one wrong twice.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ling Hao came in at twenty past five without knocking, holding two coffees.

He was an astrophysicist with a round cheerful face, the office next door, 413, and a wife who was a pastry chef, which meant he arrived most mornings smelling of butter. He’d been the postdoc down the corridor when Miles came to the department as a doctoral student nine years ago, and he was the closest thing Miles had to a friend. Ling Hao said that was like being the tallest building in a village.

“I’ve come to save your reputation,” he said, and put one of the coffees down.

“I don’t need saving.”

“You’re a lonely quantum particle.”

“I’ve been told.”

Ling Hao sat in the chair Yu Jie had been sitting in. He looked at the white mug drying by the sink. He looked at the tin of jasmine, and at the saucer of White Rabbits, and at Miles.

“Don’t,” said Miles.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has.”

Ling Hao drank some coffee. When he put the cup down, he’d stopped grinning.

“Seriously, Wei. Be careful on Wednesdays.”

Miles went on typing. “Careful how?”

“The wall’s made of cardboard. I can hear you two every week. I hear her arguing with you. I hear you laughing, nearly, which I’ve never heard in nine years. I hear you explaining things until six o’clock when you’ve got no office hours at all.”

“She’s a student.”

“I know.”

“She comes about her work.”

“I know that too.” Ling Hao leaned forward. “Professor Ruan’s noticed.”

The typing stopped.

Professor Ruan was the head of the condensed matter group and Yu Jie’s thesis supervisor, and she’d been in the department for twenty-two years. She noticed most things. The things she noticed tended to get dealt with.

“What did she say?”

“She asked me why your door’s always open on Wednesday afternoons, when you’ve kept it shut for six years.” Ling Hao held up both hands. “I didn’t tell her anything. I don’t have to. She’s got eyes.”

Miles looked at his screen without reading it.

“She’s an exceptional student,” he said. “She’s in her final year. Her record’s clean, and I don’t intend to be the thing that changes that.”

“I didn’t say you did.”

“Then what are you saying?”

“That you should decide what you’re doing,” said Ling Hao, “before somebody decides for you.” He stood up and took his coffee. At the door he looked back at the white mug and couldn’t help himself. “Lovely mug, by the way.”

“Get out.”

Ling Hao laughed all the way down the corridor.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back at ten to six, because she’d left her scarf on the back of the chair. It was a cream cashmere scarf that cost more than his bicycle, and he’d been looking at it for twenty minutes.

He handed it to her at the door.

“Thank you, Professor.”

“Miss Shen.” He hadn’t meant to say anything else. He heard himself say it anyway. “Could you come tomorrow? At three.”

She stopped winding the scarf.

“Tomorrow’s Wednesday.”

“I know.”

“Is something wrong with my derivation?”

“No. Your derivation’s fine.” He kept his hand on the door. “There’s something I need to talk to you about. It won’t take long.”

She looked at him. He could see her deciding not to ask, and then deciding to ask, and then not.

“All right,” she said. “Three.”

He watched her walk down the corridor with the end of the scarf trailing, and when she’d gone round the corner by the lifts he went back in and shut the door.

He sat down. He took a clean notepad out of the drawer, the yellow lined kind the department bought in boxes of fifty, and uncapped a pen.

He wrote one word at the top of the page in capital letters.

RULE

Then he sat looking at it for a long time.

The things that needed to go underneath it were simple. He knew what they were. He’d written dozens of documents in his life that were harder than this: grant proposals, referee reports, a reference for a student he’d failed. He knew the department’s policy, which was four paragraphs long and clear. He knew what Professor Weng had said and what Ling Hao had said. He knew what he’d say if one of his colleagues were in his position, and he knew he’d be right.

He drew a line under the word, straight, with the edge of a ruler.

Then he put the pen down without writing anything else, put the pad in the top drawer, on top of a purple pen and four paper cranes, and went home.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night Yu Jie lay on her bed with the lamp on and her notebook open on her stomach.

Tao Tao: What did he want

Yu Jie: He wants to see me tomorrow. At three.

Tao Tao: On a Wednesday??

Yu Jie: He asked me. Himself.

Tao Tao: ok that’s either very good or very bad

Yu Jie: I know.

Tao Tao: which one do you think

Yu Jie looked at the ceiling for a while. She thought about the way he’d held the door. The way he hadn’t quite looked at her when he’d said there’s something I need to talk to you about.

Yu Jie: Bad.

Tao Tao: you don’t know that

Yu Jie: He said it won’t take long. Nothing good takes not long.

Tao Tao: that’s not even a sentence

She put the phone down. In the notebook, under the equation she’d copied from the board that morning, she’d written never zero and torn the paper scribbling out the heart.

She turned to a clean page and wrote, in her neatest hand, Things I will not do tomorrow.

1. Cry.

She looked at it for a while. She didn’t add a second one.

chapters.title: Miles Wei Has One Rule
chapters.desc: Miles turns her down with a graph he drew with a metre rule. She adds an end date: the twentieth of June, four o’clock.
chapters.epigraph: “Then you should have drawn it more carefully.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past seven on Wednesday morning, Ling Hao was standing in Miles’s office with a paper cup of coffee, watching him read the same paragraph for the fifth time.

“You’re not listening to me.”

“I am.”

“What did I say?”

Miles turned a page. “Something about boundaries.”

“I said you look like a man who’s been up since four.” Ling Hao put the coffee down on the desk. “Right. We’re rehearsing.”

“Rehearsing what?”

“The conversation you’re going to have at three o’clock.”

Miles took his glasses off. “Why would I need to rehearse it?”

“Because you’ve got the emotional range of an uncooperative calculator. I’ve known you nine years. I’ve seen you tell a man his thesis was wrong in a way that made him thank you, and I’ve seen you try to buy a birthday card.” Ling Hao pulled out the chair and sat in it. “I’m her.”

“No.”

“I’m Yu Jie. I’ve come in. I’ve sat down. I’m looking at you with enormous eyes.”

“You’re looking at me with croissant on your chin.”

“Begin, Dr. Wei.”

Miles put his glasses back on. “She’s an exceptional student. She’s in her final year. I’m in her department, and there’s a policy, and a boundary, and it isn’t negotiable.”

“Good. Now say it like you’re not reading it off the back of a cereal box.”

“That’s how I say things.”

“Then why,” said Ling Hao, “are you still letting her come every Wednesday?”

Miles didn’t answer.

“She’s interested in the research,” Ling Hao offered.

“She is.”

“And the jasmine tea is part of an academic initiative.”

“Get to the point.”

“The point is you tell her the truth, kindly, and you don’t make it sound like she’s done something wrong, because she hasn’t. And then you stop watching the door on Wednesday afternoons.” Ling Hao stood and picked up his coffee. At the door he turned round. “And Wei. Whatever you do, don’t give her a mathematical explanation.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

“I can see you planning it. You’re going to draw a graph.”

He went. Miles sat and looked at the top drawer of his desk. The yellow pad was in there, with one word on it and a ruled line underneath, and nothing else, because he’d tried four times last night to write the sentence that went under it and every version had sounded either like a disciplinary letter or like an apology.

He looked at the chalkboard.

Then he got up and took the metre rule down from behind the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Jie arrived at twelve minutes to three, which was early, because she had decided that if it was going to be bad she’d rather get it over with.

She’d spent most of the morning not thinking about it. She’d also spent twenty minutes choosing between two hair clips, and chose the small white one, which nobody would notice.

The door was open. He was standing by the board.

“Good afternoon, Professor.”

He turned round. “Good afternoon, Yu Jie.”

He’d used her given name. He’d done it twice now. She was starting to keep count, which was humiliating.

“Sit down. Please.”

She sat, and then she saw the board, and forgot to be nervous.

He’d drawn a graph. He had drawn it with the metre rule, so the axes were perfectly straight and met at a perfect right angle. The horizontal one was labelled TIME. The vertical one was labelled PERSONAL INVOLVEMENT. And along the bottom, lying flat on the time axis from one end of the board to the other, was a single straight line, with a small neat arrow pointing to it and the words PROFESSIONAL DISTANCE.

Yu Jie looked at the graph. Then at him.

“Professor,” she said, “is this a lecture?”

“It’s an illustration.”

“It’s got axes.”

“Most illustrations do.” He put the rule down on the ledge. He’d meant to begin with the pad, she realised, because there was a yellow notepad on the desk in front of her chair, face up, and on it, under the word RULE in capitals and a line drawn with a ruler, was a single sentence in his small upright hand.

Nothing happens while you’re a student in my department.

She read it twice.

“Nothing,” she said.

“Nothing.” He stood beside the graph with his hands at his sides, the way he stood when he lectured. “While you’re studying here, and while I’m in a position of any kind of authority over you, that line stays flat. That’s what it means.”

She looked down at her hands. She’d known it was coming. She’d known since he’d held the door yesterday and said it won’t take long. Knowing hadn’t helped. Her chest was tight in a way she didn’t like and couldn’t do anything about.

She said, “Is that because you don’t want anything to happen?”

He was quiet.

She looked up. “Or because you can’t?”

Something moved in his face, a very little.

“Those aren’t the same question,” he said.

“I know.”

“Then you’ll understand why I’m not going to answer it.”

She sat back in the chair. “That’s a very convenient answer, Professor.”

“Yes,” he said. “It is.”

She hadn’t expected him to admit it. A smile tried to get out of her and she had to hold it in with her teeth.

“You’ve got a thesis to write,” he went on, “and a defence in May, and a lot of decisions to make about what comes after. I don’t want anything to do with me anywhere near those decisions. Not because I think you’d let it, because I don’t.” He paused. “Because it isn’t only about you. If anyone ever asked whether your degree was yours, I’d want the answer to be so obvious it was boring.”

She looked at the graph again. The line was so perfectly flat. It was infuriating.

“You’re very serious about this,” she said.

“I have to be.”

She nodded slowly. Then she got up and walked over to the board.

He didn’t move. She stood beside him, close enough that she could smell the chalk on him and the coffee, and looked at the far right-hand end of the time axis, where his arrow ran off into nothing.

“What happens here?”

“Time goes on.”

“For ever?”

“That’s generally how time works.”

“Not in a proper graph.” She picked a stick of chalk off the ledge. “A proper graph has a domain. You taught me that. Two weeks ago, about an oscillator, when you were wrong.”

“Yu Jie.”

She bent down and wrote, under the end of the axis, in her slightly slanting hand:

20 JUNE — 16:00

She underlined the twenty twice. Then she stepped back.

He looked at it. “What’s that?”

“Graduation. The ceremony’s on Saturday the twentieth of June, and it finishes at four.” She put the chalk back on the ledge, exactly where she’d found it. “After that I’m not your student, or anybody’s student in this department. I’m just a person with a degree.”

“You’ve added a condition.”

“Of course I have.”

“That isn’t how boundaries work.”

“Then you should have drawn it more carefully.” She turned to him. “There. Now it’s a complete graph.”

She wasn’t asking him to break his rule, and she wasn’t asking him to promise her anything. He could see that. She simply wouldn’t let him make the waiting look as if it went on for ever, and he understood exactly what she was doing, and he understood that it worked.

“The twentieth of June,” he said.

“Four o’clock.”

“I see.”

“Don’t worry, Professor. I’m very good at following instructions.” She smiled at him, not in triumph, just a little. “Especially when there’s a deadline.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They worked, afterwards, because that was what they did on Wednesdays and because neither of them knew what else to do.

He’d brought a problem for her. It was a stripped-down version of something his group was working on, a lopsided potential with an approximation buried in it that was wrong in an interesting way, and he gave it to her without telling her where the mistake was. She sat on the edge of the chair with her elbows on his desk and went at it.

She made a bad substitution in the second line. He pointed at it and said nothing. She frowned, and fixed it.

“Better,” he said.

“That’s all? I spent ten minutes on that.”

“Then spend another ten checking it next time.”

“You’re very unsympathetic.”

“I’m improving your habits.”

“At the expense of my happiness.”

“A necessary sacrifice.”

She laughed, and he smiled down at the page, and for a while the graph behind them belonged to a different conversation.

Then, without looking up, she said, “Do you think waiting’s hard?”

His pen slowed.

“That depends what you’re waiting for.”

“Something you want.”

“Then you have to decide whether it’s worth it.”

“Have you ever waited for something?”

“Yes.”

“What happened?”

“Sometimes I got it.” He turned the page. “Sometimes I didn’t.”

“That’s not very encouraging.”

“It’s true.”

She liked that about him, she thought. She liked it even when it was annoying. He didn’t hand you things because they sounded nice.

“All right,” she said, and went back to the problem.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly five when he said, “That’s enough for today,” and she said, “You’re dismissing me,” and he said, “I’m suggesting you go home,” and she said those were the same thing, and he agreed.

He went to the board to rub out the lower half, where they’d been working. He’d pushed his sleeves up, and he rubbed out the equations in long even strokes with the felt eraser, frowning slightly, and when he turned round there was a smear of white high on his left cheekbone where he’d pushed his glasses up with a chalky finger.

“You’ve got chalk on your face,” she said.

“Where?”

She touched her own cheek. He touched the wrong side of his.

“Other side.”

“Here?”

“Lower. No. It’s fine, I’ll...”

She stepped in and did it herself. She put her hand up and brushed her thumb once across his cheekbone, and the chalk came away on her skin.

It took about a second.

He went completely still. She felt it under her thumb, the way his whole face stopped, and then his hand came up and closed round her wrist.

He didn’t pull her hand away. He just held it there, against his cheek, with her thumb still resting under his eye and the window reflected small and bright in both lenses of his glasses, and looked at her.

She’d stopped breathing. She noticed that she’d stopped, and couldn’t start again.

“Yu Jie,” he said, very low.

“I know.”

He let go of her wrist. He did it carefully, the way you’d put down something you’d been handed by mistake. Then he took a step back, so there was the width of the desk between them again, and picked a tissue out of the box and gave it to her.

“Thank you,” he said.

She wiped the chalk off her thumb. Neither of them made a joke about it. Neither of them pretended it hadn’t happened. He turned back to the board, and she understood that the afternoon was over, and that he wasn’t angry. He was keeping the promise he’d made about an hour ago.

She put the tissue in the bin and picked up her bag.

“Good evening, Professor.”

“Good evening.”

At the door she turned round. “Don’t forget the twentieth.”

“I won’t.”

“Four o’clock.”

“I know when four o’clock is, Yu Jie.”

“Good,” she said, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t cry. She’d told herself she wouldn’t, and she didn’t, and on the bus home she was quite proud of herself, right up until she got into her flat and sat on the kitchen floor with her back against the cupboards and her coat still on, and stayed there a while.

When she got up she opened the calendar on her phone, and scrolled. October, November, December. January, February, March. April. May. June.

She tapped the twentieth. It was a Saturday.

The end of the interval

4:00 p.m. Graduation. The line stops here.

She looked at it. Then she added a note at the bottom.

Don’t be late.

Her phone buzzed while she was still holding it.

Tao Tao: well??

Yu Jie: He drew me a graph.

Tao Tao: he WHAT

Yu Jie: Professional distance. Flat line. He used a metre rule.

Tao Tao: I’m going to scream into a pillow

Tao Tao: what did you do

Yu Jie: I gave it an endpoint.

She sent a screenshot of the calendar. There was a long pause.

Tao Tao: you’re unbelievable

Tao Tao: are you ok though

Yu Jie looked at the screenshot for a while.

Yu Jie: He held my wrist.

Tao Tao: WHAT

Yu Jie: For about a second. Then he gave me a tissue.

Tao Tao: Yu Jie that man is in SO much trouble

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles stayed in his office until seven, because there were emails, and then an error in a calculation, and then because the corridor had gone quiet and he didn’t want to walk out into it yet.

When he finally stood up, the graph was still on the board.

He picked up the eraser and took it off a piece at a time. The vertical axis first. Then the horizontal. Then the long flat line and its arrow and the words PROFESSIONAL DISTANCE, which came away in white dust onto the ledge.

He stopped before the bottom right-hand corner.

20 JUNE — 16:00

It was in her writing, slanting a little to the right, with the twenty underlined twice. It would have taken less than a second.

He put the eraser down on the ledge, turned off the lamp and went home.

Ling Hao came in at eight the next morning to borrow a stapler. He stopped in the middle of the room and looked at the board, which was clean from edge to edge apart from one small date in the corner.

He looked at Miles.

“Don’t,” said Miles.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“It’s a reminder.”

“Of course it is,” said Ling Hao, and took the stapler, and on his way out he said, quite gently for him, “That’s a long way off, Wei.”

“I know.”

The date stayed. All that year it sat in the corner of the board while equations went up and came down around it, and the cleaners, who rubbed the other boards on the fourth floor every Friday, learned without being told to leave that corner alone.

chapters.title: A Countdown Disguised as a Semester
chapters.desc: Yu Jie makes a countdown calendar with an atom for every day. Miles finds it, counts the squares twice, and asks to kiss her on the back stairs.
chapters.content:
On Saturday morning Yu Jie opened her laptop at ten, made a new file, and typed THE END OF THE INTERVAL across the top in capitals.

She’d only meant to make a countdown. A date and a number, something to look at. But a number on its own was boring, and if she was going to wait from last Wednesday until the twentieth of June she might as well make it pretty.

So she drew atoms.

One for each day. A dot for the nucleus and two electrons going round it on neat little ellipses, like planets, which was completely wrong and which Niels Bohr would have forgiven and nobody else in the department would. She did them in blue and purple and pink, a different mix for every one, and by the end of the first row she was smiling at the screen.

Tao Tao came out of her bedroom in pyjamas at half past eleven, looking for coffee, and stopped behind her chair.

“What’s that?”

“A calendar.”

“Why does your calendar look like a chemistry poster?”

“It’s physics.”

Tao Tao leaned over and counted the rows with her finger, then gave up. At the bottom of the screen Yu Jie had typed the total.

255 DAYS

“You’re serious,” said Tao Tao.

“Very.”

“An atom for every day. Until June.”

“From the day he drew the graph. Wednesday the eighth. That’s square one.”

Tao Tao looked at her for a while with her coffee cup halfway to her mouth.

“Do you realise,” she said, “how much work you’re putting into waiting for a man who hasn’t even kissed you?”

Yu Jie’s hand stopped on the trackpad.

“That’s a very specific observation.”

“It’s an accurate one.”

Yu Jie printed it on the good paper, two sheets, and taped them together and stuck them on the wall above her desk. Then she took a purple marker and coloured in the first three atoms, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, one after another.

“Every day?” said Tao Tao.

“Every night before bed.”

“That’s obsessive.”

“It’s organised.”

“What’s the difference?”

“Colour coding,” said Yu Jie, and coloured in the fourth.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sunday dinner at the Shen house was never only dinner. It had an agenda.

The house sat at the top of the hill road behind a wall and a gate, with the harbour spread out underneath it like something the family had bought, which in a sense it had. There were usually three topics, two cousins’ achievements and one question about Yu Jie’s future that became the whole evening.

She arrived at three minutes past seven. Her mother was already at the table in grey silk, with her back straight, talking to Yu Ming. Her father’s chair was empty. He was in the study on a call to somebody in another time zone, which was where he usually was.

“You’re late,” said Shen Ruolan.

“By three minutes.”

“Your grandfather used to say punctuality is a form of respect.”

Yu Jie pulled out her chair. “Then I’ve only been three minutes disrespectful.”

Yu Ming laughed into his water glass. He was twenty-six, worked for their father, and looked like a good suit worn to too many meetings.

Their mother looked at him. “Don’t encourage her.”

The soup came, and for a while it was almost pleasant. Her mother asked about her thesis, and Yu Jie explained strained graphene, a sheet of carbon one atom thick that does strange things to electrons when you stretch it.

Then Shen Ruolan put her spoon down, and Yu Jie knew the agenda had arrived.

“I met someone at the consulate reception last week. Or rather, I met his mother. His name is Yan Zhiyuan.”

“All right.”

“He’s in the diplomatic service. Twenty-nine. He speaks five languages, he studied abroad, and his family is an old one.” She paused for this to settle. “He’s not married. His mother says he’d like to meet someone serious.”

Yu Jie put her spoon down too.

“Ma.”

“I thought the two of you might get on.”

“I’ve got a thesis due in May.”

“You have more than one thing in your life.”

“I’ve got a research proposal.”

“That can wait.”

“Physics doesn’t really work like that.”

Her mother’s mouth thinned slightly. “You’re graduating in June, Yu Jie. It’s time to think about your future.”

“I am thinking about it. I’m applying for doctoral programmes.”

“And then what? Five more years in a laboratory? Ten?” Shen Ruolan picked up her spoon again, as if the matter were too small to need both hands. “I’ve let you have your physics. It’s been good for you. It’s taught you discipline. But it’s a hobby, darling. A very clever hobby. You can’t build a life around it.”

The word landed harder than Yu Jie had expected.

She thought about the nights she’d sat up until two with a derivation that wouldn’t close, and the first time she’d understood why electrons in graphene behave as though they have no mass, and walked round the library twice because she couldn’t sit still.

“I didn’t do this for four years,” she said quietly, “because I needed something to fill my time.”

“You’re taking it personally.”

“It is personal.”

“Ma,” said Yu Ming, “maybe let her finish her degree first, and then...”

“You stay out of this.”

He looked down at his soup. That was the end of Yu Ming. It usually was.

Her mother turned back to her, and her voice softened, which was always worse. “I only want you to meet him. One dinner. You might like him. You don’t know.”

Yu Jie finished her soup and said nothing else, and her mother took her silence for the yes it wasn’t, the way she always did.

In the car on the way home she took out her phone and looked at a photograph of the atoms on her wall. Four coloured in. Two hundred and fifty-one to go.

For the first time all weekend she didn’t feel like smiling at them.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday her mother texted.

Ma: I’ve spoken to Zhiyuan’s mother. He’s free for dinner a week on Sunday. I’ll send the car.

Yu Jie wrote back: I told you I’m not interested.

Her mother didn’t answer, which meant the car would come anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday Miles was reading a referee report when he heard the knock he’d been listening for since two o’clock.

“Come in.”

The date was still in the corner of the board. She looked at it as she sat down, and he saw her see it, and she didn’t say anything, which he was grateful for.

He’d written her a problem. It was a simple perturbation on a simple oscillator, and she read it twice and looked up at him with her eyes narrowed.

“Is this a trick?”

“No.”

“You’ve said that before.”

“And it wasn’t a trick then either. You just didn’t see the second part.”

She bent over it. He went back to his referee report and read the same paragraph four times. For about a quarter of an hour the office was quiet apart from her pen. She was in a cream cardigan today, over the white shirt, with the sleeves pushed up, and she’d tied her hair back with a pencil through it, and she was frowning at the page in a way that made him want to stand behind her chair and read over her shoulder.

He stayed where he was.

“My mother wants me to meet someone,” she said, without looking up.

His pen stopped.

“Someone?”

“A diplomat. Yan Zhiyuan. He’s twenty-nine and he speaks five languages.” She turned a page. “There’s going to be a dinner. She’s sending the car.”

“I see.”

“Is that all?”

He looked at her. “What would you like me to ask?”

“Whether I want to meet him.”

“Do you?”

“No.”

“Then that answers it.”

“You’re not even curious whether he’s handsome?”

Miles looked at her across the desk for a moment.

“Would it change your answer?” he said.

She stared at him, and then laughed, and bent back over her problem pink to the ears, and he looked down at his report and found he’d underlined a sentence so hard he’d gone through the paper.

That was when he saw it. A sheet of folded paper was sticking out of the back of her notebook, and it was covered in colours.

“What’s that?”

“What’s what?”

He pointed. She looked down and made a grab for it, too late. He’d already seen the little atoms, rows of them, blue and pink and purple, and the words across the top.

He didn’t touch it. He just looked.

She drew it out slowly and unfolded it on the desk, because there was no point hiding it now, and sat back with her chin up.

“It’s a calendar.”

“I can see that.”

“It’s a countdown. It’s to the twentieth. Square one’s last Wednesday.”

He looked at the rows. Then he counted them. Then, because he didn’t trust himself, he counted them again, moving his eyes along each line, while she sat watching him do it with her face going slowly redder.

Two hundred and fifty-five. Seven of them coloured in, one for each day since he’d stood at his board with a metre rule and told her nothing would happen.

He thought of her sitting at a desk somewhere drawing two hundred and fifty-five atoms with their little lopsided orbits, one at a time. For a man who’d told her the line would stay flat. Who hadn’t promised her a single thing, because he’d been so careful not to.

And there was a diplomat who spoke five languages, and a car.

He got up, went to the board and picked up the chalk. Under her date in the corner, he wrote:

255 − 7 = ?

She looked at it. Then at him.

“Professor.”

“It’s a problem.”

“That’s not physics. That’s arithmetic.”

“You’re a physicist. It should be easy.”

“Two hundred and forty-eight,” she said, and laughed, helplessly, with her hand over her mouth. “You counted. You counted them twice. I saw you.”

“I calculated.”

“You counted.”

He put the chalk down. His hand wasn’t quite steady, and he didn’t like that.

“Yu Jie,” he said. “That date isn’t a promise.”

The laugh went out of her face. “I know.”

“It’s the day you stop being a student here. It doesn’t mean everything else becomes simple. I can’t ask you to spend eight months waiting for...”

“You didn’t ask.” She stood up. “I’m not doing it because you asked.”

They looked at each other across the desk.

“Come with me,” he said. “Not here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The back stairs ran down from the end of the fourth-floor corridor to a fire door into the courtyard. In the mornings second-years used them as a short cut. At half past four on a Wednesday they were empty, and the stairwell smelt of dust and cold concrete, and the light came down grey through a high wired window.

He stopped on the landing between the third floor and the fourth. She stood two steps below him, which put her eyes almost level with his.

“You’re counting,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I need you to know I’m not asking you to. Your degree. Your applications. Whatever you decide to do in June. None of it should have anything to do with what you think might happen with me.”

“It doesn’t.”

“I mean it.”

“I know you do.” She came up one step. “I’m not waiting because I think you owe me something, Miles.”

It was the first time she’d said his name. It went through him like a current.

“I’m waiting because I want to,” she said. “Because I like you. I’ve liked you since you did the normalisation integral the long way on purpose to make me feel stupid.”

She didn’t smile when she said it. She just said it, and stood there, and let him look at her.

He’d known. Of course he’d known. It was different hearing her say it, with her chin up and her hands in fists at her sides.

He’d made his rule a week ago today. He’d drawn it with a ruler. He’d stood in front of her and told her it wasn’t negotiable, and believed it, and he still believed in every reason he’d given her. And for seven days he’d watched the door anyway, and kept a sweet wrapper in his wallet, and he hadn’t rubbed out her date. That wasn’t a flat line.

“I like you too,” he said.

Her lips parted.

“Yu Jie. Can I kiss you?”

She went completely still.

“You’re asking me?”

“Yes.”

“You know what I’m going to say.”

“I’d still like to hear you say it.”

“Yes,” she said. “Yes. Obviously yes.”

He lifted his hand and stopped just short of her face. “May I?”

“Miles.”

He touched her cheek. His fingers were cold from the stairwell and her skin was hot, and she turned her face into his palm before he’d even finished the movement. He bent his head and kissed her.

He’d meant it to be careful. It was, for a moment: a slow, light press of his mouth on hers, like a question he didn’t want to ask too loudly. Then she made a small sound in her throat and took two fistfuls of his turtleneck, and he stopped being careful.

He kissed her properly. He put his other hand in her hair, and the pencil she’d stuck through it fell out and bounced down the stairs, and neither of them looked. Her mouth was soft and tasted of milk and sugar from the White Rabbits, and when he tipped her head back to get closer she came up the last step without letting go of him, so they were on the same stair and she was pressed against him from her knees to her mouth. She kissed him back like she’d been waiting to win an argument.

When he lifted his head his glasses had gone crooked. She was breathing as if she’d run up all four flights.

“Hello,” she said.

Something came out of him that was almost a laugh. Closer than before. “Hello.”

“Can I kiss you this time?”

“Yu Jie...”

She didn’t wait for the rest. She went up on her toes, took his glasses off his face, folded them one-handed the way she must have watched him do a hundred times, and kissed him so hard his back hit the stair rail. It rang all the way down the stairwell.

When she let him go he stood there with his hands at her waist, half-blind, while she put his glasses back on him, straight, and looked pleased with herself.

“You’re going to make this impossible,” he said.

“I haven’t done anything.”

“That’s the problem.”

“Is this the end of the rule?”

He thought about it, because she’d asked him seriously.

“It’s the end of pretending there isn’t anything,” he said. “Not the end of being careful. I’m not your supervisor. I don’t teach you. I won’t ever mark a single line of your work, or sit in a room where anyone decides anything about you. Nobody in that department gets to say your degree came from me.”

“Nobody will.”

“And nobody knows. Not yet. Not until June.”

“Tao Tao knows.”

“Tao Tao,” said Miles, resigned, “always knows.”

She smiled up at him. “So we’re together. Secretly. Until the twentieth.”

“If that’s what you want.”

“It is.”

“Then yes.”

“All right,” she said. “Boyfriend.”

He looked at her, and the sound came out of him again, short and rough and surprised, and he shook his head at the ceiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

They swapped numbers in the courtyard, two metres apart, like strangers comparing timetables.

She’d saved him already. She turned the screen round.

White Rabbit

“No,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re soft in the middle,” said Yu Jie, “and you lie about buying me sweets.”

“Change it.”

“What would you rather? Dr. Wei? That’s boring.”

“It’s accurate.”

“White Rabbit’s cuter.”

He held out his hand for her phone, and put his own in hers, and typed. When she got hers back she looked at what he’d saved himself as in his own phone, under her number.

Not Stuck

Her mouth fell open. “That’s my name?”

“It’s accurate.”

“That’s terrible.”

“It’s how we met.”

She narrowed her eyes at him and then laughed, and put the phone in her blazer pocket, and walked off to the bus stop without looking back, because if she’d looked back she wouldn’t have gone.

The phone buzzed before she reached the gate.

White Rabbit: Tell me when you’re home.

Yu Jie: Yes, Professor.

White Rabbit: Not at the moment.

She stopped walking and read it again.

Yu Jie: Yes, boyfriend.

There was a longer pause.

White Rabbit: Better.

She held the phone against her chest all the way home.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eleven Miles was on his sofa in the staff flat with a book open on his knee, reading the same page for the third time.

Not Stuck: Home.

He’d been holding the phone.

Miles: Good.

Not Stuck: I’ve coloured today in.

Not Stuck: Two hundred and forty-seven left.

Not Stuck: You can check my arithmetic if you want.

He looked at that for a while.

Miles: I trust your arithmetic.

Not Stuck: Goodnight, Miles.

Miles: Goodnight.

He put the phone face down on the arm of the sofa. Then he took his wallet out of his jacket, which was hanging over the chair, and opened it, and the folded wrapper was still there behind his staff card, with never zero on it in purple.

He sat with it in his hand, a man who’d kept a rule for seven days, and couldn’t make himself sorry.

chapters.title: The Coffee Cup Physics Jokes Were Not Flirting
chapters.desc: A joke on a sticky note starts a war, Dr. Ling keeps score, and Professor Ruan walks in on the worst joke yet.
chapters.epigraph: “Your jokes are still terrible. Your kisses are not.”
chapters.content:
The first note was stuck to the side of her mug.

It was the Wednesday after the back stairs, and Yu Jie had been awake since six thinking about the back stairs, and when she came into office 412 at a quarter to three the white mug was already on the desk with steam coming off it, and on the side of it, where her hand would go, there was a small yellow square of paper.

Why did the physicist break up with the mathematician?

She peeled it off. On the back, smaller:

There was no chemistry.

She looked at it. Then at Miles, who was behind his desk reading a journal with the air of a man who had no idea what anyone was talking about.

“Professor.”

“Hm.”

She held it up. “What’s this?”

“A question.”

“Is it supposed to be funny?”

“Humour is subjective.”

“I thought you had standards.”

He lowered the journal an inch. “I do.”

She drank some of her tea, deliberately, and said, “Terrible,” and put the note down beside her notebook, and he went back to his journal, and neither of them mentioned that she didn’t throw it away.

On the twenty-sixth, the Sunday her mother had promised the car, it didn’t come. Yan Zhiyuan had been sent abroad at three days’ notice to sit at the back of some conference, and the dinner was off. Yu Jie lay on her bed that night and laughed at the ceiling until Tao Tao banged on the wall. Her mother rang the next morning to say that it didn’t matter, he’d be back before Christmas, and she’d introduce them properly at the gala, where everybody would see.

That was eight weeks away. Yu Jie decided not to think about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second note came the following Wednesday.

What did the photon say at the hotel desk?

No luggage, thanks. I’m travelling light.

She stared at it for a good five seconds. He was at the board with his back to her.

“You’re doing this on purpose.”

“Doing what?”

“Leaving jokes.”

“Are they jokes?”

“Unfortunately.”

“Then I suppose I am.”

She took the purple biro out of her pencil case and wrote underneath his line: This is a low-energy form of flirting. She stuck it back on the mug.

He came back to the desk and read it, and looked at her over his glasses. “Low energy?”

“Ground state. Barely above zero.”

“That’s disappointing.”

“Try harder, Dr. Wei.”

He took the note off the mug, folded it once and put it in his top drawer. She watched him do it and said nothing, and smiled at her derivation for the rest of the afternoon.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the next week it was a routine, and the routine had rules nobody had written down. He left a note. She complained about it. Sometimes she laughed in spite of herself, and then she complained harder. The jokes weren’t good. That was the point of them. They were small and stupid and private, tucked into the ordinary business of a Wednesday afternoon: a note beside her tea, a pun written in tiny letters at the bottom of a problem sheet, a line in the margin of a paper he’d asked her to check that said Heisenberg was here, probably.

Ling Hao noticed first, because Miles had started smiling at his desk.

Not often, and not much. But one afternoon Ling Hao put his head round the door to borrow some staples and found Miles looking at a square of yellow paper with an expression on his face that Ling Hao had not seen in nine years. He backed out of the room slowly.

“What?” said Miles.

“Nothing. I’ve just witnessed something.”

“Go away.”

“You were smiling at stationery.”

“It’s a note.”

“From a Wednesday?”

Miles looked at him.

“Ah,” said Ling Hao, and came in and shut the door, delighted. “How many have you got?”

“None of your business.”
