“Oh, this is serious.” He leaned on the filing cabinet. “Wei. You do know you ought to be keeping score?”

“Why?”

“Because I strongly suspect she’s winning.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Jie had no intention of losing.

On the first Wednesday of November she arrived with a pad of pink sticky notes in her blazer pocket, and while he was frowning at a referee report she got up as if to look at a book on his shelf and stuck one to the edge of the chalkboard.

He found it ten minutes later.

Why are physicists so bad at parties?

He turned round.

“Go on,” she said.

“Why?”

“They keep trying to find the centre of mass.”

He looked at her.

“That’s worse than mine,” he said.

“Thank you.”

He took it down. He didn’t put that one in the drawer. He put it beside his keyboard, where he’d see it, and she watched him do it and her face went soft and pleased before she could stop it.

After that it was war. Yellow notes on her mug. Pink notes on his door, his monitor, the inside cover of his diary, once on the lens of his reading lamp so the whole room went faintly rosy when he switched it on. Not all of them were jokes. Some were questions. Why is your fringe always in your eyes? Is it on purpose? Some were corrections to his derivations, which he found more upsetting than the jokes. One, on the morning he had a grant meeting, just said You’ll be fine with a cat underneath it.

That one went in the drawer too.

Ling Hao started keeping the score on the inside of his own office door, in marker pen, where only people who’d shut themselves in with him could see it. It had five columns: yellow notes, pink notes, actually funny, embarrassing, and denial. Under denial, Miles had ten.

“Why’s denial ten?” said Miles, who had been shut in there to sign a form.

“Because you keep telling me this isn’t flirting.”

“It isn’t.”

“Then why are you keeping them all?”

“Throwing them away would be wasteful.”

“You’re keeping rubbish for environmental reasons.”

“Yes.”

Ling Hao added a mark under denial. It made eleven.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Wednesday after that she came early, and found him at the board in the middle of a proof.

It was his own work, nothing to do with her: a bound on how fast a particular approximation went wrong, three lines of setup and a long ugly inequality he was trying to tame. He moved over without being asked and she stood beside him, and for twenty minutes they worked on it together in near silence, passing the chalk back and forth. She questioned a step. He fixed it. He questioned one of hers and she said “No,” and showed him why, and he stood there with his mouth slightly open and then nodded.

Halfway through, she found a yellow note stuck to the corner of the board, above her date.

Why won’t the electron leave the atom?

It’s attracted to the nucleus.

“That’s terrible,” she said. “It isn’t even trying.”

“Fair.”

She took the chalk and wrote underneath it, on the board itself, in large letters: STOP ORBITING THE POINT.

He read it. Then he looked at her. They were standing shoulder to shoulder, and she could feel the warmth of his arm through her blazer, and she looked past him at the door.

It was open. He’d been propping it open every Wednesday since September.

“Yu Jie,” he said. “Someone could come in.”

She put the chalk down on the ledge. She walked to the door, kicked the stack of journals out of the way and shut it. The latch clicked. Then she turned the little lock on the handle, which she’d never seen him use, and came back across the room.

“Are you sure?” he said.

She didn’t bother answering. She took his face in both hands, chalk and all, and kissed him.

He made a sound against her mouth, half surprise and half something else, and his hand came to her waist. She pushed him back a step and his shoulders met the chalkboard, and she kissed him harder, up on her toes, her fingers in the soft hair at the back of his neck. He tasted of coffee. He kissed like he did everything else, carefully at first, paying attention, and then all at once he stopped being careful, and his hand slid up her back under her blazer and pulled her in flat against him, and she forgot entirely what the inequality had been about.

When she let him go, his glasses were askew and there was white chalk on both his cheeks in the shape of her fingers.

“That was unexpected,” he said.

“Would you prefer a written notice?”

“Possibly.”

“Dear Dr. Wei,” said Yu Jie, “I would like to interrupt your proof...”

He kissed her before she could finish. This time he turned them round, so she was the one against the board, and she felt the chalk ledge dig into her back and the dust of their unfinished proof go into her hair, and she didn’t care at all. He kissed her slowly, as if he meant to do it for a while, with his hand cupped round the back of her head so it wouldn’t knock against the board.

When he finally lifted his head she rested her forehead on his chest.

“Your derivation’s still incomplete,” she said, into his turtleneck.

“I noticed.”

“You should finish it.”

“I was planning to.”

She looked up at him. “Are you sure?”

He glanced at the board over her head. There were two smudged handprints in the middle of his inequality now, one of them hers and one his.

“Not especially,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Cen found the worst one on a Friday.

Miles had gone down to the office to collect a printout, and the head of department came into 412 looking for a journal he’d lent out and never got back, and on the way to the shelf he stopped beside Miles’s mug.

There was a pink note on it.

Cu–Te

and underneath, in case anyone was slow:

copper, tellurium. you.

When Miles came back, Professor Cen was standing by his desk holding the note between two fingers, like a specimen.

“Wei. What’s this?”

Miles stopped in the doorway. “Chemistry.”

“Cu-Te.”

“Yes.”

Professor Cen was sixty-four, the tallest man on the fourth floor, with a deep calm voice and a face that had sat on more panels than anyone in the building. He looked at the note. He looked at the mug. He looked at the empty chair on the other side of the desk. Then he gave Miles a long, measuring look over his reading glasses.

“You’re getting sentimental in your old age.”

“I’m thirty-one.”

“Hm,” said Professor Cen. He handed back the note, took his journal and went.

Miles stood with the note in his hand for a moment, and then he put it in the drawer, and shut the drawer, and sat down and stared at the wall for some time.

On Monday Ling Hao came in to return a book, found the office empty and the top drawer half open, and looked inside.

There were a great many pink notes in it. Some were folded. Some had cats on. One said you’re the only person who can make a differential equation look nervous, and one was the Cu-Te note, and underneath them all were four paper cranes and a purple pen.

By the time Miles came back from his lecture, Ling Hao was sitting in his chair holding the pen.

“Put that down.”

“Wei,” said Ling Hao. “Wei, is this her pen?”

“Put it down and get out.”

“She’s been looking for this since September. She told the whole of the third-year lab she’d lost it.”

Miles crossed the room, took the pen out of his hand, put it back in the drawer and shut it.

“Get out.”

Ling Hao went, laughing so hard he had to hold onto the door frame. Halfway down the corridor he called back, “Seven to five! She’s winning!” and a second-year coming out of the lift dropped her folder.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second Wednesday of November started like any other.

She came at a quarter to three. The tea was waiting. The note on it said What did the proton say to the electron who’d lost something? Are you positive? and she closed her eyes and said, “No. I’m begging you,” and he looked over his shoulder from the board and smiled.

They were working on a correction term together, her standing beside him with the chalk, when the door opened without anyone knocking.

“Dr. Wei. There you are.”

Professor Ruan stood in the doorway with a folder under her arm. She was fifty-eight, small and straight-backed, with short iron-grey hair and a pair of half-moon glasses on a chain, and she had two national prizes and had never knocked on a door in her life. She looked at Miles. She looked at Yu Jie. She looked, for slightly too long, at the board, where the words STOP ORBITING THE POINT were still faintly visible under a week of rubbing out.

“Good afternoon, Professor Ruan,” said Yu Jie.

“Shen Yu Jie.” Professor Ruan put the folder on Miles’s desk. “Your comments on the summer research proposals, Dr. Wei. I’ll collect them on Friday.” Then she turned to Yu Jie, and her voice didn’t change at all. “Your thesis draft.”

“My...”

“The first full draft. Which was due to me last Friday by five o’clock.”

The room went quiet.

“I was going to send it today.”

“I emailed you on Thursday. And on Monday.”

“I know. I saw them.”

“Then why haven’t I got it?”

Yu Jie had several answers, and none of them could be said in this office. She’d been revising the second section. She’d been revising it on Wednesday nights, after coming back from the fourth floor too happy to sleep, and on Thursday nights, when she sat up drawing atoms. She’d been revising it for three weeks and it wasn’t finished, because every time she opened it she thought about something else.

“I was redoing section two,” she said.

“That’s not a reason to miss a deadline.”

“No, Professor.”

“Eight o’clock tomorrow morning,” said Professor Ruan. “You’ll find me on the balcony on the fifth floor. Bring whatever you have.” She nodded to Miles. “Dr. Wei.”

She went out. The door swung shut behind her.

Yu Jie stood with the chalk in her hand.

“Your draft’s late,” said Miles.

“Apparently.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because you’d have told me to go home and finish it.”

“Yes. I would.”

“Exactly,” said Yu Jie, and her voice cracked very slightly on it, and she put the chalk down on the ledge too hard and it broke in half.

He looked at her for a moment. Then he went to the door and locked it.

“I’m not going to lecture you,” he said. “She’s done that.”

“She hasn’t started. She’ll start tomorrow at eight.” Yu Jie pressed the heels of her hands against her eyes. “On a balcony. She smokes up there. You’re not allowed on it. Nobody’s allowed on it.”

“Then she must want to talk to you very privately.”

“That’s not comforting.”

“It wasn’t meant to be.” He came up behind her. He didn’t touch her straight away. “Yu Jie.”

“What?”

“May I?”

She nodded without turning round.

He moved her hair aside, over her shoulder, and bent and kissed the back of her neck, just above the collar of her shirt, where the knob of her spine was. It was light. She felt it all the way down to her knees. He did it again, a little lower, and she shut her eyes and leaned back against him, and his arms came round her waist from behind and stayed there.

“Go home,” he said into her hair. “Finish it. Sleep for a bit. Be on that balcony at five to eight.”

“That’s very unfair.”

“What is?”

“Encouraging thesis writing like that.”

“Is it working?”

“Unfortunately,” said Yu Jie.

She went. She left her tea half-drunk, and he poured it away and washed the mug and stood it upside down by the sink, and then he took a yellow note off the pad and wrote something on it and stuck it to the inside of her mug, where she’d only find it next week, when she lifted it to drink.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty past four in the morning she sent the draft, eighty-one pages, with section two still not right. Then she sent him a text.

Yu Jie: Done. Mostly.

She didn’t expect him to be awake.

White Rabbit: Good. Now sleep.

Yu Jie: Why are you up?

White Rabbit: I wasn’t, until four.

She looked at it in the dark. He’d been lying awake waiting for her to finish.

She took a pink note from the pad on her bedside table and wrote on it, and stuck it to the back of her phone, so it would be there in the morning when she went up the stairs to the balcony.

Your jokes are still terrible. Your kisses are not.

chapters.title: Her Supervisor Is Very Interested
chapters.desc: Professor Ruan warns Yu Jie on the smoking balcony, then climbs to the fourth floor to warn Miles. He answers by reading four papers on her thesis.
chapters.content:
The balcony on the fifth floor was for staff, and only in theory.

In practice it was for Professor Ruan, who had been smoking on it every morning for twenty-two years in a building where smoking had been banned for nineteen of them. It was a narrow concrete ledge outside the condensed matter group’s corridor, with a rusted railing, a dead geranium in a pot and a view over the courtyard to the hill. Students weren’t allowed on it. Nobody had ever needed to tell them.

At three minutes past eight, Yu Jie was on it.

“Twenty pages,” said Professor Ruan.

She was leaning on the railing with a cigarette in one hand and a paper cup of coffee in the other and her half-moon glasses pushed up into her grey hair. She hadn’t said good morning.

“Professor?”

“Section two, again, properly. Twenty pages. By Monday at nine.”

Yu Jie looked down at the courtyard. A cleaner was hosing the paving stones and the water ran away in bright sheets.

“That’s a lot of pages.”

“Your thesis is a lot of pages behind.” Professor Ruan tapped ash over the railing. “I read what you sent me at half past four this morning. Eighty-one pages, of which perhaps fifty are a thesis and the rest are a collection of related thoughts.”

“It’s not that bad.”

“Section two contradicts section one in three places, and on page forty you’ve cited a paper that says the opposite of what you’ve used it to say.” She drank some coffee. “You’re the most able student I’ve had in this group in twenty years, Shen Yu Jie, and I don’t enjoy chasing you for work you could do in your sleep. So I’d like to know why I’m chasing you.”

“I’ve been distracted.”

“By what?”

It was a simple question. Yu Jie looked at the dead geranium.

Professor Ruan put her coffee down on the railing.

“Is this about Dr. Wei?”

Yu Jie turned her head so fast she pulled something in her neck. “What?”

“Don’t look so alarmed.”

“I’m not alarmed.”

“You’re holding your breath.”

Yu Jie let it out.

“I’ve been in this department for twenty-two years,” said Professor Ruan. “I know what a student looks like when she’s avoiding her supervisor. I also know what Miles Wei’s door looks like on a Wednesday afternoon, which is open, which it has not been since he joined us.” She drew on the cigarette and looked at Yu Jie through the smoke. “So.”

She could lie. She’d been lying to her mother about Wednesdays for two months. But Professor Ruan wasn’t asking out of curiosity, and she wasn’t stupid, and Yu Jie had a feeling that anything she made up now would come back later, at a worse time, with interest.

“He’s got a rule,” she said.

“A rule.”

“He made it in October. He drew it on his board. A graph, with a flat line. Professional distance. Nothing happens while I’m a student in his department.”

Professor Ruan’s face didn’t change. “And what did you do?”

“I gave it an endpoint. The twentieth of June. Four o’clock.”

There was a pause. Then Professor Ruan shut her eyes, briefly, like a woman with a headache.

“Of course you did.”

“You’re not surprised.”

“I’m trying to decide whether to be impressed by your creativity or alarmed by your priorities.” She opened her eyes. Yu Jie had opened her mouth to say more, and Professor Ruan held up the hand with the cigarette in it.

“No. Stop there.”

“But...”

“Whatever comes next, don’t tell me.” Her voice had gone quiet. “If you tell me, I have to do something about it. I’m your supervisor, I sit on your examination, and there are forms. Do you understand what I’m saying to you?”

Yu Jie looked at her. Then she nodded slowly.

“He doesn’t supervise me,” she said. “He doesn’t teach me. He’s never marked anything of mine.”

“Good. Keep it that way.” Professor Ruan picked up her coffee again. “I’ve known him since he was eighteen, you know. I taught him first-year mechanics. He sat in the front row with a notebook and never laughed at a single one of my jokes, and I’m very funny. Something had happened to that boy before he ever got to us. I never found out what.” She looked out at the hill. “He’s lonely, Yu Jie. He’s been lonely for as long as I’ve known him. Be careful with him.”

Yu Jie hadn’t expected that. She didn’t know what to say to it.

“And the twenty pages?” she said at last.

“Monday. Nine.”

“Professor...”

“Twenty.” The corner of Professor Ruan’s mouth moved. “You’re very welcome to complain once you’ve written them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past nine Professor Ruan came down to the fourth floor.

Ling Hao was in the corridor outside 413 with a croissant, reading his phone. He saw her coming and straightened like a schoolboy.

“Professor Ruan.”

“Dr. Ling. Is he in?”

“He is.”

“Alone?”

Ling Hao looked at the croissant. “At the moment.”

“Good.” She went past him and opened the door of 412 without knocking. Ling Hao watched it close behind her, and then he looked up at the ceiling and said, “Oh dear,” to nobody.

Miles was reading. He looked up, saw who it was, and put the paper down.

She shut the door and stood in front of his desk. She didn’t sit.

“Shen Ruolan rang me on Monday night,” she said.

He went still.

“Ruolan was four years below me at school. A convent on the hill, forty-odd years ago, very bad food. We still have lunch twice a year. Ruolan asked me why her daughter’s never at home on Wednesday evenings, and why she comes back on Wednesdays looking, I quote, like a girl who’s been given something.” Professor Ruan took her glasses off her head and folded them. “I told her my group has a Wednesday afternoon meeting and Yu Jie’s been running simulations in my lab until seven. I’ve never lied to Ruolan in my life, Miles. I didn’t enjoy it.”

“You didn’t have to.”

“No. I didn’t.” She looked at him. “She told me about your graph.”

He didn’t answer.

“And the date. June the twentieth.” She put her glasses down on his desk. “I’m not going to ask you what’s happened since. I’ve asked her not to tell me, and I’m asking you the same. But I want you to hear me, because I’m only going to say it once. That girl’s thesis is three weeks behind and she’s the best student I’ve had in twenty years, and if anything about this costs her one mark, one reference, one line on one form, I’ll never forgive you.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“I don’t teach her. I don’t supervise her. I’ve never seen a word of her work that she didn’t put in front of me herself.”

“That’s not what I’m asking.” Professor Ruan was quiet for a moment. When she spoke again her voice had changed. “You’ve been alone for a very long time. You have your research and your students and that dreadful office and Ling Hao, God help you. I’ve watched you since you were eighteen. You’ve never once let anyone in, and now somebody’s got in, and I’m glad. I am. But you can’t let the fact that someone’s made you happy become a reason to stop thinking.”

He looked down at his desk.

“You weren’t always this careful,” she said. “When you were younger.”

His head came up.

She looked as though she wished she hadn’t said it. She picked her glasses up again. “Never mind. The revised research allocations are in your pigeonhole. I want your comments by next Wednesday.”

“You’ll have them.”

At the door she stopped with her hand on the handle.

“Miles. She’s put an end date on your graph. Don’t make her stand there waiting while you decide whether she’s worth choosing.”

She went. Ling Hao was still in the corridor, croissant untouched.

“Everything all right, Professor?”

“That depends,” said Professor Ruan, “on whether either of you has ever had any common sense.”

Ling Hao thought about it. “I wouldn’t bet on it.”

She walked off. He waited until she’d gone round the corner, and then he slipped into 412 and shut the door.

“How bad?”

“She knows,” said Miles.

“Knows what?”

Miles looked at him.

“Oh,” said Ling Hao. “Oh, Wei.”

“She lied to Yu Jie’s mother for us. On Monday. She was at school with her.”

Ling Hao sat down on the edge of the desk. For once he didn’t make a joke. He tore the end off his croissant and held it out, and after a moment Miles took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening Miles went to the library.

He hadn’t been inside it for months. His own field was the quantum mechanics of small systems that didn’t behave, and he read papers on his laptop at his desk like everyone else. But Yu Jie’s thesis was on strained graphene, and it was next door to his field, not in it, and he’d realised on the walk home last Wednesday that he understood the outline of her work and almost none of its insides.

He found four papers in the basement stacks. One on the pseudomagnetic fields you got when you stretched graphene unevenly, so that the electrons curled about as if a magnet were there when there wasn’t one. One on the states that gathered at the edges of a sheet. One on how bending the lattice bent the bands. And one, the oldest and most battered, on what happened at the boundaries of a finite piece, where the clean mathematics ran into the ragged real edge.

He took them back to his office and read them until midnight, with a pencil, and then read them again.

He told himself he was doing it because her thesis needed to be good. That was true. It was also true that he wanted to know what she spent her nights on. What she found hard. What made her forget what time it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday she came in with a folder under her arm and the look of someone who’d slept at least twice since Thursday.

“Twenty pages,” she said, and put it on the desk. “Twenty-two, actually. She counted them. In front of me.”

“She would.”

Then she saw the stack beside his keyboard, and stopped.

“What are those?”

He turned the top one round so she could read the title. She picked it up. The margins were full of his small upright writing. There were underlinings. On the third page there was a little arrow pointing to an equation, and beside it: her section 2 depends on this.

She turned the pages slowly. She didn’t say anything for a while.

“You read these,” she said.

“Yes.”

“All four?”

“Twice.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to understand your thesis.”

Her face did something he’d remember later, in January, when he was tired and needed to.

“You didn’t have to,” she said.

“I know.” He pulled the spare chair round to his side of the desk. “Come here. Explain your model to me. From the beginning. As if I’m stupid.”

“You’re not stupid.”

“About this I am. Go on.”

So she sat beside him, and she told him.

She told him how stretching the sheet changed the way electrons hopped from one carbon atom to the next, and how if you stretched it unevenly the change worked like a magnetic field that wasn’t there, and how near the edges of the sheet the electrons collected in states that depended on exactly how the edge was cut. He asked about zigzag edges and armchair edges. He asked what happened when the strain wasn’t smooth. He asked why she’d chosen one approximation over another, and she had to stop and think, and then she answered, and then she said, “Actually, no, wait,” and gave him a better answer.

She’d stopped being nervous after about five minutes. Her hands moved as she talked. She pushed her hair behind her ear and it fell forward again, and she leaned across him to point at a diagram, her shoulder against his arm, talking fast.

“The thing is, the edge states aren’t only a consequence of the strain. The edge itself matters. If you change how it’s terminated, the whole spectrum shifts, so I think the discussion in section two has to...”

He touched her wrist.

She stopped.

He kissed her. In the middle of the sentence, in the middle of the boundary conditions, with her finger still on the diagram. It was soft and unhurried, and it went on long enough that her hand left the paper and found his collar.

When he drew back she blinked at him. Her cheeks had gone pink.

“What was that for?”

“You were explaining.”

“I was explaining.”

“You were doing very well.”

“That makes no sense at all.”

“It does to me.” He picked up the paper she’d dropped. “Go on.”

She opened her mouth. She closed it again.

“I’ve forgotten what I was saying.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

“Stop kissing me in the middle of my explanations.”

“Would that help?”

“Probably.”

“Then I’ll try.”

“That’s not a promise.”

“No,” said Miles. “It isn’t.”

She laughed, and pulled the paper back, and started again from the edges.

✦ ✦ ✦

By five the afternoon had gone cold. The window was open a crack, the way he always kept it, and the wind coming through it had an edge of the hill on it. She was rubbing her hands together without noticing she was doing it.

“You’re cold.”

“A bit.”

“Why didn’t you bring a proper coat?”

“It was warm at lunchtime.”

He got up and shut the window. Then he looked at her cardigan, which was cream and thin and hanging open over her white shirt, and came round the desk.

“May I?”

“May you what?”

He took hold of the edges of the cardigan. “Button it.”

She looked down at herself, and then up at him, and a slow smile came over her face. “Yes.”

He did up the bottom button first. Then the next. He did it carefully, the way he did everything, his knuckles brushing the cloth and not her, working upwards, and she sat still and watched his face while he did it. When he got to the top button, under her chin, his fingers touched her throat for a second, and her breath caught.

He straightened the collar.

“Now I look like somebody’s grandmother,” she said.

“You look warm.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“It’s more important.”

“You’ve done me up like a parcel.”

“A very cold parcel.” He touched her cheek with the back of his fingers, once. “Don’t get ill.”

“You’re worried?”

“Yes.”

He said it so fast that her smile went soft at the edges.

She stood up, buttoned to the chin, and gathered her folder. At the door she turned round.

“Miles. Professor Ruan said something to me. On the balcony.”

He waited.

“She said you were lonely.”

He didn’t say anything.

“I don’t think you are any more,” said Yu Jie. “Not on Wednesdays.”

He looked at her, standing in the doorway in her ridiculous buttoned-up cardigan, and he couldn’t find a single thing to say that wasn’t too much.

“No,” he said finally. “Not on Wednesdays.”

She smiled and went.

He sat down. On the edge of his keyboard, where she’d been leaning while she talked, there was a pink note he hadn’t seen her put there.

You’re my favourite boundary condition.

He read it twice. Then he opened the drawer and put it on top of the others, and sat looking at the four papers on his desk until the light went.

chapters.title: A Study Group of One
chapters.desc: She drags him to a Saturday study group, and it goes well until the head of department walks in. Miles runs, then waits fifty-six minutes for her at the bike rack.
chapters.epigraph: “Just look at me first, so I know you’re coming back.”
chapters.content:
On Friday afternoon Yu Jie made a suggestion that Miles distrusted at once.

“Come with me tomorrow.”

He didn’t look up from his paper. “Where?”

“The library café. I’ve got a study group.”

“Then you should go to your study group.”

“I want you to come.”

That made him look up. She was in the chair opposite, chin on her hand, with an expression of total innocence that he had learned meant nothing good.

“Why?”

“Because you’re good at explaining things.”

“You have lecturers.”

“I’ve got several. They’re all boring.” She sat back. “We’re doing entropy. Tao Tao’s got her biochemistry exam on Monday and she’s just found out she doesn’t understand the second law, and Ah Dong and Li Wen have a problem sheet due, and I said I knew someone.”

“I’m not tutoring a café table on a Saturday.”

“There’s coffee.”

“No.”

“Good coffee. And egg sandwiches.”

He paused for a fraction of a second. She saw it.

“Fresh ones,” she said. “From the stall by the gate. With the spring onion.”

“Is this a bribe?”

“It’s an invitation. With sandwiches.”

He put the paper down. “You’ll be discussing your thesis.”

“Probably a little.”

“Then you should be discussing it with Professor Ruan.”

“I know.” She stopped smiling. “Miles. I just want to spend a Saturday with you. In daylight. With other people there. Like a normal person.”

There it was. Not a clever argument. Just what she wanted, said plainly, across his desk.

He looked at her.

“What time?”

Her whole face lit up. “Ten.”

“Until?”

“Whenever.”

“Yu Jie.”

“One?”

“One,” said Miles. “And I’m not teaching. I’m attending. As a guest. And I expect to drink my coffee without solving anybody’s problem sheet.”

“Absolutely.”

At the door she turned round. “Oh, and don’t wear your conference shoes.”

He looked down at them. “Why not?”

“It’s a café, not a viva.”

She went. He sat looking at his shoes, which were black and polished and had been to three continents, and had a feeling Saturday was going to be a great deal less academic than he’d been promised.

✦ ✦ ✦

The library café was full by ten. Yu Jie had taken the big table under the window, where the November light came in low and gold across the notebooks. Tao Tao was arranging her coloured pens in order of the spectrum. Ah Dong, a third-year with a shaved head and a hoodie that said BOSON, was eating a custard tart over his laptop. Li Wen, who did maths and sat in on physics for fun, had a textbook open already and the face of a man who regretted his choices.

Miles came in at six minutes past with two coffees and a paper bag, in a grey jumper and, she noticed at once, trainers.

Her face did something she couldn’t stop. “You came.”

“I said I would.” He put one of the coffees in front of her. “Jasmine latte.”

“You remembered.”

“You order it every time we go past the stall.”

“That’s not the point.”

He put the paper bag down beside it. “Egg sandwiches.”

Tao Tao looked up from her pens. She looked at Miles. She looked at the latte, and the sandwiches, and at Yu Jie’s face, and a slow, enormous smile spread across her own.

“Dr. Wei,” she said. “How lovely. Thank you for coming.”

“Where would you like me?”

“Here,” said Yu Jie, too fast, and moved her bag off the chair beside her.

Tao Tao looked at the chair. “Of course,” she said. “Of course there.”

The plan to drink his coffee quietly lasted about six minutes.

Li Wen asked whether entropy could be explained without the word disorder, because he’d heard it so often he no longer believed it meant anything. Ah Dong disagreed with the question. Tao Tao drew a diagram on the back of her exam timetable that was mostly a box with some dots in it and an arrow labelled chaos?.

Miles looked at it for a while. Then he took a paper napkin out of the dispenser.

“All right,” he said. “Let’s start again.”

He drew a box, and split it down the middle with a line. He put four dots in it.

“Four particles. Each can be in the left half or the right half. Why four?”

“Why four?” said Tao Tao.

“Because eight won’t fit on a napkin.” He wrote underneath. “How many ways can you have all four on the left?”

“One,” said Li Wen.

“How many ways to have two on each side?”

Li Wen counted on his fingers. “Six.”

“So if you shook the box and looked, which would you expect to see?”

“Two and two,” said Ah Dong slowly. “Because there are more ways to get it.”

“That’s entropy.” Miles wrote it at the bottom of the napkin, small and neat.

S = k log W

“W is the number of ways the inside can be arranged and still look the same from outside. S is the logarithm of it, with a constant in front so the units work. It isn’t mess. It’s counting. Things go towards the states with the most ways to be.”

Li Wen looked at the napkin as though it had insulted his family. “That’s all it is?”

“That’s all it is. Everything else is arithmetic.”

“Then why does my room get messier,” said Tao Tao, “when I haven’t touched anything?”

“You’ve probably forgotten what it looked like yesterday.”

Ah Dong choked on his tart.

“Your room has a very large number of possible arrangements,” said Miles, “and most of them involve things you haven’t been able to find for three weeks.”

“That,” said Tao Tao, pointing her pen at him, “was personal.”

“It was an example.”

“Based on my life.”

“An unusually convenient one.”

Even Li Wen smiled.

After that he gave up pretending. He went through to the Boltzmann factor on a second napkin and to free energy on a third, and when Ah Dong got a sign wrong he didn’t correct it, he asked him how he’d got there, and waited while Ah Dong found it himself. When Tao Tao asked something that was really four questions in a coat, he took it apart and answered all four.

Yu Jie sat beside him with her cheek on her hand and watched.

He was different outside his office. Not different. He was still quiet, still careful, still let people finish talking before he answered. But here, with his sleeves pushed up and a café pen in his hand and a smear of custard tart on the cuff of his jumper that Ah Dong had given him, he seemed to fit in his own body more easily. He smiled at Tao Tao’s questions. He laughed, nearly, at something Li Wen said under his breath, and then looked startled at himself.

She liked other people seeing it. She liked it more than she’d expected.

By half past eleven the table was all napkins and empty cups. Tao Tao had moved on to enzymes. Li Wen was quietly copying out the third napkin. Yu Jie was doing a problem from Ah Dong’s sheet for fun, and Miles leaned over without warning and said, “Your sign’s wrong.”

“Where?”

“Second line. You’ve flipped the derivative.”

“I have not.”

He looked at her.

She looked at the second line. “Fine.”

He went back to his coffee.

She fixed the sign, and while he was reading over her shoulder, she moved her foot under the table until it found his.

He kept reading.

She slid it, slowly, up the inside of his ankle, under the hem of his trousers, to the bare skin above his sock.

His pen stopped. He didn’t look at her. His voice, when it came, was perfectly level.

“Next step.”

“What?”

“The next step of your derivation.”

“Oh.” She looked down at the page. She left her foot where it was.

He moved his leg. Not away. A little closer, so his calf pressed against her shin, warm through the cloth, and stayed there.

Yu Jie bit her lip so hard it hurt.

Across the table, Tao Tao looked up from her enzymes. “What’s wrong with you?”

“Nothing.”

“You’ve gone red.”

“It’s hot in here.”

Tao Tao looked at her. Then at Miles, who was reading Ah Dong’s problem sheet with the expression of a man at a funeral. Then back at Yu Jie.

“Oh,” said Tao Tao.

Yu Jie kicked her under the table with the other foot. Tao Tao grinned and went back to her enzymes.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two minutes to twelve, Professor Cen walked in.

He came through the door talking on his phone, in a camel coat, with a folder under his arm, and stopped by the cake counter, and looked round the room the way tall men do, over everybody’s heads.

His eyes found Miles.

Miles saw him at the same moment. For a second neither of them moved.

Professor Cen’s gaze went from Miles to the table. To four undergraduates. To the napkins covered in equations. To Yu Jie, sitting close beside him with her chin on her hand. And back to Miles. A small crease appeared between his eyebrows.

Tao Tao saw Miles’s face change and turned round. Ah Dong looked up. Li Wen turned his whole chair.

Yu Jie was still looking at the problem sheet. She felt his leg leave hers.

“Miles?”

He had already closed his notebook.

“I’ve got a meeting,” he said.

“What?”

He was on his feet. He had his coat. Across the room Professor Cen had finished his call, and said, “Wei?” in his deep calm voice, and Miles said, “Professor. I’m just leaving. Something’s come up,” and Professor Cen said, “I see,” and Miles went past him and out of the door into the cold, and didn’t look back at the table once.

There was no meeting. There had never been a meeting.

The door swung shut.

For a few seconds nobody at the table said anything.

“Was that a meeting?” said Ah Dong.

“No,” said Li Wen.

Yu Jie looked at the door. His coffee was still on the table, half drunk. Beside it, in the paper bag, was the sandwich he’d bought for himself and hadn’t touched.

✦ ✦ ✦

She finished the study group, because she’d organised it. She went through two more problems with Ah Dong and helped Tao Tao with an enzyme she didn’t understand either. She thanked everybody. She put the napkins in her bag, all of them, without thinking about why.

She wasn’t angry. She understood. She knew exactly what the head of department might have thought, seeing that table. She knew how easily one look could become a story.

She just hadn’t thought he’d go without looking at her.

“Do you want me to come with you?” Tao Tao said, outside the café.

“I’m fine.”

“He panicked.”

“I know.”

“He’s not very good at being surprised.”

“I know that too.”

Tao Tao squeezed her hand. “Text me when you’re home.”

It was six minutes to one. The wind had turned since the morning and came round the corner of the library with a bite in it, and she pulled her cardigan tight and walked to the bicycle racks, and stopped.

He was standing at the far end of the row, beside a black bicycle with a basket on the front, holding a paper bag.

His coat was done up to the neck. His hair was standing on end, the way it did when he’d pushed his hands through it too often. His face was pale with cold.

She walked over to him.

“You waited.”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

He looked at his watch. “Fifty-six minutes.”

“Miles. It’s freezing.”

“I didn’t know when you’d finish.”

“You could have gone home.”

“I could have.”

She looked at the bag in his hand. He held it out.

“You didn’t eat,” he said.

It was an egg sandwich, from the stall by the gate, with the spring onion. It was still warm. He’d gone back and bought another one, she realised, at some point in the fifty-six minutes, and stood holding it inside his coat to keep it warm.

She took it. Her fingers touched his, and his were like ice.

“You left without saying anything,” she said.

“I know.”

“You didn’t even look at me.”

He looked down. “I know.”

“That was horrible.”

“I’m sorry.”

He didn’t make it sound better than it was, or turn it into something noble. He just stood there by his bicycle with his hair on end and said he was sorry, and she could see on his face that he’d spent the whole fifty-six minutes saying worse things to himself.

“Was it Professor Cen?”

“Yes.”

“Did he say anything?”

“No.”

“Then why did you run?”

He was quiet. The wind went between them.

“Because I panicked,” he said. “I saw him and I thought about your examination, and the panel, and what that table looked like, and what he’d remember in May when your name came up. I thought about all of it at once. And I ran.”

“And invented a meeting.”

“Yes.”

“On a Saturday.”

“I wasn’t thinking clearly.”

She looked at him. She’d meant to stay cross for longer. She found she couldn’t.

“You’re a terrible liar,” she said, and started laughing, helplessly, with the sandwich in one hand.

“I’ve been told.”

“Something’s come up.”

“I know.”

“You said it like a man in a film. A bad film.”

“Yu Jie.”

She stopped laughing. “I wasn’t angry. I was a bit upset.”

“You were allowed to be.”

“I know why you did it.” She held the sandwich against her chest. “Next time, just look at me. You can run if you have to. Just look at me first, so I know you’re coming back.”

“I can do that.”

“And don’t invent meetings.”

“I’ll try.”

“That’s not a promise.”

“No,” said Miles.

She shook her head. The bicycle was between them, his hand on the handlebar.

“Are you cold?” he said.

“You’re the one who’s been standing out here for an hour.”

He looked round once. The racks were empty, and the courtyard beyond them was empty, and the light had gone thin and white.

“May I?”

She nodded.

He leaned over the handlebars and kissed her.

He’d meant it to be quick. It wasn’t. His mouth was cold and then it wasn’t, and his free hand found her waist inside her cardigan and pulled her against the bicycle so the basket dug into her hip, and she dropped the sandwich into it and got both hands in the front of his coat and kissed him back, hard, the way she’d wanted to all morning with her foot on his ankle. The bicycle tipped. He caught it with his knee without letting go of her. She made a small sound into his mouth and felt him shudder.

When he finally lifted his head they were both breathing fast, and his glasses had fogged.

“That,” said Yu Jie, “was a very inconvenient angle.”

“Yes.”

“You could have moved the bicycle.”

“I didn’t think of it.”

“You’re supposed to be good at problems.”

“Not all of them.”

She leaned her forehead on his shoulder, and he put his hand on the back of her head and held it there, and they stood like that by the bike racks until a delivery van turned into the service road and they stepped apart.

He fished the sandwich out of the basket and gave it back to her.

“Eat it before it gets cold.”

“You waited fifty-six minutes with an egg sandwich.”

“Yes.”

“That’s almost romantic.”

“Almost?”

She took a bite. “You forgot the coffee.”

He reached into his coat pocket and took out a small takeaway cup, with a lid, and gave it to her.

She stared at it. “You bought another latte.”

“The first one went cold.”

“Miles.”

“Hm.”

“You’re very bad,” said Yu Jie, with her mouth full, “at pretending you’re not mad about me.”

He held the bicycle steady while she ate, and didn’t answer, and didn’t need to.

chapters.title: Miles Gets Sick and Nobody Notices
chapters.desc: Miles is sick and nobody notices except Yu Jie, who turns up with soup, a thermometer and oranges, and meets his sister on speakerphone.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re allowed to need someone, you know.”
chapters.content:
On the last Wednesday of November, the second-years arrived at Lecture Theatre C to find a sheet of paper taped to the door.

Dr. Wei’s lecture is cancelled today due to illness.

At half past eight Ling Hao got a text.

Miles: Sick. Don’t come round.

Ling Hao read it by the coffee machine. He wrote back How sick? and got no answer, and rang and got no answer, and shrugged and went into his group meeting. Miles Wei didn’t make a fuss about being ill. He’d be asleep. Everyone assumed so.

Nobody thought much about it, except Yu Jie.

Yu Jie: Are you in today?

That was at a quarter to nine. At ten past, she heard about the lecture from Ah Dong.

Yu Jie: Your lecture’s cancelled. Are you all right?

Yu Jie: Miles?

Yu Jie: Are you asleep?

Yu Jie: I can bring you something if you’re ill.

Yu Jie: You don’t have to answer properly. Just send me a full stop.

At twenty past ten she rang him. It rang out.

He left his phone face down for whole afternoons. But he always answered her, even if it was only Working or Later.

Yu Jie: I’m getting worried.

By eleven she’d stopped pretending to read.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ling Hao found her just before twelve, standing by the noticeboard outside the physics building with her phone in her hand, looking at the same screen she’d been looking at for an hour.

“Yu Jie?”

“Dr. Ling. Have you heard from him?”

“He texted me this morning. Said he was ill and not to come round.”

“Has he answered you since?”

He checked. “No.”

“He’s not answering me either.” She turned the phone round without meaning to and he saw the column of grey bubbles, all hers. There were nine of them.

He looked at her face for a moment. In nine years he’d never known Miles not answer something that mattered.

“He’s probably asleep,” said Ling Hao.

“What if he isn’t?”

“Then he’s being stubborn.”

She pressed her lips together and didn’t say anything, and he sighed and took out his phone and typed, and turned the screen round.

“That’s his flat. Staff block on the north side, behind the sports hall. Third floor.”

She stared at it. “He said no visitors.”

“He did.” Ling Hao put the phone away. “Check he’s all right. If he tells you to go, you can decide what to do about that once you’ve seen his face. And don’t panic before you know anything.”

“I’ll try.”

“If he gives you any trouble, tell him I sent you.”

“Will that help?”

“Not even slightly,” said Ling Hao.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stopped on the way for plain congee in a foil tub, a bag of oranges, a thermometer and two bottles of water.

The staff flats were a low grey block with a row of bicycles outside, his black one with the basket among them. She found the door at twenty to one and knocked.

Nothing.

She checked the number. She knocked again.

“Miles?”

Nothing. Then, a long time later, slow footsteps, and a chain, and the door opened.

He was in a dark jumper and old tracksuit trousers. He didn’t have his glasses on. His hair was flat on one side and standing up on the other, and his face had gone a strange colour, grey everywhere except two hot red patches high on his cheekbones. He looked at her for a moment as though he couldn’t work out what she was.

“Yu Jie?”

“Oh my God.”

“Hello.”

“You’re ill.”

“Yes.”

“You’re really ill.”

“Apparently.” He stepped back to let her in, and put one hand on the wall to do it, and she saw that he needed it there.

The flat was dim and smelt of cold tea. There was a glass of water on the coffee table, still full, and his laptop open on the little dining table with a journal article on the screen.

She looked at it. “Are you working?”

“Reading.”

“You’ve got a fever.”

“I’d noticed.”

She put the bags down and put the backs of her fingers against his forehead, the way her grandmother used to, and nearly took her hand away again. He was burning.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“I cancelled my lecture.”

“That isn’t telling me.”

“I thought you’d be in class.”

“I’ve got a phone, Miles.”

He didn’t argue. That frightened her more than anything else had.

“Sit down,” she said.

“I’m all right.”

“You’re going to sit down.”

Something like a smile went over his face. “Very authoritative.”

“Somebody has to be.”

She got him onto the sofa. She found the thermometer in the bag and tore the packet with her teeth.

“Have you taken anything?”

“Paracetamol.”

“When?”

He thought about it, which took too long. “Eight. Perhaps.”

“Perhaps?”

“I didn’t look.”

“Open your mouth.”

He looked at the thermometer and then at her.

“Please,” she said.

He opened it. She held the thermometer under his tongue and watched the little screen and counted in her head, and when it beeped she looked down at it and forgot how to breathe.

39.1

“What?” he said.

She turned it round so he could see. He squinted at it.

“That’s quite high.”

“Quite high?”

His eyes weren’t focusing properly. His breathing was heavier than it should be and every movement he made seemed to take him a second to start. She thought of him alone in here since last night. Getting up to take tablets and not remembering when. Sitting at that table trying to read. Telling himself he was fine. What if he’d fallen? What if he’d hit his head on the corner of that table and lain on the floor, with his phone face down on the other side of the room, and nobody had come because he’d told them not to?

Her hands had started to shake. She put the thermometer down so he wouldn’t see.

He saw.

“Yu Jie.”

“Have you eaten anything?”

“Not really.”

“Water?”

He looked at the full glass on the coffee table. She followed his eyes, and shut her own for a second.

“Right,” she said, and her voice came out steadier than she was. “I’m getting you water. Then I’m ringing the health centre. If your temperature doesn’t come down, or you get confused, or you can’t breathe properly, or you can’t keep anything down, you’re seeing a doctor today. I’m not going to guess.”

“I’m not that bad.”

She looked at him.

He stopped. “All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His kitchen was spotless. It was spotless the way rooms are when nobody uses them. The fridge had a bottle of water, half a carton of milk, two eggs and a jar of something with no label, and that was all.

“Miles?” she called. “Have you got any food?”

A pause. “Some.”

“Where?”

A longer pause. “You’re looking at it.”

She shut the fridge. For now she warmed the congee in his one saucepan, peeled an orange and cut it into pieces, and carried both in on a plate.

He’d let his head fall back against the sofa. His eyes were shut.

“Eat a bit.”

He ate some, slowly, with a spoon that wavered. She gave him a piece of orange.

“Vitamin C?”

“Fruit.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the one you’re getting.”

He managed about half. She didn’t make him finish it. She sat beside him with her phone and rang the health centre, and told the nurse the reading and the time, and what he’d taken and when, roughly, and the nurse asked her some questions about his breathing and whether he’d been sick and whether his neck was stiff, and Yu Jie asked him, and he said no, and the nurse said a doctor would ring back within the hour and in the meantime fluids, rest, and the next dose at two, not before.

He protested once, about the doctor. Only once. She looked at him, and he stopped.

“You didn’t have to come,” he said, when she’d put the phone down.

“Don’t.”

“I only mean...”

“I know what you mean.” She took his hand. It was hot and dry, like something left in the sun. “I sent you nine messages, Miles. I thought something had happened to you.”

His face changed.

“I know you hate fuss,” she said. “I know you’d rather sort it out on your own and tell everyone afterwards. But you can’t just disappear when you’re ill. Not on me.”

He looked at their hands.

“I’m sorry.”

“You don’t have to be sorry for getting ill.” She rubbed her thumb over his knuckles. “You have to tell me. That’s all.”

“I’ll tell you.”

“Promise.”

“I promise.”

She leaned over and kissed his forehead, and his eyes closed.

When she drew back he was looking at her again, close up, without his glasses, and his eyes were dark and too bright and he didn’t seem to be careful about anything.

“Come here,” he said.

“I’m here.”

He put his hand on the back of her neck and pulled her down and kissed her.

It wasn’t like him. There was nothing measured in it, no question first. His mouth was hot and his hand was hot and he kissed her slowly and deeply, as if there was nothing else he had to do and nowhere he had to be. She made a small, startled sound, and then she took two handfuls of his jumper and kissed him back harder, kneeling up on the sofa, pushing him down into the cushions. For a minute the dim flat and the full glass of water and the number on the thermometer disappeared entirely.

Then she pulled away and pressed her forehead against his.

“You’re burning.”

“Still?”

“You’re like a stove.”

“That’s unfortunate,” he said, and something came out of him that was almost a laugh and turned into a cough, and she got him the water and made him drink it all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The phone on the coffee table rang at seven minutes to two.

He looked at it. “Could you...”

The screen said Lan.

“Your sister?”

He nodded.

“Should I answer?”

“Please.”

She put it on speaker. “Hello?”

There was a short silence. Then a woman’s voice, crisp and wary. “Hello? Who’s this? Where’s Miles?”

Yu Jie looked at him. He’d shut his eyes, in the manner of a man who could see what was coming and had decided not to watch.

“He’s here,” she said. “I’m a student from his department. I’m bringing him some soup.”

A pause.

“A student.”

“Yes.”

“At his flat.”

Yu Jie looked at Miles. He looked back at her, and the faintest gleam of something went through the fever.

“Yes,” she said firmly.

“Is he all right?”

“Thirty-nine point one at twenty to one. Paracetamol at about eight, the next due at two. A doctor’s ringing back. He’s eaten a bit.”

There was a different sort of silence on the line. When Wei Lan spoke again her voice had sharpened in a way Yu Jie recognised, because she’d heard nurses do it at her grandmother’s bedside.

“Put him on.”

She handed him the phone.

“Lan.”

“What have you done to yourself?”

“Nothing.”

“Don’t say nothing to me. You sound like a drain.”

“I’m fine.”

“You are not fine. A student is bringing you soup because you can’t look after yourself.”

He glanced at Yu Jie. “She’s being kind.”

“Of course she is. Someone has to.” Yu Jie had to put her hand over her mouth. “Have you been drinking water?”

He looked at the glass. Yu Jie looked at him.

“Yes,” said Miles.

“I know you,” said his sister. “Miles. Put me back on to the student.”

Yu Jie took the phone. “Hello.”

“What’s your name, sweetheart?”

“Shen Yu Jie.”

“Yu Jie. I’m his older sister, and I’m a children’s nurse, and he’s worse than any of my patients.” Her voice softened. “Give me your number, would you? So I can ask you how he is. He lies.”

“I heard that,” said Miles.

“Good,” said Wei Lan. “At least you’re conscious.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The doctor rang at twenty past two and said it sounded like flu. If his breathing changed, or the fever went over forty, they were to ring again at once.

The afternoon went slowly after that.

She gave him the second dose at two exactly and wrote the time on the back of an envelope. Every time he asked about the department she told him it would survive one afternoon.

At some point his hand moved across the cushion until it found hers, and his fingers closed round two of hers and stayed there.

“Miles?”

He didn’t answer. His breathing had slowed. His thumb moved once against her knuckle, and then he was asleep.

Once she tried to get up, and his grip tightened in his sleep, not enough to stop her. Just enough. She sat back down.

Without his glasses he looked younger. He looked less like Dr. Wei and more like a boy who’d sat in the front row of a first-year lecture and never laughed at anything.

“You’re allowed to need someone, you know,” she said quietly.

He didn’t wake.

By half past four his temperature had come down to thirty-eight and a half. She wrote that on the envelope too. When he woke for a minute and saw her writing he said, hoarse, “You’re keeping records.”

“Yes.”

“Like an experiment.”

“You’re the most inconvenient experiment I’ve ever run.”

“That’s reassuring,” he said, and went back to sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed until he was properly asleep, which was three hours after she’d arrived.

Then she went into his kitchen and washed the bowl and the spoon and the saucepan. She took the rest of the oranges out of the bag, five of them, and peeled them all. She took off the white pith, every thread of it, the way her grandmother had done for her when she had chicken pox, and split them into segments and laid them in a clean box in neat rows, and put the box on the middle shelf of the fridge with a bottle of water beside it.

She took a pink note out of her pocket.

Eat these. Don’t argue. They’re already peeled.

She stuck it on the lid. Then she added underneath, smaller, And drink the water. ALL of it.

In the living room he’d turned on his side. She bent and kissed his temple.

“I’m going. I’ll text you tonight.”

His eyes opened a little. “Going?”

“You need to sleep.”

He frowned. His hand came out from under the blanket she’d put over him, and she gave him hers, and he held it.

“I’m glad you came,” he said.

She kissed his forehead one more time and let herself out, quietly, and stood on the concrete walkway outside his door for a minute with her eyes shut, and let her hands shake as much as they liked.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes past seven her phone lit up.

Lan: Hello Yu Jie. How is he?

Yu Jie: 38.5 at half four. He’s asleep. The doctor says flu.

Lan: Thank god. Thank you for staying.

Yu Jie: It was no trouble. I left the congee in the fridge, and some oranges. Peeled. He hasn’t got any food.

There was a pause.

Lan: You peeled them?

Yu Jie: He doesn’t have anything in his fridge except two eggs and a mystery jar.

A longer pause.

Lan: Marry her.

Yu Jie stared at it.

Yu Jie: I think that was meant for him.

Lan: It was meant for both of you. I’ve sent it to him as well.

Lan: I’m serious, by the way.

Yu Jie laughed out loud on her own bed. Tao Tao, across the hall, shouted “What?”

Yu Jie: I think you should let him recover first.

Lan: Fair. But I’m keeping my opinion. And don’t let him work tomorrow. He’ll pretend he’s well the second it drops a degree.

Yu Jie: I won’t.

Lan: Thank you, sweetheart. Goodnight.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eight Miles woke on the sofa under a blanket he didn’t remember having.

There was an envelope beside him with times and numbers on it in her neat hand. His phone had a message from his sister that said only MARRY HER, and nine from Not Stuck, from that morning, which he read one after another with his chest getting tighter, and then a tenth.

Not Stuck: Your sister has very strong opinions.

He went to the kitchen and opened the fridge, and stopped.

On the middle shelf was a box of orange segments, lined up in rows like soldiers, with every scrap of white taken off. A pink note was stuck to the lid.

He stood there in the cold light of the fridge.

Then he took one segment out and ate it. It was sweet. He ate another, standing up, in his socks, and then he picked up his phone.

Miles: You peeled all of them.

Not Stuck: Yes.

Miles: That’s a lot of oranges.

Not Stuck: It took ten minutes. Don’t make a thing of it.

Miles: I’m going to make a thing of it.

Not Stuck: Go back to bed. I mean it.

He looked at the box of oranges, and the note, and the bottle of water beside it, and his empty spotless kitchen, which for the first time since he’d moved in looked as if somebody lived there.

Miles: Thank you.

Not Stuck: You don’t have to thank me for every little thing.

Miles: I know. I want to.

chapters.title: He Laughs in a Seminar
chapters.desc: Yu Jie takes apart a visiting professor’s slide in the seminar, and Miles laughs out loud for the first time in fourteen years. Then an invitation arrives with her family’s crest on it.
chapters.content:
By December, Miles’s fridge had food in it, and none of it was his doing.

Yu Jie had started bringing things. At first it was congee and soup, while he was getting better. Then it was fruit, and leftovers from Sunday dinners at her mother’s house that she smuggled out in her bag, and then, on the first Wednesday of December, four plastic boxes stacked in a cloth bag that she put down on his desk with a thump.

“What’s that?”

“Dinner.”

“I’ve eaten.”

“What did you eat?”

He thought about it for too long.

“Exactly,” said Yu Jie.

Steamed egg. Greens with garlic. Braised tofu. Chicken with ginger and spring onion, which she’d made because the woman at the market had told her it was good for men who’d had flu and didn’t look after themselves, and she’d said how did you know, and the woman had said they never do.

“You made all of these?”

“Yesterday.”

“You didn’t have to.”

She gave him the look he’d given her when she’d tried to get up off the sofa with a temperature. “Somebody has to make sure you eat.”

“You’ve become very authoritative.”

“I learned from someone.” She leaned over the desk and kissed his cheek. “Put them in the fridge. Not that fridge. The one at your flat. Tonight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The Monday after, she caught a cold.

It started with a scratchy throat at breakfast and by lunch she’d sneezed so often that Tao Tao told her to stay away from the department before she wiped out a whole year group. Yu Jie told her to mind her own business, and sneezed.

By Wednesday she was in office 412 with a tissue in one hand and her notebook in the other.

“You’re ill,” he said.

“It’s a cold.”

“You’ve said that three times.”

“Because it’s true.”

“Have you taken anything?”

“I forgot.”

He shut his laptop and got up and went out without a word, and came back ten minutes later from the department kitchen with a mug of ginger tea so strong she could smell it from the door. He’d grated the ginger himself. There was a little brown stain on his thumb.

She took a sip and made a face.

“Too much?”

“No.”

“You look unconvinced.”

“It’s good. It’s aggressive. But it’s good.” She held the mug in both hands and looked at him over it. “You’re looking after me.”

“You’re ill.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the one I have.”

She finished the tea. She did a problem set, which was a terrible idea, and he let her. At five he was at the board rubbing out the last of the afternoon, and when he turned round she’d moved from the chair to the edge of his desk, and was sitting on it with her feet swinging.

“Come here,” she said.

“You’re supposed to be resting.”

“I am resting.”

“You’re sitting on my referee reports.”

“They’re very comfortable.” She caught the front of his turtleneck and pulled him in between her knees. He glanced at the door. It was shut. “Yu Jie. You’ve got a cold.”

“I know.”

“You’ll give it to me.”

“You’ve only just stopped having flu. You’re immune. Probably. I don’t know. I’m a physicist.”

She kissed him. Her nose was cold and her mouth was hot and tasted of ginger, and he put his hands on the desk on either side of her and let her. She took her time. When he tried to draw back, to say something sensible, she smiled against his mouth and pulled him in again by the collar, and he stopped trying, and his hands left the desk and found her waist and slid round to the small of her back and held her there, and the referee reports slid off onto the floor one at a time.

When she finally let him go she rubbed her nose against his.

“All right,” she said. “Now I’ll go home.”

“Good.”

“Eat the chicken.”

“I will.”

“And drink water. And don’t read papers till midnight.”

He looked at her.

“Miles.”

“I’ll stop at eleven.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The seminar was on Friday at ten.

The speaker was a Dr. Mao from a big research institute in the north, who worked on the electronic structure of two-dimensional materials and had been cited, as Ling Hao put it, by everybody who’d ever been cited. His title was Electronic Structure and Boundary Effects in Deformed Two-Dimensional Lattices. It was so nearly Yu Jie’s thesis that she’d had it in her diary for a month.

She sat in the third row with Tao Tao, who’d come because she’d been promised there would be biscuits. Miles was at the front with Professor Cen and Ling Hao. When he turned round to look at the room his eyes found her and rested for half a second, and she smiled, and he nodded, and that was all. They’d got good at that.

“You’re going to ask a question,” whispered Tao Tao. “I can feel it.”

“Maybe.”

“Please don’t.”

“Why not?”

“Because last time you asked a question in public, a hundred and forty people turned round.”

Dr. Mao was good. His slides were clean and his diagrams were beautiful and he talked about his numbers with the ease of a man who’d given this talk at eight conferences. Yu Jie took notes. She was impressed, and then she got to slide nineteen and stopped writing.

The slide showed how electrons gathered at the edge of a stretched sheet of graphene. The equation used the boundary condition for one kind of edge, the zigzag kind. The picture beside it, on the same slide, showed the other kind, armchair, with its little paired bumps along the border like teeth.

She looked at the equation. Then at the picture. She flicked back a page in her notes, and forward.

It wasn’t notation. The kind of edge decided which states were allowed in the first place. You couldn’t take the zigzag answer and put it under an armchair picture and call it evidence.

She put her hand up.

The room went quiet. Dr. Mao looked up from his laptop and smiled.

“Yes?”

She stood up. “Thank you, Dr. Mao. I wanted to ask about slide nineteen. The boundary condition in the derivation is the zigzag one, but the figure’s an armchair edge. Is that on purpose?”

He glanced at the screen behind him. “Yes. The distinction isn’t especially important for this approximation.”

“Wouldn’t it change the edge spectrum?”

“Not qualitatively.”

“But the allowed states are different,” said Yu Jie. “If the model uses the zigzag condition, the localisation result doesn’t carry over to the armchair geometry. It’s a different system.”

People shifted in their seats. Dr. Mao’s smile stayed exactly where it was, the way smiles do when the person wearing them has decided they’re being patient.

“That’s a fair observation. But I think you’re focusing too much on the edge details. The main result is the strain effect.”

“I understand. But the figure’s being shown as evidence for localisation in the armchair case,” said Yu Jie, quite pleasantly. “If that isn’t the calculation that’s been done, then perhaps the slide should say so.”

At the front of the room, Miles laughed.

He didn’t mean to. It came up out of him before he could do anything about it, out loud, helpless, the kind of laugh that takes your whole chest with it. It wasn’t the short embarrassed breath he’d let out five years ago in a hotel ballroom when his clicker hit the floor in front of his old school. That one had been at himself. This was something he hadn’t heard come out of his own mouth since he was seventeen, and it went on for a good three seconds in total silence, and a hundred people turned and looked at him.

He put his hand over his mouth.

“I’m sorry,” he said, through it. He took his hand away. He was still smiling, and couldn’t stop. “I’m sorry, Dr. Mao. But she’s right.”

Beside him, Ling Hao had gone completely still, with a biscuit halfway to his mouth.

“The kind of edge isn’t incidental here,” said Miles, and his voice was steady again, mostly. “It decides the spectrum. If the analytical result is being used to support the numerical one, they have to describe the same edge. Could you tell us which boundary condition the numerical calculation actually uses?”

There was a long pause.

“The numerical calculation uses the armchair geometry,” said Dr. Mao. “The analytical expression is a simplified reference.”

“Then the slide should separate them,” said Miles. “As it is, the comparison’s misleading.”

Dr. Mao looked at slide nineteen for a while. “Yes,” he said. “I can see how it might be unclear.”

Yu Jie sat down.

“You did it,” Tao Tao whispered. “You actually took apart slide nineteen.”

But Yu Jie wasn’t listening. She was looking at the front row, at the back of Miles’s head, at the tips of his ears, which had gone red. He’d laughed. Out loud, in front of everybody, at something she’d said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards the room filled up with people trying to get to the speaker, and to the biscuits. Dr. Mao found Miles at the front.

“Dr. Wei. Your student raised an interesting point.”

“She isn’t my student,” said Miles. “She’s Professor Ruan’s.”

“Ah. She has a sharp eye.”

“She does.”

“I’ll revise the slide before the next meeting,” said Dr. Mao, with a little less ease than before, and went off to lunch with Professor Cen.

As the two of them went past the third row, Miles looked down at her.

“Good question,” he said. Only that. She smiled for the rest of the morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ling Hao followed him back up to the fourth floor and shut the door of 412 behind them both.

“Wei.”

“Don’t.”

“Wei. You laughed.”

“I’m aware.”

“Out loud. In a seminar. With your whole face. I’ve known you nine years and I’ve never heard that noise. I didn’t know you could make it.” Ling Hao sat down heavily in the spare chair. “Professor Ruan was in the back row. She dropped her pen.”

Miles took his glasses off and rubbed his eyes.

“You didn’t even hesitate,” said Ling Hao, more quietly. “With Mao. He’s senior to you, and that paper’s under review at the journal you referee for.”

“That doesn’t make the calculation right.”

“If it comes to you?”

“Then I’ll recommend they reject it.” Miles put his glasses back on. “It isn’t cosmetic. The central conclusion depends on the edge. You can’t fix it by changing a slide. I’ll say exactly why in the report.”

“Good.” Ling Hao looked at him for a while. “You were proud of her.”

“She asked a good question.”

“That isn’t what I said.”

“I know,” said Miles.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three he sent her a message.

Miles: Are you free?

Not Stuck: For you? Maybe.

Miles: Fire door. Fourth floor. End of the corridor.

She came up the back stairs two at a time. He was waiting on the landing, the same landing as in October, and when she came round the turn he was leaning against the rail with his hands in his pockets, and there was something in his face she’d never seen in it before. It was bright. He looked like a boy who’d got away with something.

“What’s happened?”

“I laughed,” he said.

“I know. I was there. Everybody was there.”

“Properly.”

“I know.” She stopped two steps below him, the way she had in October. “How long?”

He knew what she meant. He looked at the rail.

“Since I was seventeen. Fourteen years.”

She’d heard Professor Ruan say it, almost. She hadn’t heard him say it.

“Do you remember the last time? Before today?”

“Yes,” said Miles. “But not today.”

She didn’t push. She came up the two steps and took his hand.

“I’m glad it was me,” she said.

He took his other hand out of his pocket and put it round her waist and kissed her.

She made a small sound of surprise, and then her back was against the wall of the stairwell and his hand was flat on the wall beside her head and he was kissing her as if he’d been holding his breath since the seminar. He was smiling. She could feel it against her mouth, and it undid her completely. She got her fingers into his hair and held on. When he finally lifted his head he rested his forehead on hers, breathing hard.

“Thank you,” he said.

“For what?”

“Making me laugh.”

“Do it again.”

“I can’t do it on purpose.”

“Try.”

He looked at her, and then he did, a little, quietly, against her temple.

“See?” said Yu Jie.

Footsteps went past on the other side of the fire door. They stood still with their foreheads together until they’d gone.

“One day,” she said, “I’m going to kiss you in the middle of the corridor.”

“That would be inconvenient.”

“Very,” she said happily.

✦ ✦ ✦

The envelope was in his pigeonhole at five.

It was thick and cream and the size of a hardback book, and his name was on the front in green ink, by hand: Dr. Miles Wei. On the back, pressed into the paper, was a crest: a tree in a circle, with its roots and branches meeting at the rim.

He knew it. The Shen Foundation’s crest was on the brass plaque at the door of the physics building, on four of the department’s scholarships, on the new wing of the library, and on the back page of every annual report the university had published in his lifetime.

He’d been sent invitations to things like this before. They usually went straight into the department’s general tray. This one had his name on it.

He opened it at his desk.

The card inside was heavy ivory, printed in dark green and gold. The Shen Foundation requested the pleasure of his company at its Winter Gala, on Saturday the twentieth of December, at seven o’clock, at the harbour. Black tie. There was a list of the host committee. There was a handwritten line at the bottom of the card, in a firm sloping hand he didn’t know: With Professor Ruan’s warm recommendation.

And under the committee, under Mr. Shen Guoqiang and Mrs. Shen Ruolan and Mr. Shen Yu Ming, there was one more name.

Miss Shen Yu Jie — Young Patron

He read it twice.

Then he sat back in his chair and looked at the tree on the card, and a number of small things he’d noticed and put aside came and lined up in front of him. The car that her mother sent. The cream cashmere scarf. The house at the top of the hill road, which she’d mentioned once, and he’d thought was a figure of speech. The diplomat who spoke five languages. The way she said my family and then changed the subject.

He’d known she came from money. He hadn’t known that it was the kind of money that had its name on the door of his building.

He took out his phone.

Miles: I’ve been sent something.

He took a photograph of the card and sent it. It was read at once.

No reply came. A minute went past, then three.

Not Stuck: Oh.

Miles: Were you going to tell me?

Not Stuck: Yes.

Not Stuck: Eventually.

He looked at the word for a while.

Miles: Young Patron.

Not Stuck: It’s a title. My grandmother made it up. I go to lunches.

Miles: And the gala?

Not Stuck: We hold it every year. I stand at the top of the stairs.

Not Stuck: Are you angry?

He wasn’t. He sat with the question and turned it over, honestly, because she’d asked. He wasn’t angry that her family was rich, or that her name was on his building. He was unsettled, and it took him a minute to find out why. There was a whole part of her life he hadn’t known was there, and he had no idea how much of it she’d been keeping on the other side of a door.

Miles: No. But I’d rather have heard it from you.

The reply took a long time.

Not Stuck: Wednesday. Your office. I’ll tell you all of it. I want to do it properly, not on a phone.

Not Stuck: Please come to the gala.

He looked at the card on his desk, and the tree, and her name.

Miles: I don’t own a dinner jacket.

chapters.title: Miles in a Rented Suit
chapters.desc: He looks like he’s about to defend a thesis. His sister takes over. Dr. Ling provides croissants and terrible advice.
chapters.content:
By Monday morning Miles had established three things. The gala was on Saturday. He had no intention of going unless the department considered it professionally necessary. And Ling Hao had already decided that he was going.

“You’ve been invited personally,” said Ling Hao, in the doorway, with a paper bag. “By the Shen family. With Professor Ruan’s warm recommendation. In green ink.”

“I can read.”

“To the harbour. With trustees, donors, two ministers and about four hundred people whose watches cost more than my flat.” He put the bag on the desk. There were two croissants in it, still warm, from his wife’s bakery on Bell Street. “One’s for you. One’s my fee.”

“For what?”

“Stopping you embarrassing yourself.”

“I’m not going to embarrass myself.”

Ling Hao looked past him at the back of the office door, where Miles’s suit hung on a hook. It was grey. It had been to every faculty dinner since Miles was a doctoral student, and both elbows had gone shiny.

“No,” said Ling Hao.

“It’s a suit.”

“It’s a historical document.”

“It’s perfectly wearable.”

“The left sleeve’s reflective. The fabric’s dying, Wei. Let it go.” Ling Hao bit into his croissant. “It says black tie. You need a dinner jacket. Ring your sister.”

“Why?”

“Because she’s the only person alive who can make you look like you belong at a party,” said Ling Hao, through croissant. “Also I want to watch.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Lan answered the video call at half past eight that evening, on her sofa, in a cardigan, with her hair in a clip and a mug in her hand. She had the same eyes as him behind the same thin round glasses, and none of his patience.

“Little brother. Why are you ringing me? Is it your temperature?”

“I need your opinion.”

She put the mug down.

“On a suit,” said Miles.

She laughed until she had to put her hand over her mouth.

“Don’t,” he said.

“Sorry. Sorry. Show me.”

He turned the camera to the back of the door. She leaned into her screen and her face fell.

“Is that the one you wore to my wedding?”

“Yes.”

“That was eight years ago, Miles.”

“Oh, Miles.” She looked genuinely distressed. “You’re not going to a seminar. Why do you always dress like you’re about to defend a thesis?”

“Lan.”

“You’re going shopping tomorrow.”

“I’ve got lectures.”

“After your lectures.”

“Office hours.”

“After office hours. Do you want me to get on a train and choose it myself?”

He considered this. “No.”

“Then send me pictures. Of everything. Don’t buy anything until I’ve seen it.” She picked up her mug again, and looked at him over it, and her face changed. “You’re going for someone, aren’t you. Is it the girl? The one who peeled the oranges?”

He didn’t answer.

“Oh,” said Wei Lan, very softly.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything. I’m your sister. I’m allowed to have a face.” She picked up her phone with her other hand and held something up to the camera. It was a photograph of a ring: a thin gold band, a single small stone, very plain and very pretty.

“What’s that?”

“Isn’t it lovely? It’s in a window near the hospital.”

“Lan.”

“I’m just looking.” She put the phone down, all innocence. “Goodnight, little brother. Eat something with a vegetable in it.”

When the call ended there was already a message from her.

Lan: And don’t pick black just because it’s the least noticeable.

Lan: You’re allowed to be handsome.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ling Hao went with him the next afternoon. Miles hadn’t asked. Ling Hao announced that he was going out for lunch, walked into the formalwear hire shop on the high street ahead of him, and somehow made it impossible to leave without trying on three jackets.

Miles had decided on hiring before he went in. He couldn’t think when he’d ever wear one again. Wei Lan, on the phone propped against the mirror, said that was the saddest sentence she’d ever heard.

The first jacket was rejected by Ling Hao. The second by Wei Lan, on sight. The third by Miles.

“Why?” said Ling Hao.

“The shoulders are too narrow.”

“It’s a dinner jacket, not a medical device.”

“He’s right,” said Wei Lan. “Try the charcoal.”

“You two are a problem,” said Ling Hao.

“We’ve always been a problem,” said Wei Lan.

The fourth was dark charcoal, nearly black, with satin lapels and a good cut through the shoulders. It fitted. The trousers fell straight. When Miles came out from behind the curtain and stood in front of the mirror in it, the shop assistant stopped folding a shirt.

Wei Lan had gone quiet.

“Well?” said Miles.

“Turn round,” said his sister.

He turned round.

“That’s the one,” said Wei Lan. Her voice wasn’t quite steady. “Oh, look at you. You look like a grown-up.”

Miles looked at himself. He looked like someone he didn’t entirely know: a man who’d been persuaded to go to a party, rather than summoned to a disciplinary hearing. He pushed his fringe off his forehead and it fell straight back.

“Not bad,” said Ling Hao, which from Ling Hao was a sonnet.

“White shirt,” said Wei Lan. “Proper shoes. Black ones, polished, not the conference ones. And a pocket square.”

He looked at Ling Hao. Ling Hao shrugged. “She’s in charge.”

“Of course I am,” said Wei Lan.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday Yu Jie came to his office with her notebook held against her chest and shut the door behind her before she said anything.

The invitation was on his desk, out of its envelope, with the tree on the back.

She stopped when she saw it. Then she sat down in her chair, and put the notebook on her knee, and for a while she seemed to be looking for where to begin.

“I should have told you,” she said.

He didn’t interrupt.

“I know what you thought. That I had a rich family. Rich-ish. A big flat, a car.” She picked at the spiral of the notebook. “You didn’t think the foundation was ours.”

“I didn’t think the name on the door of my building was your grandmother’s.”

“Great-grandfather’s.” She almost smiled. “He was a shipping clerk who bought one boat. Now there’s the harbour, and the tower downtown, and Shen Holdings, and my father, who talks about quarterly growth at dinner, and my mother, who calls me the Perfect Jewel in front of guests. Not as a joke.”

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I didn’t want it to be the first thing you knew about me.”

She said it to the notebook.

“People hear the name and they know what I’m like before I’ve opened my mouth. They go polite in a strange way. Or they start asking for things. Or they decide I’m stupid, and that whatever I’ve done was arranged for me. At home I’m the daughter who goes to the right lunches and stands at the top of the stairs and is going to do something sensible with the family name.” She looked up at him. “Up here I’m just loud.”

His face changed.
