“You’re not just loud.”

“I know. I’m also very clever.”

“And frequently difficult.”

She laughed, a small one, and he saw her shoulders come down.

“I like being here,” she said. “I like arguing about equations and complaining about problem sheets. I like people knowing me because I ask too many questions and not because of a building. And I thought, if you knew, you’d have to be careful round me for one more reason.”

“Yu Jie, I’m already careful round you.”

“That’s not very romantic.”

“It isn’t meant to be.” He reached across the desk and put his hand over hers. “But I don’t want you to divide yourself in two when you’re with me. You can be the girl who takes apart a visiting professor’s slide and the girl at the top of the stairs. They’re both you. I’d like to meet the second one.”

She looked at him.

“You’re making it very hard to stay annoyed with you.”

“Are you annoyed with me?”

“A little. You keep being reasonable.” She turned her hand over under his. “There’ll be about four hundred people. My mother. My brother. Donors and trustees and half the university. I’ll have to stand at the top of the stairs and smile until my face hurts. And she’ll introduce me to men. She’s got a list. The diplomat’s on it. He’s back.”

“Do you want me to go?”

She hesitated. Then she said, “Yes.”

“Then I’ll go.”

“That’s it?”

“Would you prefer a negotiation?”

“No,” said Yu Jie, and got up, and came round the desk, and sat on the edge of it, on his referee reports, again.

“Careful.”

“I’m always careful.”

“You’re on the Mao report.”

She moved an inch. Then she leaned down and kissed him, with her hand on his cheek. It was slow, and then it wasn’t, and his hands found her waist and pulled her half off the desk into his lap, and she laughed into his mouth and kept kissing him.

When she drew back she was flushed.

“That’s for Saturday,” she said. “In advance.”

“An advance payment.”

“Because I won’t be able to touch you all night. Not once. I’ll be standing next to my mother.”

He took the hand that was on his cheek. There was a smudge of purple ink on the side of her index finger, where she wrote. He turned her hand over and bent his head and kissed it, the ink, lightly.

She went still.

“You can’t just do things like that,” she said.

“Like what?”

She kissed him again instead of answering.

At the door she turned round. “Don’t forget the pocket square.”

“You sound like my sister.”

“I’d like to meet her,” said Yu Jie.

“That,” said Miles, “might be dangerous.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ling Hao’s gala briefing took place on Thursday, in the staff canteen, over Miles’s lunch.

Miles had just picked up his chopsticks when Ling Hao sat down opposite him with a croissant and a napkin and said, “Three rules.”

“No.”

“One. Hold a plate.”

“Why?”

“So you look busy. If you hold a glass people keep filling it, and then you’re drunk, and then you’re telling a minister about the Schrödinger equation.”

“What’s two?”

“Don’t leave early. Somebody will corner you about endowments for twenty minutes and you’ll find a fire exit. I know you.”

Miles said nothing.

“Three. Don’t stand on your own by the desserts. People will think you’re waiting for someone.” Ling Hao pointed the croissant at him. “Which you will be.”

“They’re terrible rules.”

“They’re excellent rules.” Ling Hao put the croissant down and his face changed. “Listen, Wei. It’s her family’s party. There’ll be people who know exactly who you are and people who want to find out. Don’t let any of them make you small. And don’t make her feel small by pretending you’ve never met her.”

“I won’t announce anything.”

“I’m not asking you to. I’m asking you not to look at her as if she’s a stranger. She’ll notice. It’ll hurt her more than anything her mother does.” He stood up. “Also, if anybody asks whether you’re married, say no.”

“Why would anybody ask that?”

“Because you look like exactly the sort of man somebody’s aunt would try to marry off,” said Ling Hao, and went.

Miles finished his lunch. Then he finished the croissant.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday afternoon Yu Jie was at the end of a bench in Professor Ruan’s lab, running numbers, when her phone buzzed and the screen said Ma. Her shoulders went up before she’d even answered.

“Hello, Ma.”

“Where are you?”

“On campus.”

“Where on campus?”

“In the lab.”

A pause. “Again?”

“Yes.”

“Your schedule’s becoming ridiculous. Lijun says you were in her lab till seven on Wednesday as well.”

Yu Jie looked across the room at Professor Ruan’s closed office door. Professor Ruan Lijun, who had been at school with her mother on the hill, who had covered for her once already in November, had done it again. Which meant her mother had asked again.

“I had things to finish.”

“You’ve got the gala tomorrow. You should be preparing for that, not sitting with equations every afternoon. Have you decided what to wear?”

“Yes.”

“Yu Ming says you haven’t confirmed the car.”

“I’ll confirm the car.”

“Be home by five. I want you dressed by half past six, and at the top of the stairs by seven. There are people I want you to meet.” Her mother’s voice softened. “Please don’t make this difficult, darling. Your father and I have made arrangements. It would be very rude to keep anyone waiting.”

“All right, Ma.”

The call ended. She sat for a moment with the phone in her lap.

White Rabbit: Everything all right?

Yu Jie: How did you know?

White Rabbit: You stopped answering in the middle of a sentence.

Yu Jie: My mother. Tomorrow. And Professor Ruan has lied for us again. Twice now.

White Rabbit: I know. I owe her a great deal.

White Rabbit: Do you want me to ring you?

She looked at the screen for a while.

Yu Jie: No. I’m all right. I’m just tired.

White Rabbit: Eat something.

Yu Jie: Yes, Professor.

White Rabbit: I’m not your professor.

She smiled at that, alone at the end of the bench, and went back to her numbers.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday afternoon Miles stood in front of the long mirror on the back of his wardrobe door, in his staff flat, in the dinner jacket.

The shirt was pressed. The shoes were polished, black, not the conference ones. The pocket square was white and folded the way the hire shop man had shown him, in a straight line, with three points. He had shaved twice.

His phone rang. Lan.

“Show me.”

He stepped back so she could see. She didn’t say anything for a while.

“What?” he said.

“Nothing.” She’d taken her glasses off. “Nothing. You look so handsome, Miles. Are you nervous?”

“No.”

She raised her eyebrows.

“A bit,” he said.

“That’s normal. You don’t have to impress anybody. You don’t have to be clever all night. Just stand next to her.” She put her glasses back on. “And if she looks beautiful, tell her. Don’t make a graph about it.”

“Goodbye, Lan.”

She was still laughing when he hung up.

There was one more thing. He went to the desk under the window, where he’d brought it home from the office that morning in an envelope, and took it out.

The purple pen. The cat in its crown.

He’d been going to give it back to her for three months. He hadn’t. Every Wednesday he’d opened the drawer and looked at it and closed the drawer again, and he had never once been able to explain to himself why.

He turned it over. It didn’t go with anything. It was plastic and purple and frankly ridiculous, and it had no business in the breast pocket of a dinner jacket.

He slid it in behind the pocket square, where nobody would see it.

Not Stuck: Are you ready?

Miles: Yes.

Not Stuck: Nervous?

Miles: A little.

Not Stuck: Don’t be. I’ll be there. I’ll be the one at the top of the stairs who isn’t allowed to look at you.

He stood in his doorway with his keys in his hand for a moment, a man in a hired dinner jacket with a purple cat over his heart.

Miles: Look anyway.

chapters.title: The Shen Family Gala
chapters.desc: The Perfect Jewel at the top of the stairs. Two married women who recognise him across the room. And a very large man by the pillar, glaring.
chapters.epigraph: “Look at me again when you can.”
chapters.content:
Miles had given papers in six countries. He had once stood at a whiteboard for forty minutes answering questions from a Nobel laureate who thought he was wrong, and hadn’t dropped the pen. None of it had prepared him for the Shen Foundation Winter Gala.

It was in the ballroom of the Harbour Hotel. He hadn’t been inside it for five years, and the last time he’d been here he’d stood on that stage at the far end under a banner of his old school’s crest and dropped his clicker. It had been gold and ivory then. Tonight it was white and green: white orchids up the pillars, white roses and dark winter branches heaped on every table, and a ceiling so thick with chandeliers that the light came down in sheets. A string quartet was playing by the windows. Through the glass the harbour was black and full of lights.

There were four hundred people, all of whom seemed to know one another.

“Dr. Wei,” said Professor Ruan, at his elbow. “The dean’s by the second pillar. I’ll introduce you. Then his wife. Then two members of the foundation’s academic board, who will ask you about quantum computing, and you won’t sigh.”

She was in black silk to the floor, with her grey hair pinned flat and a rope of jet beads at her throat, and she had taken charge of him at the door like a parcel she’d signed for.

“You’re very quiet,” she said.

“I’m listening.”

“Good. Keep doing that.”

The dean was easy. He said he was glad Miles had come, and his wife asked about the department’s new collaboration, and Miles told her about it, and for three whole minutes he forgot he was in a hired jacket. Then Professor Ruan steered him on, to a trustee, to a councillor, to a man who wanted to talk about what quantum computers would do to his bank. Miles listened. He answered when he was asked. He held his plate.

Ling Hao’s rules, he thought, were annoyingly good.

“Miles Wei. Don’t you dare pretend you’ve forgotten me.”

He turned round.

Aurelia Chen was coming at him through the crowd in pale pink couture with pearls at her throat and a soft velvet band holding back her dark hair, looking exactly as she had looked at sixteen, when she’d been the prettiest and most frightening girl in the school. She’d organised the reunion five years ago. She’d organised, as far as he could remember, most things.

“Aurelia.”

“Good. I thought you’d blank me.” She looked him up and down. “Well. Look at you.”

“Is something wrong?”

“Your bow tie’s crooked. Don’t move.”

Before he could step back she’d reached up and taken hold of it. She retied it with four quick tugs, smoothed his collar flat with both hands and stood back to look at her work.

“There. You’re welcome.”

A step behind her stood her husband. Chen Si was in black, with black gloves on, still, with a soft fringe of black hair and a face that gave nothing away. He had been watching his wife’s hands at another man’s throat with the expression of somebody deciding which hospital to send him to.

“Si,” said Aurelia, without turning round. “Don’t look like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like someone’s stolen your wife.”

“I was watching you do up his tie.”

“It was crooked.”

“He has hands.”

Aurelia turned round, and a slow smile came over her face. “Are you jealous?”

“I’m standing here.”

“Very jealously.”

Miles looked down at his plate. Ling Hao’s first rule, he decided, was the best advice he had ever been given.

“Ignore him,” said Aurelia, taking her husband’s arm. “He gets like this when I’m helpful. Enjoy your evening, Miles. Don’t let anyone make you feel underdressed. You look lovely.”

Chen Si gave him one last long look over his shoulder as she led him away. It was not a friendly look. It was the look of a man filing something.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d got through a trustee and a woman from the arts council when someone else said his name.

“Miles.”

He turned, and it was Elowen.

She was in deep red velvet that left her shoulders bare, with her black hair loose down her back in heavy waves and a small gold clip above one ear, and a fine chain at her collarbone. People were moving out of her way without seeming to know they were doing it. Five years ago, on a hotel balcony above this same harbour, he had asked her whether she was happy, and she’d looked back through the glass at the man by the pillar and said yes.

“Elowen.”

“It’s been a long time.”

“Five years.”

“You’ve been counting.” She smiled, and her cool face went soft. “How are you?”

“Well. And you?”

“I’ve been to too many dinners this month. Everyone wants to talk about business over the pudding.” She looked at the long table along the wall. “Is any of it good?”

“The little pastries on the left. They’re better than they look.”

She laughed. “That’s a very specific recommendation.”

“I’ve been observing.”

“Of course you have.” Her eyes went past his shoulder, and something in her face changed. “Zhendong’s here too. He’s been holding up that pillar for a quarter of an hour.”

Miles looked.

By the nearest marble pillar stood a large man in a navy suit with his collar open and his arms folded, rings on his long fingers, black hair swept back with one strand falling loose. He looked like money and danger in the same breath. His eyes were on Miles, and they did not move.

Miles knew him. Five years ago, at the reunion, he’d seen him standing beside a pillar in exactly this ballroom and taken him for hotel security. He’d found out on the balcony who he was. He’d never quite recovered.

He nodded, politely.

Zhao Zhendong’s face did not change by a single muscle.

“Is he waiting for someone?” said Miles.

“Me, probably,” said Elowen. “Or he’s decided the pillar’s the most interesting person here. I’d better go and rescue it.”

She went. Zhao watched her come all the way across the room to him, and when she reached him he unfolded one arm and put it round her without looking down, and went on watching Miles over the top of her head.

Miles looked at his plate again. He was beginning to suspect the pillar wasn’t the problem.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight o’clock the music changed.

The quartet stopped in the middle of a phrase and started something else, slower and grander, and the talk in the room fell away, and every head turned towards the double staircase at the end of the ballroom.

“The family,” said Professor Ruan quietly.

Shen Ruolan came down first. She was in pale gold, with diamonds at her throat and her hair swept up and fixed, and she moved like a woman who had spent her whole life being looked at and had made her peace with it long ago. Beside her came her husband, tall and silver-haired and without any expression at all. Then Yu Ming, in black, with a cousin on each arm.

And then, alone, at the top of the stairs, Yu Jie.

For a moment Miles forgot where he was.

She was in ivory silk that fell straight from her shoulders to the floor and caught the light whenever she breathed. Her long dark hair had been put up, smooth and high and pinned with something that glittered, so that he could see the whole line of her neck for the first time, and there were diamonds at her ears. She held the rail with one hand. She was perfectly still.

And she was smiling.

It wasn’t the smile she gave him when she’d won an argument. It wasn’t the one she gave the board when a derivation finally closed, or the one she gave him across his desk when she was about to do something he’d regret. He’d never seen this one. It was beautiful and calm and polished, like something that had been worn smooth by a great many hands. It showed exactly as much of her as it was meant to and not one thing more.

The Perfect Jewel. He’d thought it was a figure of speech.

She came down the stairs beside her mother. She nodded to people. Her mother leaned and said something in her ear, and she laughed, a light little laugh he’d never heard, and the smile didn’t move.

He looked at her hand on the rail and remembered it covered in chalk.

“Quite something, isn’t she,” said Professor Ruan.

“Yes.”

“She’s been doing this since she was six. Her grandmother used to stand her at the top of those stairs in a velvet dress and make her stay there for an hour.” Professor Ruan sipped her wine. “She sits on the scholarship committee now. Ruolan’s been preparing her for the board.”

Miles said nothing. He’d understood, at last, the size of it. Yu Jie wasn’t attending her family’s party. She was one of the reasons it existed.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d seen him the moment she reached the bottom step.

She knew him by the way he stood, like a man who’d been told to look comfortable in a room he’d have given a great deal to leave, holding a plate as if somebody had handed him a specimen. He looked so handsome she had to look away.

Her mother touched her arm. “Smile, darling.”

She was smiling.

“Zhiyuan’s flight was delayed. He’ll be here by ten.” Her mother steered her gently to the left. “In the meantime. This is Mr. Pao’s son, who’s just come back from his engineering doctorate. Ask him about bridges.”

Yu Jie asked him about bridges.

Then there was a young man whose family had endowed the new chemistry building. Then a banker’s son with a good watch and nothing to say. Then the nephew of a trustee, who told her she was much prettier than her photographs, as if that were a compliment to her photographs. Then two brothers from a shipping family her father wanted something from, presented together like a set.

She smiled at all of them. She’d learned how long before she learned the Schrödinger equation. It was only tiring.

Across the room Miles watched, and counted.

The engineer. The chemistry building. The watch. The nephew. The two brothers, which made six. A man in a velvet jacket who kissed her hand. A widower in his forties, who her mother introduced herself, smiling the whole time. And a tall boy with a guitarist’s hair who made her laugh, the polite little laugh, not the real one.

Nine.

He looked down. He hadn’t realised how hard he was gripping the plate until the edge of it bit into his palm.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re staring.”

Aurelia had come back without her husband, with a fresh glass of champagne. She followed his eyes across the room to the girl in ivory, standing beside her mother listening to the widower, smiling the smile.

“She’s beautiful tonight,” said Aurelia.

“Yes.”

He’d said it too fast. Aurelia’s eyebrows went up.

“Very,” she said, slowly.

He didn’t say anything.

She watched his face for a while. He wasn’t doing anything she could have pointed at. He didn’t fidget, or try to catch the girl’s eye, or move towards her. He just stood there with his plate and looked at Shen Yu Jie as though the rest of the ballroom were a rough draft, and Aurelia, who had seen that look on exactly two men in her life and had married one of them, understood.

She lowered her voice.

“Miles. You’re in love with her.”

He could have said something careful. He’d been careful all his life. He looked at Yu Jie across the room, at the top of her head, at the glittering pins in her hair.

“Yes,” he said.

Aurelia let out a breath. “Oh,” she said. “Oh, Miles.” Then she smiled, and it was a real smile, the kind she didn’t give many people. “Well. That explains the tie.”

“What?”

“You’re in a ballroom. In a proper dinner jacket. Holding a plate. You hate all three.” She touched his sleeve. “She must matter a great deal.”

“She does.”

Over her shoulder he saw Chen Si coming back through the crowd, looking for her. Aurelia saw him see it, and turned, and took her husband’s arm as he arrived and said, “Come along, Si, we’re going somewhere else,” and steered him away before he could ask what he’d missed. She looked back once, over her shoulder, at Miles. She didn’t say anything. She didn’t have to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Jie was standing at a table of trustees, listening to a conversation about scholarships, when her clutch buzzed against her hip.

She looked down without moving her head.

White Rabbit: You look beautiful.

The smile nearly broke. She held it. The trustee beside her went on talking about bursaries. She lowered her eyes and typed under the edge of the table with her thumb.

You look

Her mother’s hand touched her elbow. Her thumb hit send.

Across the room Miles’s phone buzzed. He read it.

You look

So he looked.

She was already looking at him.

For a second neither of them moved. The quartet went on playing. Somebody laughed near the windows. A waiter with a tray of glasses walked between them and out the other side, and she was still looking, and so was he.

Then she smiled.

Not the Jewel. The other one. Small and crooked and a little bit wicked, the one she gave him across his desk when she’d caught him out. It lasted for perhaps a second and a half, and it was entirely his.

His mouth moved at the corner. He didn’t wave. He didn’t take a step towards her. He just looked back.

The clutch buzzed again.

White Rabbit: I am.

She bit the inside of her cheek, hard.

Yu Jie: That wasn’t finished. My mother touched my arm. I was going to say you look very handsome.

White Rabbit: Your mother’s looking at you now.

She turned her head. Shen Ruolan was watching her from three feet away, with her head slightly tilted, the way she looked at a painting she was thinking of buying.

Yu Jie turned back to the trustee and smiled.

Yu Jie: I know.

White Rabbit: Be careful.

Yu Jie: Look at me again when you can.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the pillar, Zhao Zhendong had been watching the whole thing.

He’d noticed the professor the minute he came in. He’d noticed Elowen go over to him, and stand too close, and laugh. He’d noticed Aurelia retie the man’s bow tie with her own hands, and Chen Si notice it too, which had cheered him up. He’d been planning, in an idle sort of way, to find out whether the professor could swim.

Then he’d noticed the professor didn’t look at Elowen once after she walked away. He didn’t look at anyone. He looked at the girl in white at the centre of the room, and every time she looked back, something happened to his face.

It was small. Zhao had made a living out of small things in other people’s faces.

Elowen came back with a glass of water and put it in his hand.

“What?”

He tipped his head at the professor. “Him.”

She looked across the room. At Miles. Then at the girl in ivory, who was smiling at a trustee and at the same time, somehow, not.

Elowen’s face went soft. “Oh,” she said.

“Oh what?”

“Nothing. Have you worked it out?”

He watched the professor look down at his phone. Across the room, a second later, the girl did the same.

Zhao unfolded his arms. He drank the water. When he folded his arms again he wasn’t glaring any more. He was just watching, the way you’d watch a man walk out onto ice.

“Poor bastard,” he said.

Elowen leaned against his shoulder and laughed into it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past nine Shen Ruolan touched her daughter’s arm.

“Come, darling. There’s someone else I want you to meet.”

Yu Jie turned with the Jewel smile already back on. “Of course, Ma.”

Miles watched her go, through the crowd, behind her mother, a white shape among the black. Ling Hao’s second rule came back to him. Don’t leave early.

He breathed out. He straightened his jacket, and felt the hard little shape of the pen in his breast pocket against his chest, under the square of white silk.

He’d promised her he’d come. He’d promised himself he wouldn’t make her night any harder than it was. So he stayed. He listened to a man from the arts council. He smiled when he was spoken to. He held his plate. And all the while, without meaning to and without being able to stop, he kept one eye on the girl at the centre of the room, who smiled for everybody and had only smiled once for real.

chapters.title: Yu Jie Is Not Jealous of Women Married to Dangerous Men
chapters.desc: She is a little jealous. She would like that noted privately. Then Aurelia Chen corners her in the powder room.
chapters.content:
Yu Jie had counted nine.

Nine men. Nine conversations about her studies and her plans and whether she’d thought of taking a bigger part in the foundation. She’d remembered which of them had done his doctorate abroad and which had a sister at her old school and which one had told her, twice, that she was prettier than her photographs. She’d smiled at every one of them at the right moment.

She deserved a medal. Or a large glass of something cold.

“Darling.” Her mother’s hand on her elbow. “Mrs. Chow wants you for the international education committee next year. Go and talk to her before the speeches.”

“Of course, Ma.”

Across the room Miles was talking to a man from the university council. He had a plate in one hand and his back straight, and the bow tie at his throat was perfectly, beautifully straight.

Aurelia Chen had done an excellent job of it.

Yu Jie looked at the bow tie. Then at Aurelia, laughing on the far side of the room on her husband’s arm. Then back at the bow tie. She remembered, in some detail, Aurelia reaching up to it with both hands. The way she’d stepped right into his space as if she’d done it a hundred times. The way he’d stood quite still and let her.

“Excuse me, Ma. I’m going to get some water.”

“Don’t disappear.”

“I won’t.”

She went to the drinks table. She wasn’t jealous. She was making an observation. Aurelia Chen was beautiful in the way a expensive doll is beautiful, and she was confident and funny and married to a man who looked as though he could take a building apart with his gloves on, and she had touched Miles’s bow tie. That was all. That was a fact. Facts weren’t jealousy.

She drank half a glass of water. Across the room he smiled at something the councillor said.

She drank the other half.

Her clutch buzzed.

White Rabbit: Have you eaten?

Yu Jie: Yes.

White Rabbit: Properly?

Yu Jie: Yes, Dad.

There was a pause.

White Rabbit: I’m nine years older than you. That isn’t old enough.

Yu Jie: It’s old enough to ask if I’ve eaten.

White Rabbit: That isn’t an age requirement.

She smiled at the screen and put it away.

She wasn’t jealous. She would like that noted, privately, somewhere.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother found her by the drinks table before the glass was empty.

“Why are you standing here on your own?”

“I wanted water.”

“There’s no need to hide in a corner.” Shen Ruolan smiled. “Come. There’s somebody you haven’t met.”

There were three more somebodies. A young man whose family had just endowed a scholarship, who asked whether she really did physics and then said, “That’s unusual,” and when she asked why, said, “Well. For someone with your background,” as if that explained it.

“Do you mean to carry on with it?” he said.

“Yes.”

“After you’re married?”

Yu Jie smiled at him until he looked away. “Physics is very interesting.”

“Yu Jie has always been very independent,” said her mother, in a voice that made it sound like a mild skin condition.

She wondered if she could get away with a laboratory emergency. It was technically possible. Her mother would never believe it.

“You’re quiet tonight,” said Shen Ruolan, when the young man had gone.

“I’m listening.”

“You’re not usually this quiet.”

“Maybe I’m tired.”

“Then make an effort, darling. These people matter.” Her mother looked at her face for a moment. Then she followed her eyes across the room, to where Miles had just finished talking to the dean’s wife.

“Dr. Wei seems to be enjoying himself.”

Yu Jie looked down at her empty glass. “He’s very polite.”

“His office is on your corridor, isn’t it?”

Her fingers went tight on the glass.

“He works on the fourth floor, Ma.”

“I know where he works.” Her mother’s voice stayed pleasant. “Lijun says you’re in her lab on Wednesdays. Every Wednesday. Until seven.”

“I’ve got simulations.”

“Of course you have.” A pause, very small. “And Dr. Wei helps with the research, does he? With the simulations?”

“He’s in the department.”

“That isn’t quite what I asked.”

Yu Jie smiled her best smile. “Ma, I don’t know what you’re asking.”

Her mother looked at her. Then she smiled too, and reached out and straightened the little diamond pin at Yu Jie’s shoulder, which didn’t need straightening.

“Nothing, darling. I only hope you’re not neglecting your future. Remember. People are always watching.”

She moved off to greet somebody. Yu Jie stood still.

Across the room, Miles wasn’t looking. He was talking to someone else. She hoped he hadn’t seen. The last thing she wanted was him spending the rest of the night worrying about something she could manage on her own.

She wished she could walk over and take his plate away and tell him he was doing beautifully. She wished she could straighten his bow tie. Just once. For scientific purposes.

✦ ✦ ✦

The powder room was marble and quiet and smelt of gardenias. She put her clutch on the counter and looked at herself in the long mirror.

Her hair was still perfect. Her make-up was still perfect. The smile, when she tried it, was still there. She let it go and looked at what was underneath, which was a tired girl in a expensive dress.

“You’re doing fine,” she told her reflection.

“Are you talking to yourself?”

Aurelia Chen was in the doorway.

“Mrs. Chen.”

“Aurelia, please. Mrs. Chen is my mother-in-law, and you wouldn’t like her.” Aurelia came in and put her own clutch beside Yu Jie’s and looked at her in the mirror. “You look beautiful tonight. And exhausted.”

“Do I?”

“Only to me. I’ve done a lot of nights like this.” She washed her hands, slowly, and dried them, and turned round and leaned against the counter. “How long have you known Miles?”

Yu Jie’s face did something. Only a little. Aurelia saw it.

“Dr. Wei?”

“Don’t,” said Aurelia kindly.

Yu Jie looked down. “Since September.”

“Only since September.” Aurelia tilted her head. “That’s interesting. He looks at you as though it’s been years.”

Yu Jie’s cheeks went hot.

“There,” said Aurelia. “That face. That’s the one.”

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“I’m usually much better,” said Yu Jie, quietly.

“I know. I watched you do nine men in a row without a crack in you.” Aurelia’s face softened. “Come here a minute. I want to tell you something about him. Nobody else is going to.”

Yu Jie hesitated. Then she came.

“I’ve known Miles since I was fifteen,” said Aurelia. “I came from Milan with no friends and a terrible accent, and he was two years above me, and the only boy in the school who’d talk to me about something other than my legs. He was different then. Stubborn. He argued about everything, even things that didn’t matter. He laughed all the time. He laughed so loudly in the library that they made a rule about it.”

Yu Jie couldn’t picture it. She tried.

“He had a notebook,” said Aurelia. “He carried it everywhere. To the canteen, to assembly. It wasn’t a diary, exactly. Equations, mostly. Questions he wanted to answer. But there were other things in it. Things about his family. Things he’d written when he was angry or frightened, at two in the morning, the way you do at seventeen. Things he’d never have said out loud to anyone.”

“What happened?”

“Some boys in his year took it out of his bag in the library one lunchtime. And read it out.” Aurelia’s mouth had gone thin. “Not just looked. Read. Standing on a table, doing voices. Half the school was in there.”

Yu Jie’s stomach turned over.

“He asked them to stop. They laughed. He asked again.” Aurelia looked at her. “Then he went over the table at the biggest one. It was a real fight. Chairs went over, books all over the floor. The librarian had to pull them apart.”

Yu Jie stared at her.

She tried to see it. Not the man who asked before he kissed her. Not the man who chose every word as if it might break. A boy of seventeen with his notebook in somebody else’s hands, going over a library table.

“They were both punished,” said Aurelia. “Eight days at home. And when he came back he didn’t bring the notebook. He never brought it again. He never laughed in the library again either, or anywhere else that I saw.”

Yu Jie had to put her hand on the counter.

“He told me years later what he’d decided,” Aurelia went on. “He’d made a rule. That he’d never again let anybody be the reason he stopped thinking clearly. That if you cared about someone you had to be more careful, not less. That feelings were dangerous if you let them make your choices for you.” She looked at Yu Jie in the mirror. “He was seventeen. He’s kept it ever since.”

Nothing happens while you’re a student in my department.

“He still thinks like that,” said Yu Jie.

“I know. He told me tonight he loves you.”

The marble room went quiet.

“He said that?”

“I asked him. He said yes. Just like that, with that face, holding a plate.” Aurelia’s eyes were bright. “In fourteen years I’ve never once heard that man say what he wanted.”

“Fourteen?”

“Since the library. He laughed at the reunion, five years ago, when he dropped his clicker in front of everyone, but that was a different thing. That was at himself.” Aurelia picked her clutch up off the counter. “And your Professor Ruan was telling the dean’s wife by the oysters that he laughed out loud in a seminar last week. At something you said. Professor Ruan dropped her pen, apparently. She was very pleased about it.”

Yu Jie didn’t say anything.

“He laughed for you,” said Aurelia. “Don’t underestimate that.”

Yu Jie looked down at the side of her finger, at the faint purple smudge of ink that wouldn’t quite wash off, and remembered him bending his head over it in his office, and her smile came up before she could catch it.

“Oh, sweetheart,” said Aurelia. “You love him too.”

Yu Jie didn’t deny it. She just said, “Yes.”

“I thought so.” Aurelia smiled at her, and it wasn’t the doll smile at all. “Now. Tell me something he’s done. Something stupid. I need it to tease him with.”

So Yu Jie told her about the study group, and Professor Cen coming in, and Miles getting up and saying he had a meeting, on a Saturday, and walking straight out of the door.

“Oh no,” said Aurelia, delighted.

“He waited for me at the bike racks afterwards. In the cold. For fifty-six minutes. With an egg sandwich inside his coat to keep it warm, and a latte in his pocket.”

Aurelia stopped laughing.

“Fifty-six minutes.”

“He felt terrible about leaving.”

“Of course he did.” Aurelia was quiet for a moment. “I’ll bet you he spent the whole fifty-six deciding what to say. And then when you got there he said something very short.”

“He said sorry.”

“Exactly,” said Aurelia. “That’s Miles. All that thinking, and then one word.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When Yu Jie went back into the ballroom the quartet had moved on to something slow. She stopped at the edge of the room by a pillar of white orchids.

He was standing with Professor Ruan. His plate was empty. He was listening to somebody, politely, with his head a little bent.

She looked at him and thought: seventeen, and a notebook, and a library table. Then she looked at his bow tie, and nearly laughed.

Then she saw his breast pocket.

There was something in it, behind the white silk square. Something with a lump at the top, and a little edge of purple showing where the silk had shifted.

She knew that shape. She’d have known it in the dark.

Her pen. Her purple cat pen. The one she’d been looking for since September, the one she’d crawled round his office floor for on her hands and knees in September while he sat at his desk and said he hadn’t seen it. He had it. He’d had it all along. And he’d brought it here, tonight, to a ballroom full of ministers, in his breast pocket, over his heart.

A laugh tried to get out of her and she put her hand over her mouth.

Then something else came up behind it, warm and enormous, and she had to stand still for a moment and let it.

She put her hand up to her hair. It had taken an hour, that afternoon, and a woman with a mouthful of pins. It was smooth and high and perfect. She found one of the pins above her left ear, and slid it out.

A strand came down by her temple. Then a little more. Not enough to spoil anything. Just enough to change it.

She put the pin in her clutch and turned towards the room.

He looked up. His eyes went over the crowd, and found her, and stopped.

For a second he only looked. Then his eyes went to her hair, to the strand lying loose against her cheek, and she saw his face change. It wasn’t much. She knew him now. She saw him notice. She saw the corner of his mouth.

His hand came up, briefly, and touched his breast pocket.

Her clutch buzzed.

White Rabbit: Your hair.

Yu Jie: What about it?

White Rabbit: There’s a pin missing.

Yu Jie: Very observant.

White Rabbit: Was it hurting?

Yu Jie: A bit.

White Rabbit: You should get someone to fix it.

Across the room Aurelia was back on her husband’s arm. She caught Yu Jie’s eye, and looked at the loose strand of hair, and raised her glass about an inch.

Yu Jie: I like it like this.

There was a pause.

White Rabbit: So do I.

Her face went hot from her collar to her hairline. She put the phone away.

“Yu Jie!” Her mother, from the middle of the room, with her hand out.

“Coming, Ma.”

She looked once more at Miles. He was still watching her. She smiled at him, the real one, for half a second, across four hundred people.

Then she went back to her family with her hair not quite perfect, and for the first time all night she didn’t feel any need to fix it.

chapters.title: Elowen Asks Him One Question
chapters.desc: Five years ago he asked her on a balcony. Tonight, on a terrace over the harbour, she asks him back.
chapters.content:
The terrace ran the length of the ballroom on the harbour side, behind a wall of glass doors, and by half past nine it was the only quiet place in the hotel.

Miles had been out there for four minutes with a glass of sparkling water. Four minutes without being introduced to anybody. Four minutes without a word about endowments. The music came out through the open doors behind him, softened by the cold, and below the stone balustrade the harbour lay black and enormous with the lights of the ferries crawling over it. It was, by any measure, the best part of his evening.

“Dr. Wei.”

He turned round.

Shen Ruolan was coming out through the doors with her daughter a pace behind her. Yu Jie’s hair was a little looser than it had been at eight, with one dark strand down against her cheek where a pin was missing, and it made her look less like a portrait and more like herself. His eyes stayed on it for a fraction of a second too long. Then he looked at her mother.

“Mrs. Shen.”

“I hope you’re enjoying yourself.”

“Very much. Thank you for having me.”

“I wanted to introduce you properly to my daughter.” Shen Ruolan put a hand on Yu Jie’s back, lightly, the way you’d present a vase. “Yu Jie.”

It was so absurd that for a moment he nearly smiled.

He knew how she took her tea. He knew which problems she pretended not to understand and which ones she really couldn’t do, and the face she made when it was the second kind. He knew the sound of her heels in his corridor and the exact weight of her when she sat on his desk. He knew she never brought a coat. And her mother was introducing them.

“Miss Shen,” he said.

Yu Jie inclined her head about an inch. “Dr. Wei.”

Her face was perfectly composed. He had to admire it. He wasn’t sure he was managing his own.

“Yu Jie’s doing physics,” said Shen Ruolan. “She’s always loved the sciences. I sometimes wish she’d choose something a little more practical.” A small smile. “Lijun tells me she’s in the department a great deal.”

“She’s very dedicated,” said Miles.

Yu Jie looked at him.

“Professor Ruan told me in November,” he went on, with his most serious face, “that your daughter is the best student she’s had in twenty years. And then she threatened me.”

Shen Ruolan’s eyebrows rose. “Threatened you?”

“With what she’d do to anyone who wasted her.” He turned the glass in his hand. “She asks very good questions, Mrs. Shen. And she doesn’t accept an answer just because someone senior has given it. Last week she took apart a visiting professor’s slide in front of the whole department, very politely, and she was right.”

Yu Jie was looking at the floor. Her mouth was doing something.

“That sounds like my daughter,” said Shen Ruolan, and laughed. “She’s never accepted anything I’ve told her either.”

“It’s a useful quality in a physicist.”

“We’ll hope she finds a use for it.” A guest called her name from the doorway. She turned. “Excuse me. Do enjoy the evening, Dr. Wei. Yu Jie, come and say goodbye to Auntie Chow before she goes.”

“Yes, Ma.”

Her mother went in. Yu Jie stayed where she was for three more seconds.

“And then she threatened me,” she said, without moving her lips.

“She did.”

“She said that to me too. On her balcony. About the twenty years.”

“I know. She said it to me the same morning.” He drank some water. “Then she said that if anything cost you a single mark, she’d never forgive me.”

Yu Jie looked up at him, and for a moment the composed face cracked straight down the middle and she was just herself, standing too close on a cold terrace with her hair coming down.

“Thank you,” she said.

“For what?”

“For saying it to her. Out loud.” She stepped back. “I have to go and kiss Auntie Chow.”

She went in. He watched her go, and smiled into his glass.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re hiding.”

Elowen came out through the doors with a glass of water and stood beside him at the balustrade. The wind off the harbour moved the hem of her red dress.

“Quite successfully,” said Miles.

“Not from me.” She looked at the water. “You look different tonight.”

“Is that good?”

“Very.” She glanced at the jacket. “Someone helped you.”

“My sister.”

“That explains it.”

For a while neither of them said anything. Out on the harbour a ferry hooted twice, low, and the sound came back off the hills.

“Do you remember the balcony?” said Elowen.

“Yes.”

“Five years ago this month. Upstairs.” She tipped her head back at the hotel. “It was raining. You came out and stood next to me and asked me a question.”

He remembered. He’d seen her across a ballroom with a man he’d mistaken for security, and seen her look at that man, and he’d gone out onto the balcony after her for no reason he could have explained, and asked her whether she was happy. She’d looked back through the glass at Zhao and said yes. He’d believed her. He’d gone home and thought about it for a week, about what it would be like to be able to answer a question like that so fast.

“I remember,” he said.

“Tonight I want to ask you.” Elowen turned and looked at him. “Are you happy, Miles?”

It wasn’t a question people asked at galas. Not like that, plainly, with nothing round it.

He looked past her, through the glass, into the ballroom.

Yu Jie was standing beside an elderly woman in a wheelchair, bending to hear her, smiling the Jewel smile. As he watched she straightened, and turned her head, and the loose strand of hair swung against her cheek.

“I’m happy on Wednesdays,” he said.

Elowen laughed softly. “Only Wednesdays?”

“Especially Wednesdays.”

She looked at his face. Then something in her own changed, and she turned and looked through the glass where he’d been looking, and found Yu Jie almost at once.

“Oh,” said Elowen. “Her.”

“Yes.”

“You’re in love with her.”

“Yes.”

He didn’t hesitate. He said it the way you say something that was settled a long time ago and that you’re slightly surprised anyone needs to ask.

“How long?”

“We’ve been together since October.”

“October?” She stared at him, and then at the ballroom, and then at him again, and laughed. “Well. That explains why you’ve been looking at that room all night as if someone hid something important in it.”

“Someone has.”

“You’re not even going to deny it.”

“No.”

She was quiet for a moment.

“I’m glad,” she said. “I mean it. I’m so glad.”

“I know.”

“She’s young.”

“Yes.”

“She’s still at university. In your department.”

“I know.”

“And you’re still the same Miles Wei who thinks every difficult thing in the world can be fixed by drawing a line and setting the boundary conditions.”

“Not every thing.”

“Most of them.”

“That’s an exaggeration,” he said, and she gave him a look, and he laughed. Not loudly. But he did, out on the terrace, and Elowen turned her head sharply at the sound and stared at him as if he’d taken off his face and shown her another one underneath.

“Miles,” she said. “You laughed.”

“It’s been happening.”

“Since when?”

“Since about a week ago. In a seminar.” He looked into his glass. “It was her fault.”

Elowen didn’t say anything for a while. She looked out at the water, and when she spoke again her voice had changed.

“We’re going north after New Year. Zhendong and I. To see the lights.” She smiled a little at the harbour. “He’s never had a holiday in his life. I had to book it myself and take two of his phones away. He still sleeps on the side of the bed nearest the door, you know. Five years. Every night. He says it’s habit. It isn’t habit.” She turned her glass round in her fingers. “He’s the most frightening man I’ve ever met and he brings me tea in bed every morning and he’s never once asked me to be anything but what I am. I didn’t know you could have both. I didn’t know that was allowed.”

Miles listened.

“When I was little,” said Elowen, “I had a rule. Whenever I was frightened of someone, I made myself look at them. Straight at them. My mother taught me. It didn’t make me braver, I was still frightened. But she said if I kept looking away, I’d decide the thing was worse than it was. So I learned to look.” She glanced at him. “I’ve been looking at people my whole life. What they show me. What they don’t say. I’m good at it now. And you, Miles, are one of the hardest people I’ve ever tried to read.”

He didn’t answer.

“You’re so careful. You keep your face still and your voice level and you never ask anyone for anything, and you think that’s how you keep people safe from you.” She shook her head. “It isn’t. People who love you need to be able to see you. When you’re frightened. When you don’t know what to say. When you’re happy on a Wednesday.” She put her hand on his arm. “Let her see your face.”

He looked into the ballroom.

Yu Jie was beside her mother again. The smile was back. But he could see, from out here, the small movement of her thumb on the clasp of her clutch, over and over, and the way she’d shifted her weight onto one foot because her shoes hurt. He knew those things. He knew her. And he knew too that he could be hard to know, and that she’d never once complained of it.

“She isn’t asking you to be someone else,” said Elowen. “I’d bet you anything she likes you exactly as you are.”

“She does.”

“Then don’t make her guess.”

He looked at her for a moment, as if he were going to say something. Then he only nodded.

“I’ll try.”

“That’s all,” said Elowen, and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the other side of the glass, by the edge of the dance floor, Zhao Zhendong had been watching them for some minutes with a glass of whisky going warm in his hand.

He’d seen Elowen go out. He’d seen her go and stand beside the professor at the rail, close, the way she stood beside people she’d decided about. He didn’t like it much. He didn’t need to like it. He knew the difference between Elowen being polite to someone and Elowen going to find someone because she had something to tell them, and this was the second kind.

He watched her put her hand on the man’s arm. He watched the professor laugh.

Then he saw the professor’s eyes go past her, into the room, to the girl in white, and stay there. And something in Zhao’s own face went quiet.

When Elowen came away from the rail he was at the terrace doors before she was, holding one of them open.

“Finished?”

“Almost.”

He looked past her at Miles. Miles nodded to him. Zhao looked at him for a moment, with those narrow heavy-lidded eyes that smiled at nobody, and then he nodded back.

He gave Elowen his arm. She took it.

“You’re very quiet,” she said.

“I’m watching.”

“That’s dangerous.”

“Why?”

“Because you always decide things before you ask any questions.”

He didn’t say anything. She leaned her head on his shoulder for a second as they walked back into the warm, and he put his free hand over hers on his arm and kept it there.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Jie was by the drinks table, listening to a trustee explain bursaries for the second time that evening, when Elowen came and waited at her elbow until he’d finished.

“Miss Shen. Could I borrow you?”

Yu Jie looked for her mother, who was across the room with a minister. “Of course.”

They moved a few steps away, beside a pillar of orchids.

“You look lovely tonight,” said Elowen.

“Thank you. So do you.” It was true, and a little frightening. Up close Elowen Zhao had cool dark cat’s eyes that seemed to see straight through to the back of your skull, and a red mouth, and she smelt of white peonies.

Elowen leaned in.

“He’s happy on Wednesdays,” she said.

Yu Jie went completely still.

“He told me,” said Elowen. “Just now. Out there. He said it very seriously.”

Yu Jie looked at the terrace doors. Her face had gone hot.

“That’s very like him,” she said, faintly.

“He’s different with you.” Elowen’s voice was gentle. “Not a different person. Less alone. I’ve known him since I was fourteen, and I’ve never seen him less alone than he was just now, looking at you through a window.”

“I know he cares.”

“Good.” Elowen touched her arm. “Then don’t let him hide too much. He’ll try. It’s what he knows.”

“I’ll try.”

Elowen laughed. “That’s exactly what he said.”

From the doorway, Zhao said her name, once.

“I’d better go,” said Elowen. She took a step, and turned back. “He’s very lucky, you know.”

“I think I am too,” said Yu Jie.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her a few minutes later at the end of a long table of white orchids, alone for once, pretending to look at the flowers.

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.” She didn’t look round. “Elowen talked to me.”

He shut his eyes briefly.

“She said you’re happy on Wednesdays,” said Yu Jie. “She said you told her.”

“I did.”

“Why?”

“She asked.”

“And you just answered.”

“Yes.”

She turned and looked up at him. “Are you? Really?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He took a moment. Then he answered quietly, standing beside her in front of four hundred people, as if there was nobody else in the room.

“Because I get to see you.”

She looked down. Her smile went small and soft at the edges. Between them, under the edge of the tablecloth, she found his hand and held it for a second.

“You’re going to make me cry,” she said.

“I hope not.”

“Why?”

“Your make-up looks expensive.”

She stared at him. Then she laughed, the real one, the one with her whole face in it, and two women by the next pillar turned round to look.

He didn’t look away. That was the thing. He stood there and looked at her laughing and let it show on his face, all of it, whatever it was, and she saw it, and stopped laughing, and just looked back.

“Elowen told me something else,” she said.

“What?”

“That you should let me see your face.”

“I think I make it hard sometimes.”

“You don’t have to tell me everything at once,” said Yu Jie. “You don’t have to be brave every second. But when you’re happy, you can look happy. When you’re worried, you can tell me.” She touched his sleeve, where nobody could see. “And when you miss me, you can say that too.”

“All right.”

“Good.”

He glanced past her. “Your mother’s looking for you.”

“Of course she is.”

“I’ll walk you back.”

“Not yet.” She moved a little closer, so her shoulder touched his arm. “Stay with me one more minute.”

So he stayed. They stood side by side at the end of the table, not touching except where her shoulder met his sleeve. A waiter went by. Somebody called Professor Ruan’s name. The quartet started something new. And in the middle of a room full of people who thought they were strangers, he looked at her, not carefully and not briefly, as if he wasn’t afraid of being caught, and she looked back.

chapters.title: The Diplomat Her Mother Chose
chapters.desc: Yan Zhiyuan is a perfect match on paper: twenty-nine, five languages, a beautiful waltz. Yu Jie hates paper. Then he offers her a deal.
chapters.epigraph: “She has a life that isn’t you.”
chapters.content:
The wind off the harbour was colder than it looked. Yu Jie found that out about three seconds after she stepped onto the terrace.

It was the second time that night she’d escaped her mother. Out here there was only the black water and the ferries and the cold, which went straight through ivory silk as if it weren’t there.

She rubbed her bare arms.

“Cold?”

Miles was further along the balustrade with Professor Ruan, a good few metres off. He’d seen her come out. He had been trying, not very well, to look as if he hadn’t.

“Not particularly.”

His eyes went to her shoulders. “Your arms disagree.”

“They’re not speaking to you.”

“They’re making a strong case.”

Professor Ruan looked from one of them to the other, and then down into her wine. “I’ll leave you to settle it,” she said, and went inside.

He didn’t come any closer. The terrace was still part of the party, and the long glass doors behind them showed the whole ballroom, which meant the whole ballroom could see out. So he didn’t come closer. He only moved. He took two steps along the stone and turned a little, and stood where he was, three metres away from her, with his back to the harbour.

The wind stopped.

It was such a small thing. She felt it all down her left side, where he’d put himself between her and the sea.

“You’re blocking the wind,” she said.

“Am I?”

“You could have brought me a coat.”

“I could have.”

“But you didn’t.”

“You didn’t ask.”

She looked down into her water so he wouldn’t see her face. “How long before my mother notices?”

“About two minutes, I’d think.”

“Then what do we do with them?”

“Stand here,” said Miles.

She laughed, quietly, at the water. When she looked up he was looking at her as though the whole long evening, the trustees and the endowments and the quantum bank man, had been worth it for that one sound.

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re pleased with yourself.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“Perhaps a little.”

The doors opened behind them and two men came out talking loudly about an auction. Miles turned to look at the harbour. Yu Jie looked at her glass. By the time the men had gone past, they were strangers again.

✦ ✦ ✦

They found another minute behind an urn.

It stood beside the terrace doors and was taller than she was, a great stone thing full of white-painted branches, and its main job seemed to be stopping people walking into the glass. It wasn’t romantic in the least. But if you stood on the far side of it you couldn’t be seen from the ballroom, and she stood on the far side of it, and he came and stood beside her.

“You’re hiding behind a plant,” she whispered.

“It’s an urn.”

“Is that better?”

“Marginally.”

He looked over the top of the branches into the room. Nobody was looking their way. Then he reached down and took her hand.

It was the first time all night he’d touched her. His hand was warm from his pocket, and she slid her cold fingers into it and held on.

“Hello,” she whispered.

“Hello.”

“You’ve been very formal tonight.”

“It’s a formal party.”

“You’re allowed to be my boyfriend behind an urn.”

His thumb moved over her knuckles. Then he lifted her hand and turned it over and put his mouth to the inside of her wrist, just where the pulse was. He held it there for a second. Not longer.

She felt it in the backs of her knees.

He lowered her hand and didn’t let go of it. “Better?”

She had to swallow before she could answer. “Much.”

“Yu Jie!”

Her brother’s voice, from inside.

She shut her eyes. Miles let go of her hand.

“Your brother.”

“I know.”

“Go.”

“You’re very quick to get rid of me.”

“I’m trying to keep you out of trouble.”

“You’re not very good at it.”

“I’ve noticed,” said Miles.

She went out from behind the urn. At the doors she looked back once, and he was watching her go, and his face was quiet and his eyes weren’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Ming was waiting just inside with a glass of champagne. He looked at his sister, and then out at the terrace.

“Where’ve you been?”

“Getting some air.”

“For a quarter of an hour?”

“It was very good air.”

He narrowed his eyes at her.

“Ma wants you to meet Yan Zhiyuan. He’s arrived.”

“Now?”

“Properly, this time, she says. Not a hello at the stairs. A conversation.”

“I’ve had about eleven conversations.”

“She says you were distracted.” He looked out at the terrace again. “Were you?”

“Yes,” said Yu Jie sweetly, “by the bursaries.”

He sighed and gave her his arm.

Yan Zhiyuan was by the foot of the staircase. He was twenty-nine and tall and neat, with a black suit that fitted as if it had been poured on and hair that had obviously been cut that morning. When he saw them coming he smiled, a pleasant, practised, well-made smile, and Yu Jie recognised it at once because she’d been wearing its twin all night.

“Zhiyuan,” said Yu Ming. “My sister. Yu Jie.”

“Miss Shen.”

“Mr. Yan.”

“I’ve heard a great deal about you.”

“Nothing too dreadful, I hope.”

“Quite the opposite.” He glanced at Yu Ming, who was already backing away into the crowd.

“I’ll leave you two,” said her brother, and went.

“He’s abandoned you,” said Yan Zhiyuan.

“He does that.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Only if you make a habit of making people vanish.”

He laughed. It was a small laugh, but it sounded real, and it surprised her. “I’ll try not to.”

The quartet had been joined by a pianist and had started a waltz. He looked towards the floor.

“Would you like to dance?”

She could see her mother on the far side of the room, quite still, watching. There was no point refusing. Refusing would just be another conversation in the car.

“All right.”

He was a good dancer. Of course he was. He took her through the first turn without any fuss, held her at a polite distance, and didn’t make the mistake of steering her about as if she’d never been taught.

“You’re at the university,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Physics, your mother says.”

“Yes.”

“What kind?”

She nearly missed a step. Nobody had asked her that all night. Not one person in four hundred.

“What kind?”

“There must be different sorts. I’m afraid I don’t know which.”

She looked up at him. He seemed to mean it.

“Condensed matter,” she said. “Strained graphene. Carbon a single atom thick. When you stretch it unevenly the electrons move as if there were a magnetic field, when there isn’t one. I’m working on what happens at the edges.”

“Is that quantum mechanics?”

“Very much.”

“I did a little physics as an undergraduate. I remember almost none of it.”

“Most people don’t.”

“That’s reassuring.” He turned her. “I’d like to hear it properly some time. The edges.”

“You’d regret asking.”

“I speak five languages, Miss Shen. I expect I can survive one explanation of graphene.”

She laughed. It came out before she could stop it, the real one, not the little polished one she’d been doing since seven. He looked pleased, and a bit surprised himself.

“Five?”

“My work needs them. Two are useful at dinner. The other three are useful when people think you can’t understand them.” He smiled. “I’m a very junior diplomat. It sounds more glamorous than it is. There’s an enormous amount of paperwork.”

“I’m writing a thesis. I know about paperwork.”

The music carried them round another turn, and over his shoulder she saw Miles.

He was by one of the pillars with Professor Ruan. He wasn’t staring. But she knew his eyes now, and she knew when they were on her, and they were. For a second she met them, and her foot went wrong, and Yan Zhiyuan caught her without seeming to.

“All right?”

“Sorry.”

“No need.” He turned her so she was facing away from the pillar. “Someone you know?”

“Someone from my department.”

“Dr. Wei,” said Yan Zhiyuan.

She looked up at him.

“We were introduced earlier. I came straight from the airport and Professor Ruan was the first person I saw. He’s very quiet.”

“That’s one way of putting it.”

“Do you know him well?”

She gave him an entirely reasonable answer. “He’s a lecturer in my department.”

“Of course,” said Yan Zhiyuan.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the waltz ended he let her go and bowed, a little, correctly. Then he said, “Would you walk with me for a minute? Somewhere less central?”

They went along the edge of the room, past a table of untouched cakes, to a corner by the windows where the noise was thinner. He waited until there was nobody within ten feet.

“I hope you won’t take this the wrong way.”

“That depends what it is.”

“I think you and Dr. Wei know each other rather better than a student and a lecturer usually do.”

Her face didn’t change. She’d had twenty years of practice.

“I’m not prying,” said Yan Zhiyuan. “But I watched you look at him. And I watched him look at you, all through that dance, as if I were standing on his foot.”

“Are you going to tell my mother?”

“No.”

He said it so fast that she believed him.

“Your mother,” he went on, “has been very clear about why she wanted us to meet. She’s been clear with my mother for two months. She thinks we’d suit.”

“On paper.”

“On paper,” he agreed, and something tired went across his face. “I don’t think either of us wants to be signed like a treaty.”

“You’re a diplomat.”

“Which is exactly how I know how exhausting treaties are.” He looked out of the window at the harbour, then back at her. “I’d like to make you a proposal.”

“That sounds dangerous.”

“Possibly. What if we helped each other?” He kept his voice low and pleasant, the voice of a man discussing the weather. “I tell my mother, and she tells yours, that we got on. That we’d like to see each other. Not an engagement. Just a courtship, slow, very proper. Your mother stops presenting you with men in velvet jackets. My family stops asking why I never bring anybody home. We go to a few dinners. We’re photographed at one or two things. And in the spring we decide, very sadly, that we don’t suit after all.”

She stared at him. “You want us to pretend to go out.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He didn’t answer straight away. He looked at the window, at his own reflection in it over the dark water.

“Because there’s someone I care about,” he said. “Someone I can’t be seen with.”

His voice hadn’t changed. But something behind it had.

“Why not?”

“Because of my work. Her situation. The people who’d be hurt if it came out.” He smiled slightly. “It’s complicated. You’ll have heard that sentence before.”

She had. She’d said it herself, to Tao Tao, about a man in an office on the fourth floor.

“You’ve thought about this,” she said.

“For about a year.”

“Why me?”

“Because you don’t want this any more than I do. And because you were looking at Dr. Wei.”

“You’re very observant.”

“It’s my job.”

“Does your job teach you to propose fake courtships at charity galas?”

“Only on the advanced course.”

She laughed again, and he looked relieved.

“You can say no,” he said. “I’ll tell your mother we simply didn’t get on, and I’ll make it sound like my fault.”

She looked at him. She thought of the car on Sundays, and after you’re married?, and nine men in a row.

“What does she think?” said Yu Jie. “The person you care about.”

His face went soft all at once, and he stopped looking like a diplomat entirely.

“She thinks I’m an idiot.”

“She sounds sensible.”

“She is.” He looked down. “She’s the most sensible person I know.”

Yu Jie made up her mind.

“All right,” she said. “We can talk about it. But I’ve got conditions. Nothing that would hurt anybody who doesn’t deserve it. No engagement. No promises to anyone. If either of us wants to stop, we stop. And you’re never to tell my mother we’re in love.”

He laughed out loud. “I wouldn’t dare.”

He held out his hand. She shook it.

“An understanding, Miss Shen.”

“An understanding, Mr. Yan.”

✦ ✦ ✦

From the pillar, Miles watched them shake hands.

He’d watched the waltz. He’d watched the man bend his head to say something to her and watched her answer, and he’d watched her laugh. Not the little laugh she’d been giving everybody since eight. Her own laugh, the one he’d thought belonged to his office and the café and the bike racks and the back stairs, given to a man in a perfect suit she’d known for ten minutes.

He’d never once imagined being jealous of her laugh.

He looked down at his glass.

“You look unhappy,” said Professor Ruan, beside him.

“I’m fine.”

She followed his eyes across the room. “Ah.”

He didn’t say anything.

“Yan Zhiyuan,” said Professor Ruan, “is a perfectly decent young man. I knew his grandfather. Good family. Good degree. He’ll be an ambassador by forty.”

“Are you recommending him?”

“I’m making an observation.” She drank some wine. “You’re jealous.”

“I haven’t said that.”

“You don’t need to. Your jaw’s saying it for you.”

He put his glass down on the ledge of the pillar.

“Dr. Wei,” said Professor Ruan, and her voice was quiet and not at all kind. “You knew what tonight was. You knew her mother would walk her round the room. You knew there’d be young men. And you’ve been standing here for ten minutes looking at that girl as if she’s betrayed you by talking to one of them.”

“She hasn’t.”

“No. She hasn’t. She’s been polite to every person Ruolan put in front of her, because that’s what she’s been trained to do since she was six, and she’s been doing it beautifully, and she’s tired. And she has every right to laugh at someone’s joke without looking over her shoulder to see whether you mind.” Professor Ruan put her own glass beside his. “You can’t walk across this room and take her hand. You know why, and you know you agreed to it. So understand the rest of it too. She has a life that isn’t you. Don’t you dare make her feel guilty for living it.”

It landed harder than he’d expected. He stood there and took it.

Across the room, Yu Jie was listening to something Yan Zhiyuan was saying. She smiled.

“You’re right,” said Miles.

“I know. It happens.”

“I don’t like it.”

“Of course you don’t. Liking it’s not required.” Her voice softened, a little. “Learn to carry it without handing it to her. That’s all anybody ever learns.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By eleven the quartet was packing up. Yan Zhiyuan had been taken off by a minister. Yu Jie was at the foot of the stairs watching the cellist put his instrument to bed when her mother came and stood beside her, looking satisfied.

“Zhiyuan seems very taken with you. His mother says he hasn’t danced with anyone in two years.”

“Ma, we danced once.”

“That’s how these things begin.” She put her hand on Yu Jie’s arm. “I spoke to his mother this evening. Properly. If things go well between you, we thought an engagement in July. After your graduation. It would give you time to finish your thesis and settle everything.”

The ballroom seemed suddenly loud, though the music had stopped.

“July.”

“After the summer would be too late for the Yans. He’s due a posting in the autumn.”

“Ma. You can’t decide that.”

“I’m not deciding anything tonight. I’m telling you what would be sensible.”

“An engagement isn’t something sensible you put in a diary.”

Her mother’s face tightened, slightly. “Don’t be dramatic.”

July. Her mother had chosen a month, and a man, and a city in another country with an autumn posting in it. And somewhere in that future Yu Jie was expected to stand at the top of a staircase in the right dress and thank everyone for arranging it.

“I’ll decide whether I give him a chance,” she said.

Her mother looked at her. Something sharp went through her eyes, and Yu Jie saw it, and didn’t know what it was. Then the polished smile came back, the one Shen Ruolan wore when there were people near.

“Of course, darling,” she said. “There’s no rush at all.”

She went away to say goodnight to a minister’s wife.

Across the room, Miles had seen. He’d seen Yu Jie’s shoulders go up and her hand close too hard on her clutch. He wanted to go to her more than he’d wanted anything all night. He wanted to cross the room and take her hand and ask her what her mother had said.

He stayed where he was. Not because he didn’t care. Because he was trying, for the first time in his life, to work out how to care for someone without taking her choices away.

Yu Jie looked up and found him.

Neither of them smiled. But he held her eyes across the whole emptying room, and didn’t look away, and didn’t pretend the distance wasn’t there.

chapters.title: Miles Takes the Long Way Home
chapters.desc: One in the morning, no coat, silver shoes that hurt. He walks her home the long way through the sleeping city, and stops one block early on purpose.
chapters.content:
By one in the morning the gala was coming apart at the edges.

The speeches were over and a long queue of guests stood in the lobby waiting for their coats.

Miles was by the cloakroom. He’d looked at his watch four times. He knew Yu Jie was tired, and he knew she’d never admit it.

She was across the lobby, saying goodnight to a line of people beside her mother. Her dress was still perfect. Her face was still perfect. But she’d been on her feet since five, and he could see it now in the way she held her shoulders, as if somebody had hung something heavy from each one.

“Still here?”

Aurelia was at his elbow in a white fur wrap, with Chen Si behind her holding her bag in one gloved hand like something that might go off.

“Apparently.”

Aurelia followed his eyes across the lobby and smiled.

“Wednesdays,” she said.

He shut his eyes. “Elowen told you.”

“Elowen tells me everything.” She tilted her head. “Happy on Wednesdays. It’s the most romantic thing I’ve ever heard.”

“Please don’t.”

“You’re allowed to be happy on other days, you know.”

“I’m aware.”

“Are you?” Her face softened. “She looks done in. Make sure she gets home.”

“That’s what I’m waiting for.”

“Good,” said Aurelia, and went up on her toes, and kissed the air an inch from his cheek, and Chen Si watched her do it with an expression that suggested he’d be thinking about it in the car.

Behind them the lifts opened and Elowen came out with Zhao. She was in a long black coat over the red dress, and he had his hand flat on the small of her back, and he steered her through the crowd in the lobby as though nobody else were in it. When they reached Miles, Zhao stopped.

The two men looked at each other for a moment.

“Don’t be stupid about it,” said Zhao.

His voice was low, and Elowen had turned to say goodnight to Aurelia, so only Miles heard it.

“About what?”

Zhao looked at him as if he’d asked what water was.

“Her,” he said, and tipped his head an inch towards the girl in ivory across the lobby. “Whatever you’re doing with her, don’t let being frightened make you careless. And don’t make her be the one who pays for it.”

From Zhao Zhendong, Miles suspected, that was an enormous speech.

“I’ll remember,” he said.

“Good.”

Elowen took her husband’s arm. “Goodnight, Miles.”

“Goodnight.”

“Happy Wednesday,” said Aurelia, from behind them, delighted, and Miles shut his eyes again, and when he opened them Zhao was laughing, quietly, all the way to the doors.

✦ ✦ ✦

A few minutes later Yu Jie was beside him.

“You’re still here.”

“So are you.”

“We’re waiting for the car.”

“Then you should go and wait for it.”

Neither of them moved.

“I hate these shoes,” she said.

They were silver sandals with heels like pencils, and beautiful.

“How long have they hurt?”

“Since eleven.”

“Why didn’t you change them?”

“Because my mother said they matched the dress.”

“They do.”

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am. I’m only acknowledging the evidence.”

She looked round the lobby. Nobody was looking.

She stepped out of the sandals, one and then the other, and picked them up by their straps.

The marble was freezing. She closed her eyes.

“Better?”

“Much.”

Outside the glass doors a long black car had pulled up under the canopy, with a driver in a peaked cap standing by the back door.

“I don’t want to go home with them,” she said.

“Why?”

“Because if I get in that car, my mother will talk about Yan Zhiyuan all the way up the hill.”

His face didn’t change. She saw it not change.

“She mentioned July,” said Yu Jie.

“July?”

“An engagement. After graduation.”

The noise of the lobby seemed to go a long way off.

“Did she ask you?” he said.

“She informed me. I said I’d decide for myself.”

“Good.”

“She didn’t like it.”

“I’d imagine not.”

She looked at him. “You’re not going to tell me what to do?”

“No.”

“Not even that I should say no?”

“That’s yours to say.”

“I know,” she said. She’d meant to tell him the rest. The handshake by the window. An understanding, Mr. Yan. She’d meant to tell him all of it on the way home, and now she looked at his face and it was so tired and so carefully still, and she thought: not tonight. He’s had enough tonight. And she didn’t.

“How are you planning to get home?” he said.

“Walk.”

He looked at her feet.

“You’re not walking home barefoot.”

“I’ve done it before.”

“In December?”

“I’ll survive.”

He looked at her a moment longer. Then he took his jacket off.

“Miles...”

He held it out to her at arm’s length, the way you’d hand something across a counter, so their fingers wouldn’t touch.

“Put this on.”

“You’ll be cold.”

“I’ll manage.”

“You’ll be in your shirt.”

“I’m very good at regulating my own temperature.”

“That isn’t how thermodynamics works.”

“I teach thermodynamics.”

“Then you should know better.”

“Yu Jie,” he said, and she took it.

It was warm from him. She put her arms into the sleeves, and the shoulders slid off hers and the hem came down nearly to her knees, and as she pulled it closed something slid out of the inside pocket and dropped onto the marble with a small plastic click.

She bent and picked it up.

A purple pen, with a fat cat on the end of it, in a little gold crown.

She looked at it. Then up at him.

“Dr. Wei.”

“Yes.”

“Why is my pen in your pocket?”

He could have said a lot of things. He’d had three months to think of something.

“Because I kept it,” he said.

“Since when?”

“Since the day you dropped it. It rolled under my chair. I found it after you’d gone.” He looked at the pen in her hand. “You came back the next week and asked me if I’d seen it, and I said no.”

“You lied to me.”

“Yes.”

“For three months.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I liked having something of yours,” said Miles.

She went completely still.

He’d kept a cheap plastic pen because it was hers, and lied to her face, and carried it to a ballroom over his heart. She’d known since the powder room. It was different hearing him say it.

“You’re sentimental,” she said, and her voice wasn’t steady.

“Apparently.”

She put the pen in the pocket of his jacket and buttoned the jacket over it.

“Then I’m keeping this.”

“I thought you might.”

Across the lobby, her mother had turned to a minister’s wife. The driver was still standing by the car.

“Help me,” said Yu Jie, very low. “I need to get out without her seeing.”

“Have you told Professor Ruan?”

“Not yet.”

“Then tell her.”

She took out her phone.

Yu Jie: Professor, I’m leaving now with a friend. Please could you tell my mother I’ve gone ahead with you? I’m so sorry.

She showed it to him. “Does that sound convincing?”

“Ask her if she’ll do it.”

Yu Jie: Will you? You don’t have to.

The answer came while she was still holding the phone out.

Professor Ruan: I’ll tell her you came with me and I dropped you at your door. That makes three times. Don’t make me regret it.

“She’s terrifying,” said Yu Jie.

“She’s very kind,” said Miles. “Both can be true.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went out by the side door, down a service corridor, into a narrow street behind the hotel.

The cold hit her like water. She stood on the pavement in his jacket and her bare feet, with her silver sandals hanging from two fingers, and laughed, because she’d done it, she’d got out.

Somewhere above them a window was open and a phone camera flashed once, a little white pop against the dark, and neither of them looked up.

“Put your shoes on,” said Miles. “Just till the corner.”

She tried. She managed three steps.

“Take them off.”

“Again?”

“Yu Jie.”

She took them off. He held out his arm.

“Are you offering me your arm, Dr. Wei? How formal.”

“I can withdraw it.”

She put her hand through it at once. “No.”

There was a convenience store on the corner, lit up green and white and empty except for a boy behind the counter watching something on his phone. Miles stopped outside it.

“Wait here.”

He went in. She watched him through the glass, a man in a white dress shirt and a bow tie at one in the morning, going down the aisle past the instant noodles and stopping at a basket by the till. He picked something out of it. He held it up to the light. He put it back and picked out another one, and looked at the label, and nodded.

He came out with a pair of cheap pink cotton slippers in a plastic packet and gave them to her.

She looked at the label.

“How do you know my size?”

“You leave your shoes under my desk,” he said, “every Wednesday.”

She stood on the freezing pavement and stared at him, and then she bent and tore the packet open with her teeth and put them on. They were exactly right. They had small embroidered rabbits on the toes.

“Miles.”

“They’re warm. That’s all.”

“They’ve got rabbits on.”

“That was the only colour.”

“Liar,” said Yu Jie, and took his arm again, and walked.

✦ ✦ ✦

The quick way to her building was twenty minutes along the main road and up the hill steps. He turned the other way, onto the back road by the water.

She noticed at the first turn.

“This isn’t the way.”

“It’s flatter. The main road’s all steps after the market. And the pavement’s broken by the bus station.”

“How do you know?”

“I’ve walked it.”

“When?”

“A few times. In November.” He didn’t look at her. “On my way home. I thought you might be in shoes that hurt one day.”

She stopped. He stopped too.

“You walked my road,” said Yu Jie, slowly, “in case I was in uncomfortable shoes.”

“I noticed which way had fewer stairs.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“Probably. Would you rather go the short way?”

“No.” She held his arm tighter. “Take the long one.”

So he did.

The city had gone quiet. A noodle place by the ferry pier was stacking its chairs, and an old man hosing the pavement in his vest watched them go past, the man in shirtsleeves and the girl in his jacket and pink rabbit slippers, and said nothing at all.

The jacket smelt of him. Chalk and old paper and coffee, and under that something warmer that was just him. She pulled the sleeves down over her hands.

“Are you cold?” she said.

“A little.”

“Then why did you give it to me?”

“Because you’re colder.”

She didn’t say anything for a while. Then she let her head rest against his arm as she walked, and he slowed down a little to match her, and didn’t tell her to walk straight.

✦ ✦ ✦

The old wall ran along the back road for a quarter of a mile, between the street and the water. It was stone, old, darker than the night, and somebody long ago had put iron lamps along the top of it, and the light came down from them in round gold pools on the pavement, one after another, all the way along.

She slowed down.

“It’s pretty.”

“Yes.”

“Did you bring me here on purpose?”

“The road happens to go this way.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

He looked down at her. “Would you like it to be?”

“Yes.”

He stopped under one of the lamps. She turned to face him.

She was in his jacket with his pen in the pocket and his slippers on her feet and her shoes in her hand, and the light was coming down on both of them, and the city was a long way off.

“I hated tonight,” she said.

“I know.”

“She talked about my future as if I weren’t standing there. Nine men. And then July.” She looked down at the rabbits on her feet. “I wish I could tell her. All of it. About you.”
